name: Crystal Street
blurb: The showpiece cul-de-sac of Glimmer Falls: twelve identical split-levels, a roundabout garden, and the purple Heartstone humming at its center like a fridge nobody can find.
art: A sunny 1980s suburban cul-de-sac of identical split-level houses with tidy lawns, a roundabout garden at its center holding a car-sized purple geode, bikes on driveways, jack-o-lanterns on porches, faint violet shimmer in the air above the stone

beats.title: Everything Must Go
beats.place: A driveway garage sale on Crystal Street
beats.text: The Okonkwo family is moving out with three days' notice, and their whole life is on card tables in the driveway: lava lamps, a Spell-a-Tron toy computer, a shoebox of loose photos. Mrs. Okonkwo won't say why they're leaving. She just keeps glancing at the Heartstone and pricing things lower.
beats.art: A cluttered suburban driveway garage sale on a sunny afternoon, folding tables of 1980s household goods, a lava lamp, a toy spelling computer, a shoebox of loose snapshots, a half-loaded moving van at the curb, a tired Nigerian American mother in a head wrap sticking price stickers on a lamp while glancing toward a huge purple crystal rock on the roundabout, a teenager digging through the shoebox, bright autumn sun, wide shot

choices.label: Haggle the whole table down to pocket change

success.text: You walk away with a box of treasures for a quarter and a handshake: a working flashlight, a pack of batteries and a Spell-a-Tron that, when you turn it on, says "W-E-L-C-O-M-E" in a voice it should not have.
success.art: A teenager walking down a sunny driveway carrying a cardboard box of garage-sale finds, a flashlight on top, a toy computer screen glowing with a single word

failure.text: You lowball so hard Mrs. Okonkwo's husband takes the box back and puts it in the moving van. Through the van's back window you see the Spell-a-Tron light up by itself and spell out your name.
failure.art: A moving van with its rear doors half shut, a toy spelling computer glowing inside among boxes, its screen showing letters

choices.label: Help pack the van and ask why they're really leaving

success.text: Between boxes, Mrs. Okonkwo finally talks. "Every October that rock hums louder. My son started sleepwalking to it." She presses an old photo of the street into your hands: the Heartstone, and a crowd of grieving faces. "Somebody should remember."
success.art: A mother handing a teenager an old black-and-white photograph of a crowd gathered around a purple geode, packed boxes stacked behind them

failure.text: You drop the box marked FRAGILE. Grandma's china, all of it. Mrs. Okonkwo is too tired to yell, which is worse. She thanks you anyway and you feel like a dropped plate for the rest of the day.
failure.art: A cardboard box marked fragile tipped on a driveway, broken blue china spilling out, a teenager wincing beside it

choices.label: Dig through the shoebox of loose photos

success.text: Most are birthdays and barbecues. But in every single one, no matter the year, the same pale kid in a striped shirt stands at the edge of the frame, never aging. You pocket the clearest one. Knowledge is armor.
success.art: A spread of old snapshots on a card table, birthday parties and barbecues from different decades, the same pale child in a striped shirt at the edge of each snapshot

failure.text: The photos are warm, like they were just pulled from a dryer. The striped-shirt kid in one of them is looking straight at the camera now. You drop the box and the photos scatter across the drive in a wind that isn't blowing anywhere else.
failure.art: Old snapshots blowing across a suburban driveway in a sudden private wind, one photo face-up showing a pale child staring out of the picture

beats.title: Mr. Pickles Is Down There
beats.place: The storm drain by the Heartstone roundabout
beats.text: Little Hector Ruiz is sobbing on the curb. His grandmother's poodle, Mr. Pickles, chased a squirrel straight into the storm drain, and now a tiny bark is echoing up from the dark, getting farther away. Something else down there is barking back, a beat too late, a pitch too low.
beats.art: A small boy crying as he kneels at a curbside storm drain on a sunny suburban cul-de-sac, a teenager crouched beside him prying at the iron grate, the shining eyes of a tiny white poodle in the dark of the drain and a second, larger pair of eyes far behind it, a package of bologna on the curb, a purple crystal rock on the roundabout nearby, bright midday light and black shadow in the drain, low medium shot

choices.label: Pry up the grate and climb down after him

success.text: The drain is cold, wet and full of echoes. You crawl twenty feet on your elbows, scoop up a shivering Mr. Pickles, and back out fast without ever turning around to see what was breathing behind him. Hector's grandmother pays you in quarters and pan dulce.
success.art: A grimy, grinning teenager climbing out of a storm drain holding a soaked white poodle aloft, a boy and his grandmother cheering on the curb

failure.text: You get Mr. Pickles, but something gets your sneaker. You come out with one shoe, a scraped knee and a dog that will not stop shaking. Hector thinks you're a hero. You think you heard your name whispered in the pipe.
failure.art: A teenager sitting on a curb missing one sneaker, holding a trembling poodle, the dark mouth of a storm drain behind them

choices.label: Lure him back with a trail of lunchmeat

success.text: Bologna, folded into a trail, works better than courage. Mr. Pickles comes trotting up out of the dark, licking his lips. Behind him, the low bark stops, like something decided it wasn't hungry for bologna.
success.art: A white poodle trotting out of a storm drain toward a trail of folded bologna slices on the asphalt, a kid clapping

failure.text: The bologna vanishes slice by slice into the dark, and Mr. Pickles does not come back. Then he does, an hour later, at Hector's front door, dry as a bone and smelling of crushed purple rock. Nobody can explain it.
failure.art: A small white poodle sitting on a suburban doormat at dusk, eerily dry and clean, a faint violet glow on its curly fur

choices.label: Run for Dr. Haddad's garage clinic

success.text: Dr. Haddad arrives with a catch pole, a headlamp and the calm of a man who once treated a three-legged goat for possession. He has Mr. Pickles out in four minutes and checks Hector for scratches too, just to be thorough.
success.art: A veterinarian with a headlamp lifting a poodle out of a storm drain with a padded catch pole, a relieved boy and grandmother beside him

failure.text: Dr. Haddad is out on a call. His answering machine plays a message about after-hours emergencies and then, under the beep, a low bark. By the time you get back, Hector's grandmother has called the fire department and you spend an hour giving statements.
failure.art: A teenager standing in a cluttered garage clinic beside a blinking answering machine, animal cages in the shadows behind them

beats.title: Neighborhood Watch
beats.place: The Delacortes' living room, 2 Crystal Street
beats.text: Folding chairs, a plate of deviled eggs and Mr. Delacorte at an easel with a pointer. The Crystal Street Neighborhood Watch is voting tonight on a Halloween curfew for "unsupervised youth" and "people who don't fit the character of the street." Everyone looks at the Ruiz family, the new couple on the corner and you.
beats.art: A crowded 1980s suburban living room in the evening, rows of folding chairs, a plate of deviled eggs on a side table, a stern middle-aged man with a pointer standing at an easel with a hand-drawn chart, neighbors turning around in their chairs to stare at a teenager in the back row, a 71-year-old Black woman in a marigold headwrap dozing in an armchair with a cane, warm lamp light, wide shot

choices.label: Stand up and speak against the curfew

success.text: Your voice shakes but it holds. You name the kids who mow lawns and walk dogs and shovel driveways, and you ask Mr. Delacorte which of them is the problem. The vote fails, eight to four. Pearl Washington winks at you from the front row.
success.art: A teenager standing up in a crowded living room meeting, neighbors raising hands in a vote, an old woman in the front row giving a wink

failure.text: Mr. Delacorte talks over you, then thanks you for your "passion" in a voice like a pat on the head. The curfew passes. On the walk home, every porch light on the street clicks on as you pass, like the houses are watching too.
failure.art: A teenager walking home along a dark cul-de-sac as porch lights click on one by one, a man silhouetted in a front window

choices.label: Get Pearl Washington to take the floor

success.text: Pearl rises with her cane. "I was on this street in 1959 when you were in short pants, Gerald, and I remember who they called unsuitable then." She names names. The room goes very quiet. The motion is withdrawn and the eggs are passed in shame.
success.alone: You stand up on your folding chair with the 1959 Watch minutes you copied off the library microfiche. "Here's who this street called unsuitable in 1959, Gerald." You name names. The room goes very quiet. The motion is withdrawn and the eggs are passed in shame.
success.art: An elderly Black woman standing with a cane in a suburban living room, finger raised, a mustached man wilting at his easel

failure.text: Pearl is asleep in her chair, and waking her would be a war crime. The vote goes through. As you leave she squeezes your hand and murmurs, "Curfews never stopped anything that walks at night, baby."
failure.alone: You stand up to speak and your voice cracks on the very first word. The vote goes through. As you leave, an old woman by the door squeezes your hand and murmurs, "Curfews never stopped anything that walks at night, baby."
failure.art: A dozing elderly woman in a floral chair at a suburban meeting, a teenager gently holding her hand as neighbors file out

choices.label: Swap the meeting tape for something funnier

success.text: When Mr. Delacorte presses play on his "Dangers of Halloween" slideshow tape, the room fills with a disco remix of a Halloween novelty song. Mrs. Kwan starts dancing. So does the mailman. Nobody can hold a curfew vote after that. They try next week; it never happens.
success.art: Neighbors in a suburban living room breaking into an awkward, joyful dance as a slide projector shows a disco ball, a red-faced man pressing buttons on a tape deck

failure.text: You're caught with the cassette in your hand. Mr. Delacorte calls your parents, then writes your name on his easel under the heading CONCERNS. Somebody draws a heart next to it in the night, which is either a kindness or a threat.
failure.art: A flip chart easel with the word concerns and a list of names, a small heart drawn in purple marker beside one name, the room empty and dim

beats.title: The Porch With Seven Papers
beats.place: Mr. Ferris's porch, Crystal Street
beats.text: Kev Park's paper route has one problem house. Mr. Ferris at the end of the block hasn't picked up his Gazette in seven days. They're piled on the porch, the TV inside is flickering through the curtains, and the screen door creaks open and shut in a breeze that isn't there.
beats.art: A suburban front porch stacked with seven rolled newspapers in plastic sleeves, the screen door hanging ajar and swinging, blue television light flickering behind lace curtains, a ceramic frog by the doormat, a skinny 12-year-old Korean American paperboy in a backwards red cap straddling a red bicycle on the walk and watching nervously, a teenager climbing the steps, overcast afternoon light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Knock, then let yourself in to check on him

success.text: Mr. Ferris is on the kitchen floor with a twisted ankle and a very dry throat, alive and furious about it. You call the ambulance, feed his cat, and he insists on tipping you three quarters and a rabbit's foot "that's done me fine for sixty years."
success.art: A teenager kneeling beside an old man on a 1960s kitchen floor, phone cord stretched, a fat orange cat watching from the counter

failure.text: The house is empty. The TV is playing a test pattern and a recording of Mr. Ferris laughing at a show that went off the air in 1971. You back out. He turns up on Tuesday, says he was at his sister's, and refuses to discuss the TV.
failure.art: A dim 1960s living room with an empty armchair facing a television showing a test pattern, a teenager backing out the door

choices.label: Ask Kev what the route knows about Mr. Ferris

success.text: Kev knows everything: Mr. Ferris has a bad ankle, a daughter in Fresno and a spare key under the ceramic frog. You let yourselves in, find him stuck in his recliner, and call his daughter. Kev adds a gold star to the house on his route map.
success.alone: You knock on doors up and down the block until you know everything: Mr. Ferris has a bad ankle, a daughter in Fresno and a spare key under the ceramic frog. You let yourself in, find him stuck in his recliner, and call his daughter. Mr. Ferris gets his paper picked up tomorrow.
success.art: A young paperboy and a teenager crouching over a ceramic garden frog to find a spare key, a hand-drawn route map in the boy's other hand

failure.text: Kev is too spooked to talk, and the only thing he'll say is "nobody on my route goes in a house where the TV's on and nobody's laughing." You leave a note. In the morning, the note is on your own porch, read and folded.
failure.alone: Nobody on the block will talk, and the only thing the man next door will say is "nobody goes in a house where the TV's on and nobody's laughing." You leave a note. In the morning, the note is on your own porch, read and folded.
failure.art: A folded handwritten note sitting on a doormat at dawn, a paperboy's bike disappearing down the street

beats.title: The Thirteenth Pumpkin
beats.place: The Heartstone roundabout, Crystal Street, Halloween morning
beats.text: It's the Crystal Street Jack-o'-Lantern Judging, and Mr. Delacorte has a clipboard, a sash and a ribbon that says BEST ON THE BLOCK. Twelve pumpkins line the roundabout curb, one for every house. A thirteenth sits right up against the Heartstone, and nobody will admit to bringing it. Its face is carved with tiny, careful teeth, and it's already lit.
beats.art: A row of twelve carved jack-o'-lanterns along a suburban roundabout curb on a bright Halloween morning, a mustached man in a judge's sash holding a clipboard and a blue ribbon, and a thirteenth pumpkin pressed against a huge purple crystal rock already lit from inside, its carved grin full of tiny careful teeth, an 11-year-old girl with blonde braids and red glasses holding a flashlight sun for her solar-system pumpkin, a teenager with an armful of gourds, crisp sunlight, wide shot

choices.label: Build a last-minute showstopper out of leftover gourds

success.text: Eleven minutes and a box of Mrs. Kwan's decorative squash: you build a pumpkin drag queen with a gourd beehive and a corn-husk boa. The street loses its mind. Mr. Delacorte, through clenched teeth, awards you BEST ON THE BLOCK and two quarters from the prize jar.
success.art: A teenager beside a jack-o-lantern dressed up with a tall gourd beehive hairdo and a corn-husk boa, neighbors laughing and clapping on a sunny cul-de-sac

failure.text: Your squash beehive collapses mid-judging, rolls off the curb and comes to rest against the thirteenth pumpkin. Its candle flares up bright and pleased. When you go to fetch your gourd back, it's warm, and its stem has been nibbled.
failure.art: A small decorative gourd resting against a glowing jack-o-lantern at the foot of a purple geode, its stem nibbled, a dismayed teenager reaching for it

choices.label: Lift the lid off the thirteenth pumpkin

success.text: Past the candle, a folded paper is pressed into the pulp: an entry form for the very first Crystal Street judging, October 1959, signed by a kid at number 13, the model home nobody ever bought. You blow the candle out. The whole street lets out a breath it didn't know it was holding.
success.art: A teenager lifting the lid of a glowing jack-o-lantern beside a purple geode, a yellowed folded paper tucked inside among the seeds

failure.text: The lid comes off with a wet sigh and a burst of warm orange seeds hits you square in the face. They stick everywhere. All day you find seeds in your collar and your socks, and every one you flick away lands pointing at the Heartstone.
failure.art: A startled teenager covered in sticky pumpkin seeds holding a jack-o-lantern lid, a purple geode glowing in the roundabout behind them

choices.label: Help Bea finish her scientifically accurate entry

success.text: Bea's pumpkin is a working model of the solar system with a flashlight sun, and with your help the planets finally orbit. Mr. Delacorte gives it HONORABLE MENTION, which Bea calls "a peer-reviewed insult." By noon the thirteenth pumpkin has quietly gone dark, outshone.
success.alone: You rig your own family's pumpkin into a working model of the solar system with a flashlight sun, and the planets finally orbit. Mr. Delacorte gives it HONORABLE MENTION, which is an insult in a sash. By noon the thirteenth pumpkin has quietly gone dark, outshone.
success.art: An eleven-year-old girl with white-blonde braids and round red glasses beside a teenager adjusting a jack-o-lantern carved as a glowing solar-system model with wire-hung planets, on a sunny curb

failure.text: The planets tangle, the flashlight sun dies and Bea's model sags into a sad orange heap in front of the whole street. Bea writes RESULTS INCONCLUSIVE in her notebook and refuses to cry. The thirteenth pumpkin's grin looks a little wider.
failure.alone: Your planets tangle, the flashlight sun dies and your model sags into a sad orange heap in front of the whole street. Mr. Delacorte makes a note on his clipboard. The thirteenth pumpkin's grin looks a little wider.
failure.art: A sagging jack-o-lantern with tangled wire planets on a curb, a small girl in a yellow slicker writing in a notebook, a toothy pumpkin glowing by a purple geode

beats.title: The Mailbox on the Corner
beats.place: The corner lawn on Crystal Street, morning
beats.text: Every morning this week, the mailbox at the corner house has been knocked flat. The new owners, Mr. Adeyemi and Mr. Lund, a retired band teacher and a florist the street keeps calling "the roommates," stand it back up and pretend it's funny. Today Mr. Lund is out with a level and a sack of cement. The post has been bent toward the Heartstone, like something leaned on it all night.
beats.art: A bent mailbox post leaning toward the street on a tidy corner lawn in morning light, a gray-haired florist in a gardening apron holding a carpenter's level beside a sack of cement, a tall retired band teacher in a cardigan holding a trumpet case on the porch, a teenager kneeling with a bucket, and down the street a purple crystal rock glowing faintly on the roundabout, soft gold morning sun, medium wide shot

choices.label: Help sink the post in fresh cement

success.text: You mix, pour and hold the post steady while Mr. Lund fusses with the level. When it sets, Mr. Adeyemi plays a victory march on his trombone from the porch, badly, on purpose. Mr. Lund tips you two quarters "for structural integrity."
success.art: A teenager holding a mailbox post upright in wet cement on a suburban lawn, a gray-haired man with a level, a second man playing trombone on the porch

failure.text: The bag splits and you end up with cement to the elbows and a mailbox leaning worse than before. Mr. Lund laughs so hard he has to sit down. In the morning the post is flat again, and the wet cement shows small bare footprints leading toward the roundabout.
failure.art: A crooked mailbox in a patch of wet cement on a lawn at dawn, small bare footprints pressed into it leading toward a purple geode in the roundabout

choices.label: Hide in the hedge tonight and see who does it

success.text: At two in the morning it's three varsity kids from across town in a pickup, laughing, and you get the plate. Before they reach the mailbox, every porch light on the block snaps on at once and they peel out screaming. Whatever the Heartstone is, tonight it was on the corner house's side.
success.art: A teenager crouched in a hedge at night watching a pickup truck of startled teens speed away as every porch light on a cul-de-sac blazes on at once

failure.text: You fall asleep in the hedge, wake up with a beetle in your ear and find the mailbox flat again. Taped to it is a note in Mr. Adeyemi's tidy hand: THANK YOU FOR TRYING. WE SAW YOU SNORING. COFFEE'S ON. It helps, a little.
failure.art: A sleepy teenager crawling out of a hedge at dawn toward a knocked-over mailbox with a folded note taped to it

choices.label: Throw them the welcome party the street never did

success.text: You round up the Ruizes, Mrs. Kwan and anyone with a folding chair, and by sundown there's a potluck on the corner lawn with paper lanterns and a boom box. Mr. Adeyemi cries into the ambrosia salad. Mr. Delacorte watches from his window and, for once, stays inside.
success.art: A sundown potluck on a suburban front lawn, folding chairs and casserole dishes, two middle-aged men laughing with neighbors under paper lanterns

failure.text: You knock on nine doors and get nine excuses. In the end it's you, the two of them and a tuna casserole on the porch steps, which is honestly a lovely evening. Still, every curtain on the street twitches while you eat.
failure.art: Three people sharing a casserole on porch steps at dusk while curtains twitch in the windows of identical houses across the street

name: Glimmer Falls Public Library
blurb: A brick Carnegie library with a modern wing bolted on: microfiche, an occult section nobody admits to using, a traveling exhibit room, and Ms. Hart's motorcycle parked out front.
art: A red-brick Carnegie library with white columns and a boxy 1970s annex, autumn leaves on the steps, a motorcycle parked by the book drop, tall arched windows glowing warm in afternoon light

beats.title: Overdue Since 1959
beats.place: The circulation desk, Glimmer Falls Public Library
beats.text: A copy of Field Guide to the Birds of the Sierra lands in the return slot with a thump. The card in its pocket shows one borrower, one date: October 26, 1959. The fine notice clipped to it is in the same handwriting as today's date stamp, and the ink is still wet.
beats.art: A library circulation desk with a battered old hardcover bird guide sliding through the brass return slot, a yellowed checkout slip in its pocket and a small fine notice clipped to it with ink still glistening wet, a date stamp and ink pad beside it, a teenager behind the desk reaching for the book, green-shaded desk lamp and afternoon window light, close medium shot

choices.label: Look up the borrower in the old patron files

success.text: The patron card belongs to Wendell Moss, age 12, who borrowed a bird book the autumn after the quarry lake was drained and was never listed as missing because his family moved that week. The address is now a parking lot. You return the book properly and stamp it paid in full. The library feels lighter.
success.art: A teenager at a wooden card catalog drawer holding a yellowed patron card with a child's signature, a stamped bird guide beside them

failure.text: The patron drawer for M is jammed. When you finally wrench it open, every card inside reads WENDELL MOSS in a child's careful cursive. The drawer slides shut on your fingers by itself.
failure.art: An open card catalog drawer stuffed with identical index cards bearing the same child's signature, a teenager pulling back a pinched hand

choices.label: Read the notes scribbled in the margins

success.text: Tiny pencil notes beside each bird: SAW ONE AT THE LAKE. SAW ONE AT THE LAKE. Then, on the last page: THE LAKE IS LEAVING. THE BIRDS KNOW. You copy the notes. Somebody, long ago, noticed something, and now you have.
success.art: Close view of a field guide page with a painted bird and tiny pencil notes crowding the margin, a teenager's hand copying them into a notebook

failure.text: The margins are full of birds drawn in pencil, more on every page, until the last pages are solid gray with wings. A rustle comes from the book as you close it. You decide it's the air conditioning.
failure.art: An old book's final pages crowded edge to edge with pencil-drawn birds, a few feathers resting on the library table

choices.label: Just pay the fine and say nothing

success.text: Twenty-seven years at a penny a day is too much, so Ms. Hart forgives all but a quarter. When the coin drops into the fine jar, a single sparrow lands on the windowsill outside, looks at you, and flies off toward the hills.
success.art: A quarter dropping into a glass fine jar on a library desk, a sparrow on the windowsill beyond, afternoon light

failure.text: You reach for your quarter and find a 1959 dime in its place. The fine jar rattles. Ms. Hart looks at the dime for a long time and puts it in her cardigan pocket without a word.
failure.art: A tarnished 1959 dime in a teenager's open palm over a library desk, a librarian's hand reaching for it

beats.title: The Fifth Player
beats.place: Meeting room B, Glimmer Falls Public Library
beats.text: Priya Raman's Friday-night campaign is short a player, and the sign-up sheet on the meeting-room door says THE DUNGEON MASTER WELCOMES ALL. Graph paper, a bag of dice, a map of a town that looks exactly like Glimmer Falls, and a dungeon drawn right where the Heartstone sits.
beats.art: A library meeting room on a Friday night, a long table covered in graph-paper maps, colorful polyhedral dice, character sheets and pizza boxes, a hand-drawn map of a small suburban town with a dungeon drawn at its center, a 16-year-old Indian American girl with a long braid, round gold glasses and a gold twenty-sided die on a cord leading from behind a folded cardboard screen, three teens and a newcomer with a fresh sheet, warm overhead light, wide shot

choices.label: Roll up a character and play the hero

success.text: Your character, a half-elf with a tape deck, saves the party with a crit on the last roll. Priya grins. "That trap was real, by the way. Not in the game. Under the roundabout." She gives you a page of her notes, just in case.
success.art: A group of teens cheering around a game table as a twenty-sided die shows its top number, a girl behind a cardboard screen grinning

failure.text: You roll a one. Then another. Your character falls into a pit Priya swears she didn't write. When you look at the map again, there's a little pencil figure at the bottom of the pit that looks a lot like you.
failure.art: A tiny pencil figure drawn at the bottom of a pit on graph paper, a pair of dice both showing one beside it

choices.label: Study the dungeon map instead of playing

success.text: Priya's map is better than the city's. She's marked the old quarry tunnels, the drained lake bed and three rooms under the roundabout she says "came to me in a dream, very rudely." You trace a copy. Maps are weapons in this town.
success.art: A teenager tracing a hand-drawn dungeon map onto tracing paper, tunnels marked under a suburban street grid, dice used as paperweights

failure.text: The longer you look at the map, the more it looks back. The dungeon rooms seem to shift a quarter-inch when you blink. Priya takes it gently out of your hands. "Yeah. It does that. Don't stare."
failure.art: A graph-paper dungeon map with ink lines subtly out of place, a girl's hand pulling it away from a dazed teenager

beats.title: The Book Drop Bandit
beats.place: Behind the library, by the book drop
beats.text: Somebody keeps checking out every copy of the library's few books about gay and lesbian lives and dumping them in the dumpster behind the building. Ms. Hart keeps fishing them out. Today a note is taped to the book drop: THESE BOOKS DON'T BELONG IN OUR TOWN. The handwriting is shaky, and young.
beats.art: Behind a red-brick library in the late afternoon, a teenager and a freckled 38-year-old librarian with gray-streaked chestnut hair and an oxblood cardigan beside a green dumpster, a stack of rescued paperbacks on the back step, a folded scrap of paper taped to a metal book drop, a cherry-red motorcycle parked nearby, long gold shadows, medium shot

choices.label: Stake out the book drop at closing

success.text: It's a sophomore from church youth group, crying, with three books in his arms. He's not throwing them away. He's been reading them and dumping them so nobody at home finds out. Ms. Hart gives him a library card in a different name, and a lot of tissues.
success.art: A tearful teenage boy clutching paperbacks behind a library at dusk, a kind librarian kneeling to hand him a library card

failure.text: You fall asleep in the bushes. When you wake, the dumpster is full of books again, the note has been replaced with one that says I'M SORRY, and you have a crick in your neck that lasts until Tuesday.
failure.art: A teenager waking up in library shrubbery at night, a dumpster full of books in the glow of a security light, a new apologetic note on the book drop

choices.label: Help Ms. Hart build a display instead

success.text: You and Ms. Hart build a whole display right by the front door: READ WHAT YOU WANT, with paper stars and every rescued book. By closing, three of them are checked out by people who leave very fast, smiling at the floor.
success.art: A library display table with paper stars and a hand-lettered sign reading read what you want, books standing upright, a librarian and teen admiring it

failure.text: Before the glue is dry, a library board member sweeps through and has the display taken down "pending review." Ms. Hart's jaw is tight. "Pending review means never," she says, and puts every book back on the shelf where it belongs, with a little star on the spine.
failure.art: A half-dismantled library display being carried off by a stern man in a suit, a librarian in a cardigan watching with arms folded

beats.title: Story Hour Emergency
beats.place: The children's corner, Glimmer Falls Public Library
beats.text: The puppeteer for story hour has the flu, and twenty-two kindergartners on a carpet shaped like a rainbow are getting restless. Ms. Hart shoves a sock puppet named Professor Hoot into your hand and a picture book in the other. In the back of the reading nook, the old marionette nobody uses has turned its head to watch.
beats.art: A library children's corner, twenty restless kindergartners on a rainbow-striped carpet, a teenager kneeling in front of them holding a brown sock owl puppet with button eyes on one hand and a picture book in the other, and in the back of the nook an old wooden marionette slumped on a shelf with its painted head turned toward the room, warm afternoon window light, wide shot

choices.label: Give Professor Hoot the performance of a lifetime

success.text: Professor Hoot does voices. Professor Hoot does a dramatic death scene and a resurrection. The kindergartners scream with joy and one of the moms slips you two quarters "for the owl." The marionette in the corner has slumped back down, satisfied.
success.art: A teenager performing with a sock owl puppet to a crowd of laughing kindergartners, one parent pressing coins into their hand

failure.text: Professor Hoot's voice cracks, the kids start crying, and a girl in the front announces that the other puppet is better. When you turn around, the marionette is sitting upright in its chair, strings slack, legs crossed.
failure.art: A wooden marionette sitting upright in a small chair with its legs crossed, kindergartners pointing at it, a sock puppet drooping on a teen's hand

choices.label: Use the old marionette instead

success.text: The strings feel warm. The marionette dances like it's been waiting decades to, and the kids go silent with wonder. Afterwards you find a tag inside its jacket: PROPERTY OF THE RIALTO, 1948. Some things just want to perform again.
success.art: A teenager working a vintage wooden marionette in a graceful dance before awestruck children, a faded tag visible inside its jacket

failure.text: The marionette dances, all right. It dances when you stop moving your hands, too. Ms. Hart gently takes the control bar from you, locks the puppet in a cabinet, and tells the kids it was a magic trick.
failure.art: A librarian locking an old marionette inside a glass cabinet, its painted face pressed to the glass, children applauding behind her

beats.title: The Lost and Found Column
beats.place: The microfiche room, Glimmer Falls Public Library
beats.text: Ms. Hart asked you to check the microfiche reader before the history club arrives, and it keeps stopping on its own. Every time, it lands on the November 1 edition of the Glimmer Falls Gazette, a different year each time: 1961, 1968, 1974, 1983. Every time, the Lost and Found column runs the same tiny ad. FOUND: ONE SNEAKER, NEAR THE ROUNDABOUT. CLAIM AT LIBRARY. On top of the cabinet, as if waiting, sits one small sneaker.
beats.art: A dim library microfiche room, a teenager at a glowing green reader screen showing an old newspaper page, stacks of film reel boxes, and on top of a gray filing cabinet a single small child's sneaker sitting alone, damp at the toe, a single desk lamp and green screen glow, medium shot

choices.label: Crank through every Halloween and count the sneakers

success.text: Twenty-seven Halloweens, twenty-seven sneakers, and you match them to the kids who lost shoes to the storm drains, every one of whom grew up fine and a little jumpy. You tape the list to the cabinet. The reader stops misbehaving, as if somebody finally got the count right.
success.art: A teenager at a microfiche reader with a long handwritten list taped beside the glowing screen, film reels stacked high on the table

failure.text: The reels spin faster than you can read and the screen fills with sneaker after sneaker, until the machine smells like hot rubber and pops a fuse. Ms. Hart finds you in the dark with the small sneaker in your lap and decides not to ask.
failure.art: A teenager in a dark library room lit only by a smoking microfiche reader, a small sneaker resting in their lap

choices.label: Take the sneaker to the desk and claim it, like the ad says

success.text: Ms. Hart opens a drawer behind the circulation desk you've never noticed: dozens of single sneakers, each tagged with a year. She adds yours. "The town never claims them," she says. "Someone should keep count." She gives you a quarter from the fine jar for honesty.
success.art: A librarian in a cardigan opening a deep wooden drawer full of single sneakers with paper tags, a teenager handing over one more

failure.text: The moment you pick it up, the sneaker is soaking wet, dripping storm-drain water across the carpet in a trail toward the door. You drop it. When you look again it's dry and gone, and your own left shoe feels a size too loose all afternoon.
failure.art: A small wet sneaker on library carpet with a trail of dripping water leading toward the front doors, a startled teenager stepping back

choices.label: Ask the history club's oldest member what it means

success.text: Mr. Stroud, ninety and sharp as a tack, laughs. "Every Halloween some kid loses a shoe to that drain, and every year the library finds it. Never the kid. Always the shoe." He makes it sound like a tradition instead of a warning, which helps more than it should.
success.art: A ninety-year-old man in a tweed cap laughing at a library table with a teenager, old newspaper printouts spread between them

failure.text: Mr. Stroud goes pale, gathers his notes and leaves the meeting early without a word. The rest of the history club spends the whole hour staring at your feet.
failure.art: Elderly history-club members around a library table all staring down at a teenager's sneakers, an empty chair pushed back

beats.title: The Shush
beats.place: The reading room, Glimmer Falls Public Library, Sunday afternoon
beats.text: Sunday hours are short and sleepy, and today they're too quiet. Every time anyone speaks above a whisper, a long soft SHHHH answers from somewhere in the stacks, and the speaker can't make a sound for a minute afterward. A toddler has been silenced mid-giggle. Two old men are arguing in furious, total silence. The SHHHH is drifting closer to the front desk.
beats.art: A sunlit library hall of tables on a lazy Sunday afternoon, patrons pressing hands over their open silent mouths, a toddler frozen mid-giggle on her mother's lap, two old men glaring at each other across a table with their lips moving silently, a faint ripple in the air drifting between the tall shelves toward the front desk, a teenager holding a heavy dictionary over their head, gold dust in the sunbeams, wide shot

choices.label: Drop the big dictionary and sing back at it

success.text: BOOM goes the unabridged dictionary, and you follow it with the loudest show-tune note you own. The SHHHH tries to answer and chokes on it. All at once everyone's voice comes back, mid-argument, mid-giggle, and the reading room erupts in the happiest noise it has heard in years.
success.art: A teenager singing at full voice beside a giant dictionary flat on a library floor, patrons cheering and laughing as dust motes dance in the sunlight

failure.text: You get out half a note before the SHHHH lands on you like a wet towel. You spend the rest of the afternoon mouthing words nobody can hear, and Ms. Hart has to write GO HOME AND REST on a notepad for you.
failure.art: A teenager clutching their throat in a quiet library, a librarian in a cardigan holding up a notepad toward them

choices.label: Tiptoe into the stacks and follow the SHHHH to its source

success.text: Deep in the 900s you find it: a hand-painted QUIET PLEASE placard from 1931, trembling on its nail. You take it down and tuck it gently into the donation bin for the Glitter Box prop room, where it will finally be in a show. The stacks go back to an ordinary hush.
success.art: A teenager in a narrow aisle of tall library shelves lifting an old hand-painted wooden placard off a nail, dust swirling in a shaft of afternoon light

failure.text: You round the end of an aisle and the SHHHH is right in your ear, warm and disapproving. Your footsteps vanish, then your breathing, then your own heartbeat, until you bolt back to the sunny front desk and the world rushes back in.
failure.art: A teenager running out of a dim aisle of library shelves toward a sunlit front desk, a shadowy ripple of air close behind them

choices.label: Run the whole library on passed notes with Priya

success.text: Priya hands out graph paper and pencils like it's a dungeon crawl: Silent Library Mode, house rules. In twenty minutes everyone is passing notes and laughing without a sound. Starved of noise, the SHHHH thins out, and by closing it's just the hum of the lights.
success.alone: You hand out scratch paper and golf pencils from the card catalog and declare Silent Library Mode. In twenty minutes everyone is passing notes and laughing without a sound. Starved of noise, the SHHHH thins out, and by closing it's just the hum of the lights.
success.art: Library patrons of all ages passing folded paper notes and laughing silently around a big reading table, an Indian American teen girl with a long braid and gold glasses directing them

failure.text: Someone passes a note that says SO FUNNY, and someone else laughs out loud. The SHHHH sweeps the whole table at once. Priya, mute, writes NAT 1 on the back of her hand and shows it to you.
failure.alone: Someone passes a note that says SO FUNNY, and someone else laughs out loud. The SHHHH sweeps the whole table at once, you included, and you can't so much as hum on the walk home.
failure.art: A reading table of startled library patrons covering their mouths, paper notes scattered, a gust stirring their hair, a teen girl in a purple cardigan holding up her hand

name: Pump Iron Gym and Aerobics
blurb: Chrome weights, mirrored aerobics studio, a sauna that is always too hot, and a roller-rink annex where the disco ball still spins. The high-school gym is next door, all trophies and old prom banners.
art: A 1980s strip-mall gym with a neon Pump Iron sign, chrome weight machines visible through the front window, a mirrored aerobics studio and an attached roller rink with a spinning disco ball, afternoon sun on the parking lot

beats.title: Skate or Die
beats.place: The roller-rink annex, Pump Iron Gym
beats.text: The Velvet Wheels, four seniors in matching satin jackets, have claimed the rink every Saturday since August. Today they've thrown down: one couples skate, winner takes the rink, loser buys everyone nachos. The DJ cues up a synth track and the disco ball starts to spin faster than any motor should allow.
beats.art: A neon-lit 1980s roller rink on a Saturday afternoon with a disco ball spinning fast, four teens in matching purple satin jackets posing on skates in the middle of the floor, a young woman with dark curls and an orange headband rolling up in a neon-orange racing wheelchair, a teenager lacing up rental skates on the bench at the edge of the floor, colored spotlights, wide shot

choices.label: Skate fast, skate fearless, go for the spin

success.text: You hit the spin and it keeps going, a perfect blur of light and wheels, and the rink erupts. The Velvet Wheels buy the nachos with good grace, and their captain hands you her satin jacket for the week. "You earned it, freak." It's the nicest thing anyone's said to you all month.
success.art: A teenager mid-spin on roller skates under a disco ball, light scattering everywhere, a crowd of skaters cheering in satin jackets

failure.text: Wheels, floor, ceiling, floor. You wipe out spectacularly into the carpeted wall. The disco ball stops dead. Everyone looks up at it. Nobody touched the switch. You buy the nachos.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled against a carpeted rink wall in rental skates, a stopped disco ball overhead, skaters staring up at it uneasily

choices.label: Skate with Sunny and let her lead

success.text: Sunny Castellanos rolls onto the floor in her racing chair and you skate beside her, hands linked, cutting the corners so tight the Velvet Wheels just stop and watch. It isn't a contest after that. It's a show.
success.alone: You roll onto the floor alone and skate the couples number solo, cutting the corners so tight the Velvet Wheels just stop and watch. It isn't a contest after that. It's a show.
success.art: A woman in a racing wheelchair and a teenager on roller skates gliding hand in hand around a neon rink, other skaters stopping to watch

failure.text: You and Sunny are in perfect sync until the lights go out. In the dark, you hear more wheels on the floor than there should be, circling. When the lights snap back, it's just the two of you, and Sunny says, quietly, "Let's go get nachos."
failure.alone: You are in perfect sync with the music until the lights go out. In the dark, you hear more wheels on the floor than there should be, circling. When the lights snap back, it's just you out there, and you decide, quietly, that it's time to go get nachos.
failure.art: A roller rink plunged into darkness, only the disco ball's faint glints showing fresh wheel tracks across an empty rink

choices.label: Bring the camp with a full choreographed routine

success.text: Jazz hands. A hairbrush microphone. A slide on your knees to the final note. The Velvet Wheels laugh so hard they forfeit. Somebody's little brother asks for your autograph on his skate.
success.art: A teenager on roller skates in leg warmers ending a flamboyant routine on their knees with arms raised, rival skaters doubled over laughing

failure.text: Your big finish involves a scarf that catches in a wheel. You spin out into the snack bar, taking a tray of soft pretzels with you. The Velvet Wheels win, but their captain helps you up and says it was "honestly iconic."
failure.art: A teenager tangled in a scarf sliding into a roller-rink snack bar, pretzels flying, a rival skater offering a hand

beats.title: Locker 31
beats.place: The sauna and locker room, Pump Iron Gym
beats.text: The sauna is empty and fogged solid. As you sit, letters appear in the steam on the glass, written from the inside by a finger nobody owns: LOCKER 31. Locker 31 has had the same rusted padlock on it since the gym opened, and the staff swear nobody's ever had the key.
beats.art: A steamy wood-paneled gym sauna with a fogged glass door, a finger-traced line appearing in the steam on the inside of the glass, and outside the door a row of old metal gym lockers with one sealed by a rusted padlock, a huge teenage boy with a curly sandy mullet in a cream sweater holding a flashlight beside a teenager crouched at the lock, warm amber sauna light, medium shot

choices.label: Snap the padlock off with your bare hands

success.text: The lock gives with a shriek. Inside: a 1974 gym bag, a pair of lucky leg warmers, and a bodybuilding trophy for M. TESSARO, who, the manager says, disappeared on a dare. You leave the trophy on the front desk. The fog on the sauna glass never writes again.
success.art: An open gym locker with a snapped padlock hanging off it, inside a vintage duffel bag, striped leg warmers and a small gold trophy

failure.text: Your hands slip on the hot metal and the lock doesn't budge. When you look up, the steam on the locker-room mirror says NOT LIKE THAT, and the sauna door slams shut on its own.
failure.art: A steamy locker-room mirror with words traced in condensation, a teenager rubbing sore hands beside a padlocked locker

choices.label: Get Moose to help you pick it

success.text: Moose holds the flashlight and talks you through it like knitting: "gentle, gentle, now loop." The padlock clicks open. Inside is an old letter, never mailed: I'm sorry I left. Tell the guys I'm okay. Moose quietly folds it and promises to track down M. Tessaro's family.
success.alone: You hold the flashlight in your teeth and talk yourself through it like a tricky knot: gentle, gentle, now loop. The padlock clicks open. Inside is an old letter, never mailed: I'm sorry I left. Tell the guys I'm okay. You fold it quietly and promise yourself you'll track down M. Tessaro's family.
success.art: A huge gentle football lineman holding a flashlight for a teenager picking a padlock with a bobby pin, a folded old letter visible inside the locker

failure.text: The bobby pin snaps off inside the lock. Moose winces. "Okay, so that's in there forever now." As you walk away, a slow, polite knock comes from inside locker 31. Three times. Then nothing.
failure.alone: The bobby pin snaps off inside the lock. You wince. That's in there forever now. As you walk away, a slow, polite knock comes from inside locker 31. Three times. Then nothing.
failure.art: A broken bobby pin jammed in a rusty padlock on a gym locker, two teens backing away down a tiled locker room

beats.title: The Sweat-a-Thon
beats.place: The aerobics studio, Pump Iron Gym
beats.text: Pump Iron is running a Sweat-a-Thon to raise money for the free clinic, and every minute you last earns pledges from the regulars. The music is loud, the leg warmers are many and the mirrors along the wall show a few more people in the back row than are actually in the room.
beats.art: A packed mirrored aerobics studio, sweaty people in headbands and leg warmers doing step-touch to a boombox, a painted paper strip for a charity sweat-a-thon taped above the mirrors, a teenager in the front row, and in the mirror reflection three extra pale gray figures dancing in the back row of the reflection, with the real back row empty, bright fluorescent light, wide shot

choices.label: Last the full ninety minutes

success.text: Ninety minutes. Your legs are noodles, your headband is soup, and the clinic jar is full. Your share of the pledges comes to three quarters and a free smoothie. The extra figures in the mirror applaud as you leave, and then they're not there.
success.art: An exhausted, triumphant teenager collapsed on an aerobics mat holding up a full donation jar, faint figures in the mirror applauding

failure.text: At minute forty you get dizzy and see the back-row people clearly for a second: gray faces, frozen smiles, still doing jumping jacks from some other decade. You sit down hard. Someone hands you a Bolt Cola and you drink it all.
failure.art: A dizzy teenager sitting on an aerobics studio floor, in the mirror behind them a row of gray figures in old-fashioned workout clothes mid-jumping-jack

choices.label: Skip the workout and work the pledge sheet

success.text: You hit up every lifter on the floor and the manager's mother for pledges, and you get the car dealership next door to match. The clinic gets double. You get two quarters and the manager's eternal respect.
success.art: A teenager with a clipboard grinning at a muscular man signing a pledge sheet, a full charity jar on a gym counter

failure.text: Nobody wants to pledge to someone who isn't sweating. The manager suggests, kindly, that you either dance or leave. Behind her, the mirror shows you dancing, perfectly, though you're standing still.
failure.art: A mirrored aerobics studio where a teenager's reflection is dancing while they stand still holding a clipboard

beats.title: Top of the Rope
beats.place: The high-school gym next door
beats.text: Coach Pruitt's makeup fitness test is running in the old high-school gym, and a freshman named Arlo is frozen at the top of the climbing rope, thirty feet up, white-knuckled and crying. The rope is creaking. The ceiling beam it hangs from has a crack you've never noticed before.
beats.art: An old high school gymnasium, a scared freshman boy clinging white-knuckled to the top of a climbing rope thirty feet up near a cracked ceiling beam, a tall broad woman coach with a red-blonde perm under a green cap and students staring up from the floor, blue crash mats being dragged across the boards, a teenager starting up the rope, faded prom streamers on the walls, high window light, low angle shot

choices.label: Climb up and talk him down hand over hand

success.text: You get above him, talk about anything but heights, and guide his feet one knot at a time. When you both hit the mat, the beam groans and the rope drops an inch. Coach Pruitt writes you both an A and walks you to the nurse herself.
success.art: Two teens descending a climbing rope together in a gym, one guiding the other's feet, a coach below with arms out ready to catch

failure.text: Halfway up, the rope swings and you both slide down hard, rope-burned and shaking. Arlo is okay. You are mostly okay. Coach Pruitt has the rope taken down, and nobody can explain why the crack in the beam is shaped like a grin.
failure.art: A crack in a gym ceiling beam shaped like a crooked smile, a climbing rope lying coiled on a mat below, two teens nursing rope-burned palms

choices.label: Rally the class to drag every crash mat underneath

success.text: You get the whole class hauling blue mats until there's a padded mountain under the rope. Arlo lets go, lands like a starfish in the middle and laughs for the first time all week. Coach Pruitt says she's never seen a class move that fast for anything.
success.art: A crowd of teenagers dragging blue crash mats into a towering pile beneath a climbing rope, a boy dropping safely into the middle

failure.text: The class drags their feet and the mats don't cover enough. Coach Pruitt climbs up herself, which she should not do at forty-five, and brings Arlo down with a cussing streak that would peel paint. She glares at all of you.
failure.art: A big fierce softball coach climbing a gym rope with a frightened freshman on her back, students below looking guilty

beats.title: Spot Me
beats.place: The weight room, Pump Iron Gym
beats.text: Big Lorraine Mbeki, fifty-two, regional bench-press champion and owner of the loudest laugh at Pump Iron, is going for the state record today, and her usual spotter has the flu. Between warm-up sets, you notice the plates on her bar keep changing. Forty-five pounds becomes fifty, then fifty-five, stamped with numbers that aren't on any plate in the rack. Lorraine hasn't noticed. She's chalking up.
beats.art: A chrome 1980s weight room, a powerfully built fifty-two-year-old Black woman in a red singlet chalking her hands beside a loaded bench-press bar, one extra iron plate at the end of the bar glowing faintly, a teenager standing at the head of the bench staring at the plate, lifters watching from the racks, bright overhead light and mirror reflections, medium shot

choices.label: Spot her and trust your arms

success.text: She drives the bar up, it stalls, and you're there with two fingers and everything you've got. It goes up. The room explodes. Lorraine hugs you off the floor and swears it felt heavier than it should. The strange plate is gone when you rack it, and you're a little stronger for having held it.
success.art: A teenager spotting a straining woman on a bench press as the bar locks out, lifters around them cheering with fists raised

failure.text: The bar dips, you both strain, and two lifters have to haul it back to the rack. Lorraine is fine, and furious at the bar instead of you. The strange plate rolls under the squat cage, and when the manager fishes it out, it's a dusty 1979 hubcap.
failure.art: Two burly lifters hauling a heavy barbell off a bench as a woman sits up gasping, a dusty hubcap rolling across the rubber floor

choices.label: Pull her aside and do the math on the bar

success.text: You add it up on a towel with a marker: the bar is carrying thirty pounds more than the record. You strip the strange plates off before her attempt and stack them in the corner, where they sulk. Lorraine breaks the record clean, then breaks it again for fun.
success.art: A teenager sliding odd iron plates off a barbell and stacking them in a corner of a weight room while a champion lifter watches with arms crossed

failure.text: Your math says the bar is fine. Your math is wrong. Lorraine misses the attempt by an inch, and when she sits up, the strange plates are stacked neatly in the corner, waiting, as if they had been there all along.
failure.art: A disappointed champion lifter sitting up on a bench, a neat stack of strange iron plates in the corner of the weight room behind her

choices.label: Get the whole gym chanting her name

success.text: LOR-RAINE. LOR-RAINE. You get the lifters stomping, the aerobics class banging tambourines and the sauna regulars yelling from the doorway in towels. She lifts on pure adrenaline and the extra weight doesn't stand a chance. She buys you a protein shake that tastes like chalk and victory.
success.art: A packed 1980s weight room chanting and stomping, an aerobics class shaking tambourines in the doorway, a woman pressing a heavy barbell up in triumph

failure.text: Nobody chants. One guy claps twice. Lorraine shoots you a look that says "baby, please" and lifts in total silence, and the strange plate seems to drink up the quiet.
failure.art: A silent weight room of unimpressed lifters, one man clapping limply, a teenager with raised arms looking embarrassed

beats.title: Cubby Zero
beats.place: The skate-rental counter, the roller-rink annex at Pump Iron
beats.text: Dwayne at the rental counter has a problem in cubby zero. A pair of white 1950s boot skates with pink pom-poms keeps turning up there, laced and polished, no matter how many times he locks them in the back. The wall of fame says they belonged to Bunny Albescu, who skated here every Saturday until she was eighty-one and passed last spring. Today they're in your size.
beats.art: A roller rink skate-rental counter with wooden cubbies full of brown rental skates, one pair of polished white 1950s boot skates with pink pom-poms sitting laced in the bottom cubby with a soft glow, a young man behind the counter rubbing his neck, framed black-and-white photos of skaters on the wall behind, a disco ball overhead, a teenager reaching for the skates, warm counter light, medium shot

choices.label: Lace them up and take one lap for Bunny

success.text: The skates know the floor better than you do. They carry you through a perfect slow lap under the disco ball, finishing in the little backward spin Bunny was famous for. The old regulars on the rail stand up and clap. The skates go back in cubby zero and stay there, finally resting.
success.art: A teenager gliding backward in white vintage boot skates under a spinning disco ball, elderly regulars standing at the rail applauding

failure.text: The skates want a faster song than the DJ is playing. They take you twice around the rink at a speed nobody should reach in rentals and deposit you in a heap at the snack bar, in the nachos. By the time you get them unlaced, Dwayne is already putting them back in cubby zero.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled at a roller-rink snack bar with nachos scattered everywhere, white vintage skates on their feet still spinning their wheels

choices.label: Read the wall of fame for what she left unfinished

success.text: In the 1957 photo, Bunny is mid-couples-skate with a woman in a matching pom-pom pair, but the caption names only Bunny. The partner's name is penciled on the back of the frame: Marguerite Ferreira. Dwayne adds it to the caption with his label maker and gives you a free skate pass. The pom-poms stay quiet after that.
success.art: A teenager studying a framed black-and-white photograph on a roller-rink wall, showing two women in matching pom-pom skates skating arm in arm

failure.text: The photos are faded and the captions are mostly skating puns. When you turn around, the white skates are sitting on the counter right in front of you, laces loose, toes pointed at you, waiting.
failure.art: A pair of white vintage boot skates sitting on a rental counter with loose laces, toes pointed toward a nervous teenager

choices.label: Find Bunny's granddaughter and bring the skates home

success.text: Her granddaughter Rosa runs the alterations shop across the parking lot and bursts into tears at the pom-poms. She hangs the skates over her sewing machine, where Bunny can watch the whole street go by. She swears she'll hem your jeans for free, forever.
success.art: A tearful woman in a tailor's shop hanging white vintage roller skates above a sewing machine, a teenager smiling in the doorway

failure.text: Rosa thanks you politely and takes them inside. By the time you walk back across the parking lot, Dwayne is waving at you from the rink door, holding up a pair of white skates with pink pom-poms and looking haunted.
failure.art: A rink employee in the doorway of a roller rink holding up white vintage pom-pom skates with a haunted look, a parking lot in late afternoon

name: Glimmer Falls High
blurb: Home of the Fighting Prospectors: endless lockers, a trophy case nobody dusts, a yearbook darkroom and a shop class building the homecoming float out of chicken wire and hope.
art: A sprawling 1960s brick high school with a marquee sign reading go geodes, a football field behind it, rows of lockers glimpsed through glass doors, kids with backpacks on the front steps in autumn light

beats.title: Saturday Detention
beats.place: The library annex, Glimmer Falls High
beats.text: Saturday detention, 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. Vice Principal Kroll locks the door and leaves you with a jock, a burnout and a girl in black lace who has not blinked once. The wall clock reads 1:13 and doesn't move. Hours pass. The clock doesn't. The door is still locked.
beats.art: Five mismatched teenagers slumped at long tables in a high school library annex during Saturday detention, a jock in a letter jacket, a long-haired burnout, a girl in black lace staring with wide unblinking eyes, a teenager and a quiet freshman, a round wall clock stuck at one-thirteen, a locked door with a wire-glass window, gray light through tall windows, wide shot

choices.label: Get everyone talking, for real

success.text: It starts with snacks and ends with secrets. The jock wants to dance. The burnout writes poems. The girl in lace just wanted someone to ask. When you all laugh at the same time, the clock jumps to 3:00 and the door clicks open.
success.art: Five teenagers sitting in a circle on a library floor sharing snacks and laughing, a wall clock behind them suddenly reading three

failure.text: Nobody wants to talk. The silence gets heavier until you can hear the clock not ticking. At 3:00, which you know only because the janitor unlocks the door, you all leave without a word, and the girl in lace is gone before she reaches the hall.
failure.art: A school hallway with four teens walking separately and silently away from detention, an empty space where a fifth figure should be

choices.label: Escape through the air vent

success.text: The vent leads to the teachers' lounge, where you liberate a box of doughnuts and the master key to the vending machines. Back through the vent before Kroll checks in. The clock starts ticking again, as if it lost interest.
success.art: A teenager crawling out of a ceiling air vent into a cluttered 1980s teachers' lounge, a box of doughnuts on the table, a ring of keys on a hook

failure.text: The vent goes on much farther than the building does. You crawl for what feels like an hour past grates that look into classrooms from other years. You come out in detention again, exactly where you started. The clock still says 1:13.
failure.art: A long metal air duct receding into darkness, slatted grates along it showing faded classrooms from different decades

choices.label: Climb up and fix the clock

success.text: Somebody wedged a pencil in the clock's gears. Under the pencil, a note in old ballpoint: DETENTION 10/25/66, THEY FORGOT ABOUT ME. You free the gears, the hands spin forward, and the door unlocks. You keep the note.
success.art: A teenager standing on a chair prying open a school wall clock, a pencil stuck in the gears, a folded old note falling out

failure.text: You fall off the chair and take the clock with you. It shatters on the floor, and in the broken glass you see every detention since 1959, faces staring up. Kroll writes you up for property damage.
failure.art: A smashed school clock on linoleum, the broken glass reflecting a crowd of faces from different eras, a vice principal looming in the doorway

beats.title: Somebody Else in the Picture
beats.place: The yearbook darkroom, Glimmer Falls High
beats.text: The yearbook editor, a frazzled junior named Yolanda, swears the darkroom is broken. Every photo she develops of the empty hallway comes out with a figure in it, standing in a different spot each time, getting closer to the camera. Deadline is Monday. She needs someone to print the last roll.
beats.art: A small high school darkroom glowing red under a safelight, black-and-white prints hanging from a clothesline, each one of the same empty school hallway with a blurry figure standing a little closer to the camera in every print, a nervous junior girl with frizzy hair holding print tongs, a teenager leaning in at the developer tray, deep red light, medium shot

choices.label: Develop the last roll yourself

success.text: You print the roll steady-handed. In the last frame, the figure is right at the lens: a smiling boy in a 1962 letterman jacket holding up a sign that says DON'T FORGET ME. Yolanda finds his photo missing from the 1962 yearbook and puts it in this one.
success.art: A wet photograph hanging in a red darkroom showing a smiling boy in a vintage letterman jacket holding a hand-lettered sign, two teens staring at it

failure.text: The last print is just your face, in close-up, from behind the camera, taken a second ago. You drop the tongs. Yolanda decides the yearbook will feature cartoon drawings this year instead.
failure.art: A dripping photograph in a darkroom tray showing a close-up of a startled teenager's face from an impossible angle

choices.label: Test the hallway with your instant camera

success.text: Your instant photo of the hallway shows the figure too, which rules out bad chemicals. You find the spot it's always nearest to, a dented locker, and inside the vent slats someone has jammed a lost class ring from 1962. You hand it to the office.
success.art: A teenager in a school hallway holding a freshly developed instant photo next to a dented locker, a tarnished class ring glinting in the vent slats

failure.text: Your instant photo develops slowly, and the figure in it raises a hand and waves. You decide to stop taking pictures of hallways for the rest of your life.
failure.art: An instant photograph of an empty school hallway in a teenager's hand, a faint figure in it with a hand raised in greeting

beats.title: Chicken Wire and Hope
beats.place: The shop class garage, Glimmer Falls High
beats.text: The homecoming float is a giant papier-mache geode named Rocky, the Prospectors' good-luck rock, and it's due Friday. Class president Chip Merriweather is losing it: half the committee quit, the glue gun is on fire and Rocky's head keeps turning toward the window when nobody's looking at it.
beats.art: A school shop garage after hours, a giant half-built papier-mache purple rock mascot with googly eyes on a parade trailer, chicken wire, tissue paper, a smoking glue gun and paint cans everywhere, the rock's head turned toward the window, a preppy 17-year-old boy with side-parted chestnut hair, a pink oxford shirt and a navy blazer clutching a clipboard in despair, a teenager with wire cutters, work lights, wide shot

choices.label: Roll up your sleeves and build

success.text: You and Chip work until the janitor kicks you out. Rocky is magnificent: googly eyes, tissue-paper sparkles, a tiny football helmet. Chip, glue in his hair, says you're the first person who's helped him this year without wanting something.
success.art: Two teenagers covered in paint and tissue paper high-fiving in front of a finished glittering purple rock mascot float, the shop garage lit by a single bulb

failure.text: The chicken wire fights you, and wins. You leave with scratches on both arms and Rocky still headless. In the morning his head is back on, finished, painted in perfect detail. Nobody admits to doing it.
failure.art: A parade float of a purple rock mascot in a dim garage at dawn, its head mysteriously complete and gleaming, a teenager with scratched arms staring at it

choices.label: Talk the quitters back onto the committee

success.text: You promise pizza and credit in the yearbook. Eleven kids show up. Chip looks like he might cry, then makes a speech so earnest that the whole room cheers. Rocky is finished by Wednesday.
success.art: A crowded shop garage full of teens painting a giant rock mascot float together, pizza boxes stacked on a workbench, a class president mid-speech

failure.text: The quitters all say they're busy, and one of them says the float "gives her the creeps" and won't explain. Chip pretends he's fine. He isn't. Rocky's head turns to watch you go.
failure.art: A preppy teen sitting alone on an overturned bucket in a shop garage beside a half-finished rock mascot whose head is turned toward the door

beats.title: Notes in Locker 214
beats.place: The B-wing lockers, Glimmer Falls High
beats.text: For a week, folded notes have been slipping into your locker. HELP. THEY WON'T STOP. Today's says GYM BLEACHERS, 3:15. Under the bleachers you find a freshman, Teddy Albright, whose backpack has been dumped and stomped three days running by the same pack of seniors.
beats.art: A shy freshman boy sitting under high school gym bleachers among scattered homework and a muddy stomped backpack, a teenager crouching beside him holding a small folded paper, slatted afternoon light falling through the bleacher seats in stripes across them, gum wrappers on the floor, medium shot

choices.label: Walk him to his locker and face the seniors

success.text: The seniors try their usual routine. You stand in front of Teddy and don't move. Coach Pruitt happens to round the corner at exactly the right moment and spends ten very loud minutes educating them. Teddy walks home with his head up.
success.art: A teenager standing protectively in front of a freshman in a school hallway, a group of senior bullies backing off as a fierce coach rounds the corner

failure.text: The seniors laugh and knock your books out of your hands too. But Teddy picks up your books for you, and you pick up his, and now there are two of you. That counts for something. It doesn't feel like enough.
failure.art: Two teenagers kneeling in a school hallway gathering each other's scattered books, laughing bullies walking away in the background

choices.label: Set up a buddy system with your friends

success.text: You get five people to rotate walking Teddy between classes. By Thursday the seniors give up out of sheer boredom. Teddy draws you a comic where you're a superhero with a walkie-talkie. You tape it inside your locker.
success.art: A hand-drawn comic taped inside a school locker showing a teenage superhero with a walkie-talkie, a freshman grinning beside it

failure.text: Your friends forget their shifts, and Teddy gets cornered in the bathroom. He finds you after school, damp and furious and quietly brave. "I'm still glad you tried," he says. You'll do better.
failure.art: A damp, defiant freshman standing in an empty school hallway after hours, facing a guilty teenager

beats.title: Paging Daniel Wexler
beats.place: Homeroom and the main office, Glimmer Falls High, a school morning
beats.text: After the pledge and the cafeteria menu, the PA crackles and a different voice comes on, older, with a hiss under it like a worn record. "Daniel Wexler, report to the principal's office." Your homeroom teacher goes white. Daniel Wexler graduated in 1966 and runs the night shift at the Thriftee-Mart now. The announcement repeats every school morning, and every morning it sounds a little more impatient.
beats.art: A 1980s high school homeroom on a school morning, startled students at wooden desks looking up at a crackling wall-mounted PA speaker box, a pale homeroom teacher frozen at the chalkboard with chalk in hand, an empty desk by the window, a teenager half standing, warm morning sun through tall windows, wide shot

choices.label: Go to the office in his place

success.text: The principal's office is empty, but the old intercom on the wall is warm. You press the button and say, "Danny grew up, sir. He turned out okay." A long pause, a click, then a sound like a man finally exhaling. The PA plays the school song, slightly off-key, and goes quiet for good.
success.art: A teenager speaking into a wall-mounted vintage intercom in an empty principal's office lit by morning sun through venetian blinds

failure.text: The secretary, Mrs. Delgado, looks at you like you're the ghost. "You're not Daniel," she says, and the PA says it too, from every speaker in the building at once. You get a tardy slip and a chill that lasts until lunch.
failure.art: A startled school secretary at her desk staring at a teenager, PA speakers mounted high on the office wall

choices.label: Tape the announcement and play it backward in the AV room

success.text: Backward, under the hiss, the old principal is saying something else: "I was wrong to call him in that day. I was wrong to tell his folks." You bring the tape to Mr. Wexler on his break at the Thriftee-Mart. He listens twice, nods slowly and presses two quarters on you "for the tape."
success.art: A teenager in a cluttered high-school AV room wearing headphones beside a portable cassette recorder, a reel-to-reel deck and cables behind them

failure.text: Backward, the announcement is just your name, over and over, in that old impatient voice. The recorder eats the tape. Vice Principal Kroll confiscates it for being in the AV room without a pass, which is honestly the least scary part of your morning.
failure.art: A stern vice principal holding up a tangled cassette tape in a high-school AV room, a sheepish teenager beside a jammed recorder

choices.label: Ask Mrs. Delgado in the office what happened in 1966

success.text: Mrs. Delgado has been the school secretary since 1964. She closes the door. "Principal Harlan called Danny in and told his parents he'd been seen holding hands with the Fischer boy. Harlan regretted it until the day he died." She writes Danny's number on a pink message slip. "Somebody should tell him that."
success.art: A gray-haired school secretary leaning across her desk to confide in a teenager, a pink message slip in her hand, the office door closed

failure.text: Mrs. Delgado's smile goes stiff. "Ancient history, sweetheart," she says, and hands you a hall pass to anywhere else. As you turn to go, the PA crackles and the old voice says, "Mrs. Delgado, hold my calls." She drops her coffee.
failure.art: A school secretary dropping a coffee mug in surprise beneath a crackling PA speaker, a teenager holding a hall pass in the doorway

beats.title: Costume Code
beats.place: The quad at lunch, Glimmer Falls High, Halloween
beats.text: Halloween lunch means the costume parade around the quad, and Vice Principal Kroll has taped a list of APPROPRIATE COSTUMES to the cafeteria door. A sophomore named Ozzie Brandt is in a sequined swamp-queen gown he sewed by hand, with a glittering train of felt lily pads, and Kroll is pointing at the list and then at the bathroom, telling him to change. The trophy case behind them flickers like it's watching. Ozzie's chin is up, but his hands are shaking.
beats.art: A sunny high school quad at lunchtime decorated with paper bats and pumpkins, a sophomore boy in a glittering hand-sewn green swamp-queen gown with a long train of felt lily pads standing with his chin up, a stern vice principal with a clipboard pointing toward a doorway, students in Halloween costumes watching, a teenager stepping up to offer the boy an arm, a trophy case flickering through the glass doors behind, bright noon light, wide shot

choices.label: Offer Ozzie your arm and start the parade yourself

success.text: You offer Ozzie your arm and walk. The drama kids fall in, then the softball team, then half the quad, until Kroll is standing alone with his list while the parade sweeps past him. Ozzie wins Best Costume by a landslide and wears the sash to every class.
success.art: A sophomore in a glittering swamp-queen gown walking arm in arm with a teenager at the head of a cheering costume parade across a sunny school quad

failure.text: Kroll steps between you and writes you both up before the parade can start. You spend lunch on the bench outside the office together. Ozzie fixes a sequin and says, very quietly, "Thanks for being the only one." It counts. It still stings.
failure.art: Two teenagers on a bench outside a principal's office at lunchtime, one in a glittering gown fixing a sequin, the other holding a detention slip

choices.label: Pull the student handbook and read Kroll the actual rules

success.text: Page 41, dress code: there is no costume rule at all. Kroll invented the list this morning. You read the page aloud in front of the principal, who is judging the parade in a witch hat. The list comes off the door, and Kroll goes to check on the cafeteria for a very long time.
success.art: A teenager holding up an open student handbook to a frowning vice principal in a school quad while a principal in a witch hat looks on

failure.text: The dress code is vague enough that Kroll can call anything a distraction, and he smiles and says so. Ozzie changes into gym clothes and folds the gown into his locker. The trophy-case lights stay dark all afternoon.
failure.art: A gloomy school hallway beside a darkened trophy case, a teenager in gym clothes folding a glittering gown into a locker

choices.label: Raid the drama closet so everyone shows up in a gown

success.text: Twenty minutes later the football team is in ball gowns, the chess club is in feather boas and Coach Pruitt is in a tuxedo with tails, refereeing. Kroll can't send the whole school to change. Ozzie leads the parade in a crown somebody made out of a pie tin.
success.art: A school quad full of laughing teenagers in mismatched ball gowns and feather boas, a sturdy coach in a tuxedo with a whistle, a sophomore in a pie-tin crown leading them

failure.text: The drama teacher catches you with an armful of gowns and marches you to Kroll, who gives you detention and keeps the gowns "as evidence." Ozzie walks the parade alone in his. He gets a few cheers and a lot of stares.
failure.art: A drama teacher catching a teenager carrying an armful of sparkly gowns out of a costume closet, a stern vice principal in the doorway

name: Rewind Video
blurb: Wall-to-wall VHS and a few loyal Betamax holdouts, a horror aisle lit like a crypt, a beaded curtain to the back room, and a night-drop slot that sometimes returns tapes nobody rented.
art: A cozy 1980s video rental store in a strip mall, walls of VHS boxes, a horror aisle lit purple, a retro counter with a rewinder machine, a night-drop slot beside the glass door, afternoon sun through window posters

beats.title: Returned by Mr. Gill
beats.place: The night-drop bin, Rewind Video
beats.text: Zelda Fishbein empties the night-drop and goes pale. A Betamax copy of Blood Harvest, returned in its case with a sticky note in shaky pencil: SORRY IT'S LATE. The membership card it's checked out on belongs to Walter Gill, who rented it in October 1979. Zelda went to his funeral that November.
beats.art: A video store counter in the morning, a 63-year-old woman with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain and a red staff vest gone pale as she holds an old Betamax tape case with a yellow sticky note on it, the metal night-drop bin open beside her, a dusty paper membership slip on the counter, a teenager leaning in, soft morning sun through the front glass, medium shot

choices.label: Put the tape in the old Betamax deck in back

success.text: The tape plays Blood Harvest, and then after the credits, Mr. Gill sitting in his recliner. "Tell Zelda the ending still gets me." He smiles and the tape runs out. Zelda laughs until she cries. Some people just want to finish the movie.
success.art: An old Betamax deck glowing in a cluttered back room, a television showing a smiling old man in a recliner waving, a woman with tears and laughter watching

failure.text: The tape plays nothing but snow, and in the snow, a shape leans closer to the glass. The deck ejects the tape hot to the touch. Zelda puts it in the freezer, which she says is what you do, according to every movie.
failure.art: A television screen of static with a faint shape pressing toward the glass, a smoking Betamax tape ejecting from a deck

choices.label: Help Zelda close out his account properly

success.text: Zelda waives seven years of late fees and stamps the card RETURNED, THANK YOU. The bell over the door rings once, though nobody comes in. Zelda says Walter always said goodbye like that. She gives you a free rental and a hug.
success.art: A woman stamping an old video store membership card at a counter, the bell over the glass door swinging gently on its own

failure.text: You type the old account into the computer and the screen fills with late fees, then rows of the same title, then the word SORRY, over and over. The computer shuts off with a pop. The tape is back in the night-drop the next day.
