failure.art: An early 1980s computer terminal at a video store counter with a green screen filled with the repeated word sorry

beats.title: Be Kind, Rewind
beats.place: The counter, Rewind Video
beats.text: Two hundred tapes came back un-rewound this week, and the manager will pay a quarter for every forty you run through the rewinder. It's a dull job, until one tape keeps rewinding past its start. The counter keeps going, into negative numbers, and the motor whines like it's in pain.
beats.art: A teenager behind a video store counter surrounded by tall stacks of videotapes, a little boxy rewinder in the shape of a red sports car whirring with smoke curling from its seams, its red digital counter running into minus numbers, the teen staring at it with a tape halfway to the next slot, warm counter light and purple horror-aisle glow behind, medium shot

choices.label: Finish the stack and ignore the weird one

success.text: You rewind all two hundred, sort them alphabetically and put the weird one in a drawer marked DO NOT RENT. The manager pays you five quarters, and Toby Nakamura asks if he can borrow the weird one for "research." You say absolutely not.
success.art: A teenager handing coins across a video counter beside neatly stacked tapes, a single tape locked in a drawer with a red warning label

failure.text: You get bored, you get careless, and you jam three tapes in a row. Ribbons of tape spill across the counter. The manager docks your pay. The weird one sits on top of the pile, perfectly rewound, waiting.
failure.art: Tangled ribbons of magnetic tape spilling across a video store counter, one pristine cassette sitting on top of the mess

choices.label: See what's on the tape before the beginning

success.text: Before the movie's opening titles: shaky footage of this very store at 3 a.m., lights off, the horror aisle glowing. A woman in a shop apron puts a tape on the shelf and looks into the camera. "Pick me up anytime." You know a strange shop when you see one.
success.art: A small TV showing grainy footage of a dark video store at night, a mysterious woman in an apron placing a tape on a shelf and looking into the camera

failure.text: Before the beginning is static, then a test pattern, then you, sitting at this counter, watching this tape. Then the you on screen turns around. The power goes out. You don't finish the job.
failure.art: A dark video store during a power outage, the only light a television showing a teenager at a counter looking over their shoulder

beats.title: Toby Needs a Zombie
beats.place: The horror aisle, Rewind Video
beats.text: Toby Nakamura is shooting a zombie short on his camcorder in the horror aisle after hours and his lead zombie went home sick. He has a jar of homemade fake blood, a bag of oatmeal guts and a borrowed fog machine that has started making fog shaped like hands.
beats.art: A video store horror aisle after hours lit purple, a 15-year-old Japanese American boy with a black bowl cut, big wire-rimmed glasses and a yellow windbreaker filming on a bulky shoulder camcorder with a red recording light, a teenager in torn clothes and gray zombie makeup shambling down the aisle, a borrowed fog machine pouring mist that curls into the shapes of reaching hands, a jar of fake blood and a bag of oatmeal on a shelf, purple light and gray fog, wide shot

choices.label: Shamble, moan and commit to the role

success.text: You are the best zombie in Glimmer Falls history. Toby screams "CUT!" in joy. Your death scene, eaten by the fog, will play at the Glitter Box midnight show. You're famous for about four minutes, which is plenty.
success.art: A teenager in pale zombie makeup lurching dramatically down a VHS aisle in fog, a filmmaker with a camcorder shouting with delight

failure.text: You trip over the fog machine cord and land in the oatmeal. The tape catches the fog-hands grabbing your ankle a second before you fell. Toby wants to use it. You want to go home.
failure.art: A teenager in zombie makeup sprawled face down in oatmeal guts in a foggy video aisle, misty hand shapes curling around an ankle

choices.label: Run sound and keep an eye on that fog

success.text: You hold the boom mic and unplug the fog machine the second it starts reaching for Toby. In the playback you both hear it: a tiny sigh on the audio when it switches off. Toby gives you a producer credit and two quarters.
success.art: A teenager holding a boom microphone and an unplugged fog machine cord, a filmmaker reviewing footage on a camcorder screen

failure.text: You miss the cue, the fog machine chugs on, and the shot fills with gray hands. Toby, white as paper, says "okay, that's a wrap" and you both leave through the front instead of the back.
failure.art: A video store aisle drowning in fog full of gray hand shapes, two teens bolting for the front door

beats.title: Staff Pick
beats.place: The new-release wall, Rewind Video
beats.text: A handwritten STAFF PICK card has appeared on the new-release wall, in handwriting nobody at Rewind recognizes. It recommends Nightmare on Crystal Street (1986): "A real scream! You'll feel like you're in it!" The box is there. The cover shows your street. The back cover shows your house.
beats.art: A video store new-release wall of videotape boxes, a small folded paper tent propped on one shelf, a box whose painted front shows a sunny suburban cul-de-sac with a glowing purple crystal rock in the roundabout, a teenager reaching for it with a puzzled face, a 63-year-old woman in cat-eye glasses watching from the counter, fluorescent store light, medium shot

choices.label: Rent it and read the back cover closely

success.text: The back-cover blurb lists the cast as "you and your friends" and the tagline: THE ONLY WAY OUT IS TOGETHER. A useful thought. You return it unwatched. The rental is free; the card says "staff discount."
success.art: A teenager reading the back of a VHS box under a desk lamp, the cover showing a suburban street at night with a gang of silhouetted kids holding flashlights

failure.text: The box is empty. Inside the case, someone has written in red marker: COMING SOON. The staff pick card on the wall has changed. Now it says the movie is "too scary to rent."
failure.art: An empty VHS case open on a counter with coming soon scrawled inside in red marker, a staff pick card on the wall behind it

choices.label: Ask Zelda how this kind of movie ends

success.text: Zelda leans on the counter. "Final girl, final boy, final whoever. It ends when the kids stop splitting up and start listening to each other." She gives you a flashlight from under the counter. "And always check the batteries."
success.alone: You lean on the counter and run through every horror movie you've ever rented. Final girl, final boy, final whoever. It ends when the kids stop splitting up and start listening to each other. You grab the store flashlight from under the counter. And you check the batteries.
success.art: A retired scream queen leaning on a video store counter handing a flashlight to a teenager, posters of 1950s monster movies behind her

failure.text: Zelda looks at the box and her face changes. "I don't remember making this one," she says, "but that's my scream." She takes it into the back room and doesn't come out for an hour.
failure.alone: You flip the box over and your stomach drops: the scream on the back cover is yours, and you don't remember making this one. You shove it in the back room and don't go near that wall for an hour.
failure.art: A woman staring in shock at a VHS box on a counter, a beaded curtain to a back room swinging behind her

beats.title: Mangler Mack Moved
beats.place: The front window, Rewind Video, opening time
beats.text: The life-size cardboard standee of Mangler Mack, the masked janitor from Summer Camp Carnage IV, faced the street when Zelda locked up last night. This morning he's facing the counter, one cardboard arm raised in a little wave, and there are dusty prints on the carpet between the window and the register. The manager wants him out by the dumpster before customers arrive. Mack weighs two pounds and somehow feels heavier.
beats.art: A video store at opening time, a life-size cardboard cutout of a masked movie janitor holding a mop standing in the aisle facing the register with one cardboard arm raised in a small wave, a trail of dusty prints on the carpet leading from the front window to the counter, a teenager and a store manager staring at it, morning sun through the glass, medium wide shot

choices.label: Drag him out to the dumpster yourself

success.text: You fold Mack in half, march him out the back and wedge him behind the dumpster. When you come back in, the bell over the door jingles behind you and you refuse to turn around. He stays out there. The manager pays you two quarters for the haul.
success.art: A teenager hauling a folded cardboard cutout out a back door toward an alley dumpster in morning light

failure.text: Mack catches on the door frame, tears down the middle, and the top half flops over your shoulder like a hug. By lunchtime he's back in the window, taped together, waving at the street. Nobody admits to the tape.
failure.art: A taped-together cardboard cutout of a masked janitor standing in a video-store window waving at the street, a dismayed teenager on the sidewalk outside

choices.label: Raffle him off to the horror regulars, a quarter a ticket

success.text: The horror regulars go feral. A sixth-grader named Lupe wins and rides him home on her bike like a prize marlin. She calls the store the next morning: he moved again, and she loves him. You clear two quarters after the prize.
success.art: A kid on a bicycle riding away from a video store with a life-size cardboard cutout of a masked janitor strapped to her back, regulars cheering in the doorway

failure.text: Three kids buy tickets, and one of them wants a refund the moment Mack's head turns toward him. Then they all do. You refund everybody. Mack stays in the window, having made his point.
failure.art: A teenager handing coins back to a frightened kid at a video-store counter, a cardboard cutout in the window turned to watch them

choices.label: Check the store's overnight security tape

success.text: On the grainy tape, at 3:12 a.m., an opossum squeezes in through the night-drop slot, knocks Mack over, props him up the wrong way around and spends an hour in the candy rack. You laugh until you cry. You decide to skip the part where it looks right at the camera.
success.art: A grainy security monitor in a video-store back room showing an opossum in a candy rack beside a toppled cardboard cutout, a teenager laughing at the screen

failure.text: The tape shows the store empty all night. Mack faces the street, then the counter, with nothing in between. Then, at the very end, the frame jumps and Mack is standing right in front of the camera.
failure.art: A teenager recoiling from a security monitor in a dark back room, the screen filled by a cardboard masked face up close

beats.title: For Nico, When He's Older
beats.place: The returns counter, Rewind Video
beats.text: Inside the case of a returned copy of Beach Blanket Bigfoot is the wrong tape: a home-video cassette with a peeling label, FOR NICO, WHEN HE'S OLDER, XMAS '76. The account belongs to Nico Ferrante, nineteen, who dropped off eleven tapes in a laundry bag and left for basic training this morning. The cassette is warm. From inside the case comes the faint sound of a woman humming a carol.
beats.art: A video store returns counter at closing time, an open rental case holding a worn home-video cassette with a peeling paper strip on its spine, a canvas laundry bag spilling eleven tapes beside it, a teenager leaning close to the case with one ear turned toward it, a warm desk lamp on the counter and dark shelves behind, close medium shot

choices.label: Watch it in the back room to find out whose it is

success.text: It's Christmas 1976, and a young woman with the camera in her lap is talking to a baby in a high chair. "When you're big, Nico, and someone tells you who you're allowed to be, play this." Then she sings him a carol, badly and joyfully. You know exactly where it needs to go.
success.art: A teenager in a dim video-store back room watching a TV that shows a young woman singing to a baby in a high chair beside a decorated tree

failure.text: The tape is chewed in the middle, and the deck mangles the rest, spooling a long ribbon of Christmas onto the floor. You wind it back by hand with a pencil for an hour. The humming in the case stops, and you hope it's resting.
failure.art: A teenager sitting on a back-room floor winding a long ribbon of spilled videotape back into a cassette with a pencil

choices.label: Find the family through the membership file

success.text: The emergency contact is Rita Ferrante on Larkspur Lane. She opens the door, sees the label and sits right down on the step. "That's his mother. My sister. I'll send it to him at basic." She presses two quarters into your hand and won't take them back.
success.art: A woman sitting on her front step clutching a home-video cassette to her chest, a teenager on the front walk in afternoon light

failure.text: The address on file is a house that sold last month, and the new owners have never heard of any Ferrantes. You leave a note at the post office. The tape sits in Rewind's lost-and-found, humming quietly to itself every evening at closing.
failure.art: A teenager on the porch of an unfamiliar house with moving boxes stacked inside the screen door, holding a cassette and looking lost

choices.label: Dub a copy with Zelda so it can never be lost again

success.text: Zelda runs two decks at once like a pro and narrates the whole time about how home movies are the only horror films with happy endings. The dub comes out perfect. One copy goes to Nico's aunt, one goes in a drawer marked KEEP, and Zelda calls you a born archivist.
success.alone: You chain two decks together with a cable from the back room and sit with the tape the whole way through. The dub comes out perfect. One copy goes to Nico's aunt, and one goes in a drawer under the counter marked KEEP.
success.art: A woman in her sixties with a silver-streaked black bouffant and cat-eye glasses beside a teenager watching two stacked VCRs dub a tape, a TV glowing with a family Christmas

failure.text: The dub comes out with a second voice humming under the carol, lower and wrong. Zelda erases the copy without a word and hands you back the original. "Some things you don't copy," she says.
failure.alone: Your dub comes out with a second voice humming under the carol, lower and wrong. You erase the copy fast and put the original back in its case with both hands.
failure.art: A video-store counter at dusk, a TV showing static over a faint Christmas tree, a woman in cat-eye glasses ejecting a cassette from stacked VCRs beside a teenager

name: Starlight Mall and Arcade
blurb: Two floors of neon, a food court that smells like pretzels and orange-cream smoothies, the Galaxy Zone arcade, and a dead wing behind plywood where the old department store went dark in 1983.
art: A bustling two-story 1980s shopping mall atrium with neon signs, a fountain full of coins, escalators, a glowing arcade entrance, and at the far end a plywood barrier sealing off a dim abandoned wing

beats.title: DTH
beats.place: The Galaxy Zone arcade, Starlight Mall
beats.text: There's a fight brewing at the Galaxy Gobbler cabinet. Every top-ten score has been knocked off the board by three initials, DTH, and nobody has ever seen who plays. The regulars are accusing each other. A kid named Vince is about to throw a punch. The machine is warm, and nobody's touched it all morning.
beats.art: A crowded 1980s mall arcade, teenagers shouting around one glowing upright cabinet whose high-score screen shows the same three initials in every slot, a kid in a jean jacket winding up a punch, a wiry 15-year-old Vietnamese American boy with a lightning bolt shaved into his hair and a teal windbreaker with hot pink sleeves leaning on the next cabinet, a teenager stepping between them, blue and magenta arcade glow, wide shot

choices.label: Drop a quarter and take the score back

success.text: Two hours, one quarter, zero blinks. You beat DTH's score by forty points and type your initials in gold. The arcade erupts. On the next screen, DTH's initials are gone, replaced with GG. Good game. The machine cools down.
success.art: A teenager at an arcade cabinet surrounded by a cheering crowd, the high-score screen showing new initials at the top

failure.text: You die on level nine. The screen flashes DTH, and then, slowly, it types your initials beneath it, in the slot marked NEXT. The crowd goes quiet. Vince buys you a soda.
failure.art: An arcade game over screen showing the initials DTH with a teenager's initials typed beneath under the word next, a crowd gone silent

choices.label: Break up the fight before it starts

success.text: You get between Vince and the other kid and point out that nobody in this room could have done it. They all look at the machine. The machine looks back. Everybody agrees to hate it together, which is the closest thing to peace an arcade has.
success.art: A teenager standing between two angry kids in an arcade, everyone slowly turning to look at a glowing cabinet game

failure.text: Vince swings anyway. You catch it on the shoulder and the manager throws all three of you out. From the doorway you see the Galaxy Gobbler start a game all by itself.
failure.art: Three teens being shoved out of an arcade by a manager, behind them a cabinet game starting a round by itself at empty controls

choices.label: Ask Lou Tran to watch the machine with you

success.text: Lou plays one round and frowns. "Those scores aren't possible. Board's got a ghost or a short." He pops the back panel and finds a burned-out 1981 quarter jammed in the coin mech, etched with the initials D.T.H. Mystery solved, mostly.
success.art: An arcade champion with the back panel off a game cabinet, holding up a scorched old quarter between two fingers, wires and circuit boards glowing

failure.text: Lou plays one round, gets very quiet and walks away from the cabinet. "Something was playing with me," he says, which is the first time you've ever seen him lose. He doesn't want to talk about it.
failure.art: A young arcade champion stepping back from a cabinet game with a stunned expression, the screen glowing with a game over message

beats.title: The Kid at the Fountain
beats.place: The wishing fountain, Starlight Mall
beats.text: A girl of about six sits on the lip of the wishing fountain, holding a balloon and not crying, which is worse. Her name is Penny, her mom said she'd "be right back" two hours ago, and she says the fountain told her to wait. The coins at the bottom are all arranged in a spiral.
beats.art: A six-year-old girl in a pink coat holding a red balloon sitting alone and dry-eyed on the edge of a tiled mall wishing fountain, coins on the fountain floor arranged in a perfect spiral, shoppers with bags walking past with their eyes on the shop windows, a teenager kneeling beside her, skylight sun and neon storefronts, medium wide shot

choices.label: Comb the mall for her mom

success.text: You find Penny's mom in the dead-end corridor by the restrooms, dazed, swearing she only stepped away for a minute. When they hug, the coins in the fountain scatter out of their spiral. Her mom presses three quarters into your hand and won't take them back.
success.art: A tearful mother hugging her small daughter by a mall fountain, a teenager standing nearby with a balloon string, coins scattered in the water

failure.text: You search every store and find nothing. When you come back, Penny is with mall security and her mother, who never looks at you. As they leave, Penny waves and says, "The fountain says you owe it one."
failure.art: A small girl waving over her shoulder as a mall guard leads her away, a teenager standing alone by a fountain glinting with coins

choices.label: Toss a coin and make a wish for her

success.text: You flip your last quarter. It lands at the center of the spiral and the water goes still as glass. A second later, Penny's mom comes running down the escalator, calling her name, saying she got "turned around for hours." You decide not to wish for anything else today.
success.art: A coin landing at the center of a spiral of coins in a still mall fountain, a mother running down an escalator toward a child

failure.text: The coin hits the water and the spiral swallows it. Penny's balloon pops. Her mom appears and scoops her up, but looks right through you. So does everyone else, for the rest of the afternoon.
failure.art: A popped balloon string dangling over a mall fountain, a teenager looking around a crowded concourse while shoppers walk through them unseeing

beats.title: The Dead Wing Dare
beats.place: Behind the plywood, Starlight Mall
beats.text: The mall rats have a rule: you're not one of them until you bring back a mannequin head from Woolmart, the department store that closed in 1983 behind the plywood. Dani Ortega is holding the loose board open. Inside, the escalators are still, the fountains are dry and somewhere far in the dark, music is playing.
beats.art: A group of teenage mall rats holding back a loose sheet of plywood that reveals a dark abandoned mall wing, a frozen escalator, a dry fountain full of pennies and a dusty closed department store full of mannequins all facing the opening, a 16-year-old Chicana skater with a shaved undercut and pink-tipped black hair holding the board with her skateboard under her arm, a teenager stepping through, a thin beam of light in the dust, wide shot

choices.label: Walk in alone and grab a head

success.text: Dust, mannequins, a dry fountain full of pennies. You grab the first head you see and walk out without running, which is the real test. The mall rats chant your name. Dani gives you a glow-stick bracelet as membership.
success.art: A teenager walking out of a dark abandoned mall wing holding a mannequin head aloft, a group of punks cheering at the plywood

failure.text: Every mannequin in Woolmart is facing the door. You don't remember them all facing the door. You run. The mall rats laugh, but kindly, and Dani says nobody makes it the first time.
failure.art: A dim department store aisle full of dusty mannequins all turned toward the camera, a teenager fleeing in the far distance

choices.label: Skate it with Dani, fast and loud

success.text: You and Dani bomb down the dead escalator on skateboards, scream through Woolmart, snag two heads and are back in ninety seconds. Whatever lives in the dead wing has no idea what just happened. Neither do you. It's the best day of the week.
success.art: Two teens on skateboards rocketing through a dark abandoned department store, each holding a mannequin head, wheels sparking

failure.text: Your wheel catches a crack and you go down hard in the dark. Dani drags you out by the back of your jacket. Your knee is bleeding and your skateboard stays in there. In the morning, someone has propped it against the plywood, outside.
failure.art: A skateboard leaning against a plywood barrier in an empty mall at dawn, a single mannequin hand resting on its deck

beats.title: Pretzel Pete
beats.place: The food court, Starlight Mall
beats.text: The pretzel stand needs someone in the Pretzel Pete costume for the afternoon rush, a giant foam pretzel with eyes, paying a quarter an hour plus all the salt you can eat. The suit smells like old cheese and a stranger's sweat. Something in the left arm moves when you put it on.
beats.art: A mall food court back room, a giant foam pretzel mascot costume with big googly eyes hanging on a hook, its stuffed left arm bulging and twitching, a teenager holding up the costume's head skeptically with wrinkled nose, crates of pretzel dough and a neon food stall glow through the doorway, warm fluorescent light, medium shot

choices.label: Wave, dance and hand out samples

success.text: Pretzel Pete becomes a legend: you do the robot, you dance with a grandmother, you lead a conga line through the food court. The stand sells out by four. You get four quarters, a pretzel and a fan club of six toddlers.
success.art: A foam pretzel mascot leading a conga line of laughing shoppers through a neon food court, a cluster of toddlers trailing behind

failure.text: Kids kick Pretzel Pete. Teenagers kick Pretzel Pete harder. Inside the suit, something in the left arm squeezes your hand, sympathetically. You quit at the first break and leave the costume very carefully on its hook.
failure.art: A pretzel mascot costume slumped on a food court bench being poked by a gang of kids, its left foam arm curled oddly

choices.label: Check what's inside the left arm first

success.text: Tucked inside the arm is a raccoon kit, very small and very scared. You smuggle it out the service door to the drainage creek, where its mother is waiting. Then you do the shift with a lighter heart and an emptier sleeve.
success.art: A tiny baby raccoon peeking out of a foam costume sleeve, a teenager gently lifting it out by a mall service door

failure.text: There's nothing in the arm. Nothing at all. You put the suit on and the arm moves again, waving, all on its own. The manager says it's always done that, and that's why the job pays a quarter an hour.
failure.art: A pretzel mascot costume standing alone in a back room with one foam arm raised in a wave, hollow and empty

beats.title: Ho Ho Ho, October
beats.place: Center court, Starlight Mall
beats.text: It's still October and the mall is already building the Holly Jolly Village at center court: fake snow, a plywood gingerbread house and eleven animatronic elves in their shipping crates. The setup crew is two people short and paying two quarters for the afternoon. The problem is elf number seven. He's unplugged, his batteries are in a bag on the floor, and he keeps singing "Up on the Housetop" in a slow, deep voice.
beats.art: A shopping mall center court half built into a Christmas village in October, fake snow, a plywood gingerbread house, animatronic elves standing in open wooden shipping crates, one elf in a green felt vest with glowing eyes and its mouth wide open singing, its batteries in a plastic bag on the floor, a teenager holding a string of lights, paper bats still hanging from the railings above, wide shot

choices.label: Pitch in with the setup crew for the pay

success.text: You haul crates, spread fake snow and hang lights for three hours while the elf sings. By the end you're humming along. The crew boss pays you two quarters and tells you elf seven "does this every year, kid, just don't let him finish the song."
success.art: A teenager hanging strings of lights on a plywood gingerbread house in a mall center court beside a row of animatronic elves

failure.text: You lift elf seven's crate and he finishes the song. Every elf in the village turns its head toward you at once, with a little whir. The crew boss sends you home early for scaring the merchandise, with fake snow in your ears.
failure.art: A row of animatronic elves in a fake-snow Christmas village all turned to stare at a startled teenager holding an empty crate

choices.label: Open elf seven up and find out what's powering him

success.text: Behind his felt vest, wedged in the gears, is a cassette from 1983, the year the old department store closed: a Woolmart holiday jingle on a loop. You pull it and elf seven stops mid-ho. The silence is enormous. The crew boss lets you keep the tape, and it turns out to have a great B-side.
success.art: A teenager with a small screwdriver opening the back of an animatronic elf's felt vest, gears and an old cassette tape visible inside

failure.text: You get the vest open and find gears, wires and no power source of any kind. Elf seven stops singing, turns his head all the way around to look at you and says, in that deep voice, "Naughty." You button him back up very gently.
failure.art: An animatronic elf with its head turned all the way around staring at a frozen teenager in a half-built mall Christmas village

choices.label: Sing along and turn it into a show for the shoppers

success.text: You grab a candy-cane prop and duet with elf seven at full volume, adding harmonies and a kick line. A crowd gathers. The elf, bewildered, speeds up to match you and finishes in a perfectly normal chipper squeak. Shoppers toss quarters into the fake snow.
success.art: A teenager doing a kick line with a candy-cane prop beside a singing animatronic elf in a fake-snow mall village, shoppers clapping

failure.text: Your harmony makes it worse. Elf seven drops an octave lower than any speaker should, and every Christmas light in center court flickers in time. Mall security asks you to take your act to the parking lot.
failure.art: A mall security guard escorting a teenager away from a flickering Christmas village, an animatronic elf singing with wide glowing eyes

beats.title: Lap Eleven Hundred
beats.place: The upper concourse, Starlight Mall, 7 a.m. before the gates go up
beats.text: The Starlight Striders, a dozen retirees in matching teal tracksuits, walk laps of the mall every morning before the shops open. This morning they flag you down. Ida Feeney, seventy-eight, started walking on Tuesday and hasn't stopped. She's polite, she's chatty, she waves every lap, and her eyes lock on the dead-wing plywood every time she passes it. Her sneakers are worn through to the socks.
beats.art: An empty upper mall concourse at seven in the morning with metal gates still down on every store, a dozen retirees in matching teal tracksuits gathered with worried faces, and a 78-year-old woman with a white bob in a teal tracksuit walking briskly past a tall plywood wall in sneakers worn through to her socks, waving, a teenager falling into step beside her, pale early light from the skylights, wide shot

choices.label: Fall into step beside her and slow her down lap by lap

success.text: Sunny rolls up alongside, sets the pace and talks Ida down lap by lap, slower and slower, like a cooldown. On the last lap Ida blinks, looks around and says, "Goodness, I'd love a cinnamon roll." The Striders cheer, and you get a cinnamon roll too.
success.alone: You set a pace beside her and talk her down lap by lap, slower and slower, like a cooldown, while your legs scream. On the last lap Ida blinks, looks around and says, "Goodness, I'd love a cinnamon roll." The Striders cheer, and you get a cinnamon roll too.
success.art: A Puerto Rican woman in a racing wheelchair with an orange headband and a teenager pacing an elderly woman in a teal tracksuit along an empty mall concourse at dawn

failure.text: She speeds up to match you. For three laps you're both nearly running, and the plywood seems to lean out as you pass. A Strider finally catches Ida's arm and she sits, confused and exhausted, and you both get fanned with a food-court menu on the pretzel bench.
failure.art: An exhausted elderly woman and a panting teenager slumped on a mall bench at dawn, retirees in teal tracksuits fanning them with menus

choices.label: Look behind the plywood she keeps staring at

success.text: Through a gap you see the old Woolmart lunch counter and a faded sign for a 1983 seniors' special: walk ten laps, coffee's free. Ida worked that counter from the day the mall opened. You bring her a coffee in a paper cup, and she stops, takes it and says, "Oh, they finally remembered."
success.art: A teenager peering through a gap in plywood at a dusty abandoned department-store lunch counter with chrome stools, faint morning light

failure.text: Through the gap there's only dark, and then a pair of teal sneakers walking toward you inside, worn through to the socks. You stumble back. When you look at Ida again, she's walking the concourse in her stocking feet.
failure.art: A pair of worn teal sneakers walking by themselves across the dark floor of an abandoned department store, seen through a gap in plywood

choices.label: Talk your way into the PA closet and change the music

success.text: You talk the maintenance man into the PA closet and swap the bouncy tape for a slow-dance standard. Ida's pace drops to a stroll, then a sway, and then she's slow-dancing with a Strider named Herb by the fountain. She sits down afterward like nothing happened, and Herb tips you a quarter.
success.art: Two retirees in teal tracksuits slow dancing beside a mall fountain in early-morning light, other walkers applauding

failure.text: The only other tape in the closet is a marching-band album. Ida's laps get faster and crisper, and three more Striders fall in behind her, swinging their arms. It takes until opening to get them all to stop.
failure.art: A line of determined retirees in teal tracksuits marching briskly along a mall concourse, a teenager chasing after them with a cassette tape

name: The Glitter Box Playhouse
blurb: A converted 1920s vaudeville house: community theatre by day, drag revue by night and a Saturday midnight double feature. Sequins in every crack of the floorboards, and the bravest people in town.
art: A small ornate 1920s vaudeville theatre with a bulb-lit marquee reading drag revue and midnight double feature, gold paint peeling on the facade, a glass display case of sequined performer photos, afternoon sun on the sidewalk

beats.title: The Show Must Go On
beats.place: Backstage, The Glitter Box Playhouse
beats.text: Twenty minutes to curtain on the matinee revue and Miss Coco Mango has a broken heel, a bad back and a sold-out house. Glory Hallelujah's eyes land on you. "You know the choreography. Don't lie, I've seen you mouthing it in the wings for weeks." There's a sequined jumpsuit in your size, which is suspicious and also perfect.
beats.art: A chaotic theater dressing room twenty minutes before curtain, bulb-ringed mirrors and wig heads, a tall drag queen with a platinum bouffant wig in a pink feathered robe holding up a sparkling sequined jumpsuit to a startled teenager, another drag performer on a stool holding a broken high heel and pressing a hand to her back, warm bulb light, medium shot

choices.label: Take the stage and lip-sync for your life

success.text: You hit every beat, every hair flip, every dramatic collapse. The house roars. Miss Coco cheers from the wings with an ice pack on her back. Glory hugs you so hard sequins stick to your face for a week.
success.art: A teenager in a sparkling jumpsuit striking a dramatic pose center stage under a spotlight, an audience on its feet, a drag queen cheering from the wings

failure.text: You blank on the second verse and freeze. Then the audience starts singing it for you, all of them, every word, and you finish to a standing ovation for the worst performance in Glitter Box history. Glory says it was honestly the best kind.
failure.art: A frozen teenager in sequins on a theatre stage as the audience sings along with arms in the air, warm spotlight

choices.label: Talk Coco through it with a stool and a slower number

success.text: You rework the number into a torch song Coco can do sitting on a stool. She brings the house to tears. Afterward she presses a silver lame scrunchie into your hand. "For my stage manager. You've got an eye, baby."
success.art: A drag performer singing a torch song seated on a stool in a single spotlight, a teenager watching proudly from the wings holding a clipboard

failure.text: The rewrite doesn't come together in time, Coco goes on in pain, and Glory has to cover with a twelve-minute monologue about her divorce. The audience loves it. Coco does not. You owe her a heating pad.
failure.art: A drag queen in sequins delivering a long monologue to a laughing audience, a pained performer limping off in the background

beats.title: Reel Two Is Missing
beats.place: The projection booth, The Glitter Box Playhouse
beats.text: Saturday midnight double feature, and reel two of Attack of the 50-Foot Prom Queen has vanished from the booth. Frankie Fontaine has her headset on, a flashlight in her teeth and an audience of two hundred stamping their feet below. The empty film can is labeled in someone else's handwriting: BORROWED. BACK SOON.
beats.art: A cramped theater projection booth at midnight with a big old film projector, a 24-year-old trans woman stage manager with long dark curls in a high side ponytail, a black headset and a flashlight in her teeth, an empty round film can on the bench, a teenager searching a shelf, and through the small booth window an audience of two hundred stamping their feet below, projector glow and dark booth, medium shot

choices.label: Search the theatre for the missing reel

success.text: You find it in the balcony, seat M13, threaded neatly on its spool as if someone was holding it in their lap to watch. You rush it up to Frankie and the movie roars back to life. Seat M13 is empty, but the cushion is warm.
success.art: A film reel resting on a velvet theatre seat in a dark balcony, a teenager reaching for it, the projector beam cutting overhead

failure.text: You search every seat and every closet. When you come back to the booth, the reel is on the projector, already running. Frankie didn't put it there. The movie that plays is not the one on the label.
failure.art: A projector running in an empty booth, its beam throwing a strange flickering image on a distant screen, a teenager in the doorway

choices.label: Help Frankie rig the next film early

success.text: You and Frankie swap in the second feature on the fly, splice a cartoon in between, and the audience never knows. Frankie lets you announce the switch on the PA. Afterward she hands you a roll of tape and a headset. "You're crew now."
success.art: A stage manager and a teenager working side by side splicing film at a booth workbench, a cartoon flickering on the screen below

failure.text: The splice snaps, the film burns on screen in a bubbling brown blot, and the audience howls. Frankie keeps her cool, kills the lamp and leads a sing-along in the dark until the second feature is ready.
failure.art: A movie screen with burning celluloid melting in bubbles of light, an audience in the dark lit by lighters

beats.title: Two Signs on the Sidewalk
beats.place: The sidewalk outside the Glitter Box
beats.text: Two picketers are back on the sidewalk outside the matinee: a hard-jawed man with a sign that reads TURN BACK, and a teenage boy holding a sign he won't look at. Patrons are hesitating at the curb. The boy keeps glancing at the poster of the revue like it's a window he wants to climb through.
beats.art: A sunny sidewalk outside a sparkling vaudeville theater with a bulb-lit marquee, a stern hard-jawed man holding a protest placard on a stick, a teenage boy beside him holding his own placard limply at his side while staring at a glamorous painted billboard of drag performers in sequins, patrons hesitating at the curb, a teenager walking up to the boy, bright afternoon light, wide shot

choices.label: Quietly talk to the boy

success.text: His name is Caleb, and his dad drags him here every Saturday. While his dad is arguing with the usher, you slip him a program and tell him the stage door is always open on Thursdays. He folds it into his sock. He smiles, a tiny real one.
success.art: A teenager discreetly handing a folded theatre program to a nervous boy on a sidewalk, a man arguing with an usher in the background

failure.text: His dad sees you talking and drags Caleb away by the arm. Caleb looks back once. You don't know if you made his week better or worse. It sits in your chest all day.
failure.art: A man pulling a teenage boy away down a sidewalk by the arm, the boy looking back over his shoulder at a theatre

choices.label: Lead the line in a show-tune sing-along

success.text: You start the first line and the whole ticket line joins in: grandmothers, couples, a busload of theatre kids. The picketer's chant disappears under four-part harmony. Patrons stream in. Glory comes out to take a bow on the sidewalk.
success.art: A long line of theatregoers singing joyfully outside a theatre marquee, a drag queen bowing on the sidewalk, a picketer drowned out

failure.text: You get two lines in before your voice cracks, and the man laughs at you. The ticket line goes quiet. Then an old woman in a fur hat takes your hand and walks you to the door, head high, past him.
failure.art: An elderly woman in a fur hat leading a teenager by the hand past a picketer to a theatre door

beats.title: The Lady in M13
beats.place: The balcony, The Glitter Box Playhouse
beats.text: Everyone at the Glitter Box knows not to sell seat M13 in the balcony. It belongs to the Lady, a silent-film actress who opened here in 1926, who leaves a lipstick print on a program every closing night. This week there's no program on the seat, and the chandelier keeps swaying even when the doors are closed.
beats.art: A dim gilded theater balcony, rows of red velvet seats with one seat at the end of a row empty and softly lit, the faint translucent silhouette of a woman in a 1920s cloche hat and beaded dress sitting in it, a crystal chandelier swaying slightly overhead, a teenager sitting in the seat beside her with one hand resting on the armrest, gold and blue shadows, medium wide shot

choices.label: Leave her a program with a note

success.text: You leave a program on M13 with a note: The show's not the same without you. By the next morning the program has a perfect red lipstick print, and the chandelier is still. The house manager tips you two quarters for "keeping the Lady happy."
success.art: A theatre program on a velvet seat bearing a crisp red lipstick kiss, morning light through dusty balcony windows

failure.text: The program is torn in half by morning. The chandelier swings so hard during rehearsal that Frankie clears the stage. Somebody upset the Lady, and now the whole theatre has to apologize for it.
failure.art: A torn theatre program on a velvet seat, a crystal chandelier swinging wildly over a cleared stage

choices.label: Sit in M14 and ask her what's wrong

success.text: You sit beside her seat in the dark and wait. A cool hand rests on yours. A whisper: "They took my picture down from the lobby." You find it in the basement, dust it off and rehang it by the box office. The chandelier never sways again.
success.art: A teenager sitting in a dark theatre balcony with a translucent gloved hand resting on theirs, a framed old headshot of a 1920s actress in their lap

failure.text: You wait an hour in the dark. Nothing. Then, as you stand to go, a voice right behind your ear says "Shh, it's starting," and the stage lights snap on for a show nobody is performing.
failure.art: A dark empty theatre stage suddenly lit by spotlights on an empty stage, a teenager frozen in a balcony seat

beats.title: Letters on the Marquee
beats.place: The marquee ladder, The Glitter Box Playhouse, Saturday afternoon before the midnight double feature
beats.text: Frankie Fontaine hands you a crate of plastic letters and points up. Tonight's midnight double feature is ATTACK OF THE 50-FOOT PROM QUEEN and REVENGE OF THE ROLLER GHOULS, and the marquee has to say so by sundown. But every time you climb down for more letters, the ones already up have rearranged themselves. First it was COME IN. Then it was SIT TOGETHER. Now it just says TONIGHT, three times.
beats.art: A teenager on a tall ladder against the bulb-lit marquee of a 1920s vaudeville theater on a sunny Saturday afternoon, a plastic crate of marquee letter tiles hooked on the ladder, the tiles already on the board sliding around by themselves, a young woman in a black headset on the sidewalk pointing up with a frown, peeling gold paint on the facade, bright afternoon light, low angle shot

choices.label: Climb up and set the whole thing in one go

success.text: You haul the crate up the ladder and slam letters in faster than they can move, until both titles are up and spelled right. Frankie whoops from the sidewalk and slips you a quarter. The letters stay put, though at sundown the 50 in 50-FOOT looks suspiciously like it's winking.
success.art: A teenager atop a ladder slotting the last plastic letters into a theatre marquee at sunset, a woman in a headset cheering from the sidewalk

failure.text: The crate tips, and plastic letters rain down on the sidewalk like hail. When you gather them up, there are exactly enough to spell TONIGHT three times, and not one letter more. Frankie chalks the titles on a sandwich board by the door.
failure.art: Plastic marquee letters scattered across a theatre sidewalk at golden hour, a teenager on hands and knees gathering them, a tall ladder above

choices.label: Leave the letters be and work out what they want

success.text: You copy every message down and line them up: COME IN. SIT TOGETHER. TONIGHT. It's an invitation, not a threat. You add one line under the titles, ALL WELCOME, and the letters settle like a cat that's finally been understood. That night the line wraps around the block.
success.art: A theatre marquee glowing at dusk above a line of costumed moviegoers wrapping around the block, a teenager looking up with a notebook

failure.text: You stare at the marquee until your neck hurts, and the letters spell your name, then your street, then your house number. Frankie climbs up herself, pulls every letter, drops them in the crate and sits on the lid.
failure.art: A woman in a headset sitting firmly on the lid of a crate of marquee letters at the foot of a ladder, an empty marquee glowing above her

choices.label: Glue every letter down with Frankie's stage adhesive

success.text: Frankie mixes a glue she swears could hold a chandelier through an earthquake, and you slap every letter in place. They twitch, hard, then give up. At midnight she lets you announce the double feature over the lobby PA, which is the best ten seconds of your life.
success.alone: You find a tub of stage adhesive in the scene shop that could hold a chandelier through an earthquake, and you slap every letter in place. They twitch, hard, then give up. At midnight the house manager lets you announce the double feature over the lobby PA.
success.art: A young Portuguese American trans woman with dark curls and a headset and a teenager pressing glue-smeared letters into a theatre marquee from a ladder, afternoon sun

failure.text: The glue sets on your hands before it sets on the letters. You and Frankie spend an hour on the curb peeling it off your fingers while the marquee spells out HA HA, very slowly, above you.
failure.alone: The glue sets on your hands before it sets on the letters. You spend an hour on the curb peeling it off your fingers while the marquee spells out HA HA, very slowly, above you.
failure.art: A teenager and a woman in a headset sitting on a theatre curb peeling glue off their fingers, a glowing marquee above them

beats.title: The Mermaid Tail
beats.place: The costume-rental loft, The Glitter Box Playhouse
beats.text: Halloween week, the Glitter Box rents its costume loft to the whole town, and you're working the racks. A boy of about nine named Mateo has both hands pressed to a sequined mermaid tail like it's an aquarium. His mother keeps steering him toward the pirate rack, saying, "Something normal, mijo." Behind them, the tail's sequins ripple on the hanger, though every window in the loft is shut.
beats.art: A cluttered theater costume loft with racks of sequined gowns and capes, a nine-year-old boy pressing both hands against a shimmering green sequined mermaid tail on a hanger, its sequins rippling, his mother holding a plastic pirate hat toward him, a teenager behind the rental counter with a pincushion on their wrist, dusty skylight sun, medium wide shot

choices.label: Talk to his mom, gently

success.text: You tell her what Glory told you once: Halloween is the one night a year everyone gets to be what they love. She watches Mateo's face for a long moment, then sighs and pays for the tail. "He gets the pirate hat too," she says. He wears both, and the sequins go perfectly still.
success.art: A mother paying at a theatre costume counter while her son twirls in a shimmering mermaid tail and a pirate hat, a teenager smiling behind the register

failure.text: She thanks you stiffly and rents the pirate suit. Mateo doesn't argue. He just touches the tail once on his way out. That evening the tail is gone from its hanger, and you find it folded neatly on the loft steps, damp and smelling of the sea.
failure.art: A sequined mermaid tail folded neatly on the steps of a dim theatre loft, damp and glittering in a slant of evening light

choices.label: Pin and hem the tail so it fits him right now

success.text: You pin it on him in ninety seconds flat and he walks out of the dressing room glowing. His mother's whole argument dies in her throat when she sees his face. She pays and tips you a quarter for the tailoring. The tail's ripple settles into a contented shimmer.
success.art: A teenager kneeling with a pincushion hemming a sequined mermaid tail on a beaming nine-year-old boy, his mother softening in the dressing-room doorway

failure.text: You drop the pin box and half the sequins come off the hem in one long glittering ribbon. His mother takes it as a sign. "See? It's falling apart." They leave with the pirate suit, and you spend an hour picking sequins out of the floorboards.
failure.art: A teenager on hands and knees picking sequins out of old floorboards in a costume loft, a half-stripped mermaid tail on the counter

choices.label: Model the tail yourself and make it a fashion show

success.text: Glory hears the fuss, sweeps up the stairs and declares a fashion show. You flop down the aisle in the tail like a beached glamour queen while Glory narrates, and Mateo's mom laughs so hard she has to sit down. She rents him the tail. Glory hands you a can of Aqua-Glow Max Hold for commitment to the bit.
success.alone: You declare a fashion show and flop down the aisle between the racks in the tail like a beached glamour queen, narrating yourself. Mateo's mom laughs so hard she has to sit down. She rents him the tail. The loft manager hands you a can of Aqua-Glow Max Hold for commitment to the bit.
success.art: A teenager in a shimmering mermaid tail posing dramatically on the floor of a costume loft as a tall drag queen in a magenta sequin gown narrates with a feather fan, a mother and son laughing

failure.text: The sequins ripple up your legs and lock tight, and for one awful minute you can't stand up. Glory hauls you upright, and in the confusion Mateo's mom hustles him down the stairs with a pirate hat. "Next year, baby," Glory calls after him.
failure.alone: The sequins ripple up your legs and lock tight, and for one awful minute you can't stand up. In the confusion Mateo's mom hustles him down the stairs with a pirate hat. It takes you an hour to wriggle free.
failure.art: A teenager stuck in a tight mermaid tail on a costume-loft floor being hauled upright by a drag queen in a magenta sequin gown, a mother and boy heading down the stairs

name: St. Jude's and Pinecrest Cemetery
blurb: A stone church with a basement that hosts bingo, AA and punk band practice, and the cemetery out back: mausoleums, crooked oaks and the founders' graves on the hill, where the grass grows wrong.
art: A small stone church with a bell tower beside a hilly cemetery of crooked oaks, mausoleums and leaning headstones, fallen leaves, a groundskeeper's shed and a wrought-iron gate in late afternoon light

beats.title: Otis Lost the Key
beats.place: The groundskeeper's shed, Pinecrest Cemetery
beats.text: Otis Fenn has been groundskeeper at Pinecrest for forty years, and this morning he lost the key to the Whitcomb mausoleum. Not misplaced. Lost. It was on his ring at dusk and gone at dawn, and the mausoleum door, which was locked, is now standing an inch open.
beats.art: An old groundskeeper in faded overalls holding up a jangling key ring with one empty hook, a gray stone mausoleum behind him with its iron door standing an inch ajar, morning mist drifting among the leaning graves, a crow on the branch of an oak by the gate, a teenager beside him looking toward the door, cool gray morning light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Search the grounds for the key

success.text: You follow the trail of wet, tiny footprints from the shed to a crow's nest in the oak by the gate. The key is in it, along with bottle caps and a ring. Otis tips you three quarters and lets you keep the bottle caps.
success.art: A teenager reaching into a crow's nest in a cemetery oak, a shiny old key glinting among bottle caps, an old groundskeeper pointing from below

failure.text: The footprints lead to the mausoleum. Inside, the key is resting on a stone coffin lid, placed there neatly. When you pick it up, something inside the coffin knocks, twice, polite as a houseguest.
failure.art: A small brass key resting on a stone coffin lid inside a dark mausoleum, a teenager's hand reaching for it, light from the open door

choices.label: Push the mausoleum door shut and hold it

success.text: You put your shoulder to the iron door. It fights you, then slams. In the quiet afterward, the lost key drops from the lintel above into your hand, as if returned by someone who has decided you're all right.
success.art: A teenager straining with a shoulder against a heavy iron mausoleum door, a key falling from the stone lintel above

failure.text: The door pushes back. Hard. You land in the leaves, and the door swings open another inch. Otis helps you up and says, "Well, they want air, I suppose." He brings out a padlock and chain.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled in fallen leaves in front of a mausoleum, its iron door opened wider, an old groundskeeper bringing a chain

choices.label: Ask Father Iggy to bless the door first

success.text: Father Iggy shows up in a hand-painted punk band T-shirt and a stole, blesses the door, then the shed, then Otis, then you. The key turns up in Otis's coffee can. Iggy fills your squirt gun with holy water on the way out, no questions asked.
success.alone: You borrow a bottle of holy water from St. Jude's and bless the door yourself, then the shed, then Otis, then your own sneakers. The key turns up in Otis's coffee can. You fill your squirt gun with what's left of the holy water on the way out, no questions asked.
success.art: A young priest in a punk band T-shirt and a stole sprinkling holy water on a mausoleum door, a teenager holding out a squirt gun

failure.text: Iggy's blessing gets interrupted by a sudden gust of leaves that blows his prayer book shut. He laughs it off, but he walks you to the gate and tells you to stay off the hill after dark this week.
failure.alone: Your homemade blessing gets interrupted by a sudden gust of leaves that blows your borrowed prayer book shut. Otis laughs it off, but he walks you to the gate and tells you to stay off the hill after dark this week.
failure.art: A priest's prayer book snapped shut by a swirl of autumn leaves in a cemetery, the priest and a teenager shielding their faces

beats.title: B-13
beats.place: The church basement, St. Jude's
beats.text: Afternoon bingo in St. Jude's basement: folding tables, dabbers, a coffee urn and fifty serious grandmothers. The caller, a cheerful volunteer named Mrs. Petrakis, keeps calling numbers that aren't on anyone's card. B-13. B-13. B-13. She doesn't seem to notice. The grandmothers have noticed.
beats.art: A church basement on a weekday afternoon full of folding tables and fifty elderly women with paper bingo sheets and ink dabbers, a cheerful volunteer at a wire ball cage holding up one old wooden ball, every player looking up uneasily, a 71-year-old Black woman in a marigold headwrap squinting at the cage, a teenager at the end of a table with a dabber, a coffee urn steaming, fluorescent light, wide shot

choices.label: Play your card straight and win the pot

success.text: You dab every legitimate number and catch the caller's real calls between the B-13s. BINGO. The grandmothers applaud, the pot is four quarters and the B-13 calls stop the second you win, as if the game just wanted a winner.
success.art: A teenager standing up with a bingo card raised in triumph in a church basement, elderly women applauding, a stack of coins on the table

failure.text: Your card fills up with B-13 even though you never dabbed it. The ink is still wet. The grandmothers move their chairs away from you, politely. You lose.
failure.art: A bingo card covered in identical dabbed squares all marked B-13 in wet ink, elderly women edging their chairs away

choices.label: Check the bingo cage while nobody looks

success.text: Among the balls is one too many: an old wooden B-13 from the 1950s, carved by hand. Pearl Washington, at the next table, recognizes it: "That's from the quarry-workers' benefit night in '52. Lot of those men never came home." You hand it to the priest to keep safe.
success.alone: Among the balls is one too many: an old wooden B-13 from the 1950s, carved by hand. A grandmother at the next table recognizes it: "That's from the quarry-workers' benefit night in '52. Lot of those men never came home." You hand it to the priest to keep safe.
success.art: A teenager holding up a hand-carved wooden bingo ball beside a wire bingo cage, an elderly woman at the next table recognizing it

failure.text: You stick your hand in the cage and something cold closes around your fingers. You yank it out holding nothing, and all the balls in the cage now read B-13.
failure.art: A wire bingo cage full of balls all marked with the same number, a teenager clutching their hand, startled grandmothers

beats.title: The Name Chiseled Off
beats.place: The founders' hill, Pinecrest Cemetery
beats.text: Your history teacher assigned grave rubbings from the founders' hill. Six tall stones of the families who built Glimmer Falls in 1859, and a seventh, smaller, off to the side, its name chiseled away so hard there's a groove. The grass around it grows in a perfect circle, greener than anything else on the hill.
beats.art: A grassy cemetery hilltop on an autumn afternoon with six tall weathered founders' headstones in a row and one small stone set apart, its face gouged deep where a name used to be, a perfect ring of bright green grass around it, a teenager kneeling with paper and a charcoal stick, an olive-skinned goth teen in a plum velvet coat watching, low golden sun, wide shot

choices.label: Make a rubbing of the chiseled stone

success.text: The charcoal finds what the chisel missed: a faint name, a date in 1859 and a carved sprig of herbs. Raven, reading over your shoulder, says that whoever this was, the town wanted them forgotten. Now someone remembers.
success.alone: The charcoal finds what the chisel missed: a faint name, a date in 1859 and a carved sprig of herbs. Sitting back on your heels, you understand that whoever this was, the town wanted them forgotten. Now someone remembers.
success.art: A sheet of paper held against a small worn headstone, charcoal rubbing revealing a faint name, a date and a carved sprig of herbs, a goth teen peering over

failure.text: The rubbing comes out black, solid black, no matter how lightly you press. When you hold it up to the sun, there's a handprint in the middle of it, smaller than yours.
failure.art: A sheet of paper rubbed solid black with charcoal held up against a bright sky, a faint small handprint visible in the middle

choices.label: Pull the weeds and leave flowers

success.text: You clear the moss and leave a handful of wild chicory from the fence line. The green ring of grass shivers once in no wind. On the way down the hill, you feel lighter, like you did a favor for someone who doesn't get many.
success.art: A small bouquet of wildflowers resting at the base of a nameless headstone in a ring of green grass, a teenager walking away down a cemetery hill

failure.text: The weeds have roots like wire. You pull and pull and the ground pulls back. You fall into the founders' stones and scrape your palms. The green ring is wider than it was when you came.
failure.art: A teenager fallen against tall weathered founders' headstones with scraped palms, a ring of bright green grass spreading across a cemetery hill

beats.title: Nobody Came
beats.place: The chapel, St. Jude's
beats.text: Father Iggy is about to say a funeral mass for Mrs. Edna Lowry, ninety-four, no family, no friends left alive. The pews are empty. He catches you in the doorway and asks, quietly, if you'd stay. As you sit, the guestbook on the stand by the door starts filling with names, one by one, in different handwritings.
beats.art: An empty stone church chapel at midday, a single closed casket with a spray of roses at the altar, a 31-year-old Filipino American priest with a black spiked pompadour in white vestments standing at the front, a teenager sitting alone in a wooden pew, and by the door a guestbook on a stand with a pen writing by itself across its pages, colored light through stained glass, wide shot

choices.label: Stay, and say something kind about her

success.text: You didn't know Mrs. Lowry, but you read the obituary and you tell the empty church she grew roses that won the county fair four times. Every candle flickers at once. The guestbook has forty names now. Iggy hugs you at the door.
success.art: A teenager speaking at a church lectern to empty pews, every candle on the altar flaring at once, a priest bowing his head

failure.text: You stand to speak and your words dry up. The silence stretches. Then, in the back, the pew creaks under a weight nobody can see, and someone softly starts to hum a hymn. You sit back down and let them.
failure.art: An empty church pew in the back of a chapel, its cushion dented under an invisible weight, a teenager at the front turning to look

choices.label: Read the names in the guestbook

success.text: The names are all from the 1952 quarry collapse: workers, a foreman, a water boy. Iggy reads them aloud at the end of the mass. Mrs. Lowry, it turns out, was the town telephone operator who called every family that night.
success.art: A priest reading aloud from an old guestbook at the altar of an empty chapel, a teenager beside him holding the book open

failure.text: The names start appearing faster than you can read, filling page after page, until the pen by the book rolls off the stand and lands at your feet. You pick it up. Something wants you to sign.
failure.art: A guestbook overflowing with handwriting on a stand by a chapel door, a pen lying at a teenager's feet

beats.title: The Eleven O'Clock Folk Mass
beats.place: The nave and organ loft, St. Jude's, Sunday morning
beats.text: Sunday at St. Jude's means Father Iggy's folk mass: two acoustic guitars, a bongo and a tambourine player who is home with the flu. Iggy presses the tambourine into your hands before you can object. Then the first hymn starts, and up in the loft the old pipe organ, silent since the organist retired in 1979, joins in on one low, held note. The pews hum under everyone's knees.
beats.art: A small stone church nave on a sunny Sunday morning, a young Filipino American priest with a spiked pompadour playing an acoustic guitar beside two parishioners on guitar and bongo, a teenager at the front holding a tambourine, the congregation clapping in the pews, and high in the dim loft an old pipe organ with its brass pipes glowing faintly and an empty bench, sunbeams through stained glass, wide shot

choices.label: Play the tambourine like it's a stadium show

success.text: You find the beat, then you find the congregation, and by the second verse fifty parishioners are clapping on two and four. The organ's low note climbs, wobbles and slides into the right key, like it just wanted to be in the band. Iggy mouths "Hired" from the altar.
success.art: A teenager shaking a tambourine high overhead in a church aisle, smiling parishioners clapping along, a young priest grinning over his guitar

failure.text: On the big chorus the tambourine slips out of your hand, sails over the front pew and lands in the holy water font with a jingling splash. The organ lets out one long, low note that sounds exactly like a sigh. A grandmother in the second row pats your arm.
failure.art: A tambourine splashing into a stone holy water font at the front of a church, startled parishioners turning in their pews, a teenager covering their face

choices.label: Slip up the spiral stairs to see who's playing

success.text: The loft is empty. A gray cardigan hangs on the organ bench, and a fat old hymnal has slid onto the lowest pedal. You lift it off, the note stops, and you play the hymn's last chord with one careful finger. The church below thinks it was planned. In the cardigan pocket is a wrapped peppermint, and somehow it feels like a thank-you.
success.art: An empty church organ loft with a gray cardigan draped on the bench, a teenager lifting a heavy hymnal off a wooden organ pedal, dusty sunbeams through a round stained-glass window

failure.text: Halfway up the spiral stairs, the note stops. At the top, the organ bench is warm, the cardigan is gone, and the hymnal on the music stand is open to a hymn for the dead, with your street's name penciled lightly in the margin. You take the stairs back down two at a time.
failure.art: A narrow stone spiral staircase in a church tower, a teenager peering up toward a shadowy organ loft, an open hymnal on a music stand lit by one slanting sunbeam

choices.label: Check the organ's bellows in the basement

success.text: Down past the bingo tables, the organ's big leather bellows is wheezing with its motor switched off. Behind it, a family of mice has built a nest of shredded bingo cards right in the wind valve. You move the nest into a shoebox, the note upstairs stops mid-hymn, and the old sexton gives you two quarters from his own coin purse.
success.art: A church basement with folding bingo tables, a teenager carrying a shoebox of tiny mice away from a huge old leather organ bellows, an elderly sexton smiling with a coin purse

failure.text: The bellows is breathing. Its motor is unplugged, the cord coiled neatly on the floor, and the great leather lung swells and settles, swells and settles, in time with the hymn upstairs. When you step closer, it holds its breath. You decide the basement can keep its secrets.
failure.art: A huge old leather organ bellows swelling in a dim church basement, its unplugged cord coiled on the stone floor, a teenager backing slowly toward the stairs

beats.title: The Angel Moves at Night
beats.place: The children's section, Pinecrest Cemetery
beats.text: Otis Fenn swears the marble angel from the 1902 Halloran plot stood ten rows deeper in the cemetery last Monday. Every morning this week it's a little closer to the front gate, and every morning it faces a little more toward Crystal Street. It weighs half a ton. There are no drag marks in the grass, only a trail of small, perfect footprints pressed into the dew.
beats.art: A weathered half-ton marble angel statue with folded wings and green moss streaks under its eyes standing among small leaning children's headstones near a wrought-iron cemetery gate, a line of small perfect footprints pressed into the morning dew behind it, an old groundskeeper in overalls scratching his head, a teenager kneeling with a stick of chalk at its base, pale morning mist, wide shot

choices.label: Chalk a ring around its base and keep watch

success.text: You chalk the base, stretch a string from the statue to the gate and sit in Otis's shed doorway with a thermos until the light goes orange. It never budges while anyone watches, but the string's angle tells the story: it isn't heading out the gate. It's heading for the Heartstone, like a mourner walking to a grave. You write that down.
success.art: A teenager kneeling to draw a chalk ring around the base of a marble angel statue, a ball of string stretched from the statue to an iron gate, late afternoon light

failure.text: You chalk the ring, look down to cap your chalk and look up again. The angel is outside the ring now, a full step closer to you, its marble hand lifted a little higher than before. Otis says, very calmly, that it's time for both of you to get some lunch somewhere else.
failure.art: A marble angel statue standing one step outside a chalk ring on the grass with its stone hand slightly raised, a startled teenager and an old groundskeeper backing away

choices.label: Scrub the moss streaks off its face

success.text: Green moss has run down from the angel's eyes like tear tracks. You scrub them clean with Otis's bucket and brush, and under the grime the plaque on its base comes clear: FOR OUR LITTLE BRIDGET, WHO LOVED THE LAKE. When you finish, the stone face looks less sad, and it stays exactly where it is all day.
success.art: A teenager on a stepladder gently scrubbing green moss from the face of a marble angel statue, a bucket of soapy water below, a small brass plaque on the base gleaming

failure.text: The moss comes off, then comes back while you watch, two green lines running fresh down the marble cheeks. Your brush water turns as cold as a lake in November. You leave the bucket behind, and when you glance back from the gate, the angel's head has turned to follow you.
failure.art: Fresh green moss streaks running down the cheeks of a marble angel statue, an abandoned bucket and scrub brush at its base, a teenager glancing back from a cemetery gate

choices.label: Have Raven lay a tarot spread on its pedestal

success.text: Raven lays three cards on the pedestal with enormous ceremony: the Star, the Six of Cups, the World. "It's homesick," they say. "Six of Cups is childhood. It wants to go back to the water it remembers." A single dry leaf settles on the World card like a finger pointing. Knowing what it wants makes the whole hill feel kinder.
success.art: A goth teen in thrifted velvet laying three tarot cards on the pedestal of a marble angel statue, a single dry leaf drifting onto the middle card, autumn oaks behind
success.alone: You lay three cards from a borrowed deck on the pedestal with enormous ceremony: the Star, the Six of Cups, the World. The little booklet says the Six of Cups means childhood and going home. It's homesick, you realize, for water it remembers. A single dry leaf settles on the World card like a finger pointing.

failure.text: Every card Raven turns over is the same card, the Tower, and on the fourth flip they gather the deck up fast and wrap it in black silk. "Nope," Raven says. "Not today. We ask again when it's in a better mood." The angel's shadow is lying across both of you, though the sun is on the other side.
failure.art: Four identical tarot cards showing a lightning-struck tower on a marble pedestal, a goth teen wrapping a deck in black silk, a long statue shadow falling across them
failure.alone: Every card you turn over from your borrowed deck is the same card, the Tower, and on the fourth flip you gather the deck up fast and stuff it in your pocket. Not today. You'll ask again when it's in a better mood. The angel's shadow is lying across you, though the sun is on the other side.

name: KGLM 103.3 and the Water Tower
blurb: A cinderblock radio station on the hill under the town water tower, all blinking consoles and a call-in line that rings a little too late at night. Climb the tower ladder and you can see the whole valley.
art: A small cinderblock radio station on a grassy hilltop beneath a tall round water tower painted Glimmer Falls, a red-blinking transmitter antenna, a pickup truck parked outside, golden afternoon light over the valley

beats.title: Line Three
beats.place: The broadcast booth, KGLM 103.3
beats.text: Mix Bell is covering the afternoon show before his overnight shift and lets you sit in, and line three lights up. The caller asks for a song from 1958 in a voice full of bubbles, like she's calling from under water. The light on the console says the call is coming from the old quarry pay phone, which was flooded and removed in 1959.
beats.art: A small radio booth on a rainy afternoon, a 17-year-old Black DJ with a high-top fade, big padded headphones and a purple satin station jacket at the console, a teenager beside him holding up a dusty 1958 seven-inch record pulled from a crate, a single call-line button blinking on the phone, beads of water collecting on the phone and rain streaking the window, gray window light and warm console glow, medium shot

choices.label: Find the record and play her song

success.text: You find the single in the station's dusty archive and Mix spins it on air. The caller sighs, happy, and the line clicks off. For the rest of the afternoon, every radio on Crystal Street plays a little warmer. Mix gives you the record.
success.art: A teenager handing a vintage vinyl single to a DJ in a radio booth, the record spinning on a turntable, a call button going dark

failure.text: You can't find the record. Mix plays something close and the caller goes very quiet, then says "That's not it" in a voice right next to your ear instead of in the headphones. The whole console fizzes.
failure.art: A radio console sparking with static in a dim booth, two teens leaning away from a microphone, a blinking call line

choices.label: Keep her talking on air

success.text: You ask her name, Lillian, and her favorite dance, the stroll. She tells you about the lake before it drained, the dock, the boy she was meeting. The town hears her on air. A dozen old folks call in to say they remember her. The line clicks off kindly.
success.art: A teenager speaking gently into a radio microphone, a phone board lighting up with incoming calls, an old photo of a lakeside dock taped to the wall

failure.text: You ask the wrong question. "Where are you?" The bubbles get louder, the line fills with rushing water, and the booth's floor is suddenly wet. Mix pulls the plug. The puddle doesn't dry for a day.
failure.art: A radio booth floor with a spreading puddle of dark water around the chair legs, a DJ yanking a cord from the console

beats.title: Halfway Up the Tower
beats.place: The water tower ladder, above KGLM
beats.text: A kid named Jun climbed the water tower to paint his crush's initials on the tank, and now he's stuck forty feet up, clinging to a ladder rung that's peeling away from the rivets. Below him is a can of red spray paint, dented. Above him, painted by someone else, letters older than both of you: GO BACK.
beats.art: A boy of about twelve clinging to a rusty ladder high on the side of a round water tower above a grassy hilltop, one rung peeling away from its rivets under his hands, a dented can of red spray paint on the ground far below, faded old painted marks on the tank above him, a teenager starting up the ladder from the base and a small cinderblock radio station beside the tower, golden afternoon light, low angle shot

choices.label: Climb up and guide his feet down

success.text: You climb, steady and slow, and talk about anything else: cartoons, cereal, his crush. You guide his sneakers rung by rung. At the bottom, he tells you the crush is a boy named Eli, and he's going to tell him with words instead of paint.
success.art: A teenager on a water tower ladder guiding a younger boy's sneaker onto a rung below, sunset behind them, the valley spread out far below

failure.text: The rung snaps under your hand and for one long second you're both hanging. Mix comes running with a rope from the station and gets you both down. Jun is okay. Your hands shake until dinner.
failure.art: A snapped ladder rung falling through the air beside a water tower, two figures clinging to the ladder, a DJ running with a coil of rope

choices.label: Run inside and get on air for help

success.text: You grab the mic and ask anyone with a ladder truck to come to the KGLM hill. Within ten minutes three pickups and the volunteer fire department show up. Jun comes down in a bucket. The whole valley heard you save him.
success.art: A fire department ladder truck extended to a water tower, a boy climbing into its bucket, pickup trucks and onlookers gathered on the hill

failure.text: Your voice goes out on dead air, the transmitter hiccuping static, and nobody hears. By the time you run back out, Jun has climbed down himself, pale and furious, and the words on the tank above now read GO BACK NOW.
failure.art: A pale boy standing at the base of a water tower glaring at a teenager, painted letters high on the tank reading go back now

beats.title: Be Caller Thirteen
beats.place: A pay phone outside the Quik-Stop, then KGLM
beats.text: KGLM is giving away two tickets to the Halloween night Thrash Bash at the fairgrounds to caller number thirteen. Every phone in town is ringing the station. You've got one quarter, a pay phone and a busy signal. The busy signal, if you listen closely, is counting.
beats.art: A teenager at a strip-mall pay phone on a bright afternoon pressing the receiver to one ear and holding a single quarter ready, finger on the hook, a convenience store glowing behind them, a parked car nearby with its windows down and its dashboard radio on, a bicycle leaning on the phone post, long late-day shadows, medium shot

choices.label: Redial with lightning fingers

success.text: Eleven. Twelve. You hit the hook, redial, and Mix's voice says "Caller thirteen, you're on KGLM!" You win the tickets, which you sell to Wade for three quarters and a ride wherever you want this week.
success.art: A teenager shouting with joy into a pay phone receiver, fist in the air, a convenience store parking lot at dusk

failure.text: You get through, but you're caller fourteen. Mix sounds sorry. Then, behind him, a different voice on the line says "I'll take thirteen" and the call drops. On air, the winner never gives a name.
failure.art: A pay phone receiver dangling on its cord at a lonely strip-mall wall, a teenager staring at it

choices.label: Skip the phone and bike to the station

success.text: You pedal up the KGLM hill like your life depends on it and barge through the door just as the twelfth caller hangs up. Mix laughs so hard he lets you win in person. Also, he gives you a station mixtape for pure nerve.
success.art: A sweaty teenager bursting through a radio station door with a bike behind them, a DJ in the booth doubling over laughing

failure.text: The hill is steeper than you remember. You arrive gasping as the winner is announced, then coast all the way back down with no brakes and land in a hedge. The radio in the hedge-owner's kitchen is playing your heavy breathing on air.
failure.art: A teenager tangled in a hedge beside a crashed bicycle, a kitchen window above with a radio on the sill

beats.title: Live From Sal's Mattress Kingdom
beats.place: The production booth, KGLM 103.3
beats.text: The station manager's voice talent quit, and Sal's Mattress Kingdom's Halloween Spooktacular ad runs live in ninety seconds. The copy is three pages of puns. The manager shoves it at you. The microphone has a little piece of tape on it that says DON'T SAY IT THREE TIMES, and nobody will tell you what IT is.
beats.art: A cluttered radio production booth, a vintage silver microphone with a strip of masking tape wrapped around its neck, a panicked station manager in a short-sleeved shirt and loose tie shoving three pages of ad copy at a teenager, a red on-air bulb above the door about to light, a wall clock ticking toward the hour, fluorescent light and red glow, medium shot

choices.label: Read the copy like your life depends on it
