success.text: "At Sal's, our prices are SO LOW, they're SIX FEET UNDER!" You nail every pun. Sal himself calls the station crying with joy. You get four quarters and a lifetime offer of a free mattress, which you decline, because nobody should own a free mattress from Sal.
success.art: A teenager leaning into a microphone with dramatic gestures in a radio booth, a station manager giving a thumbs-up through the glass

failure.text: You say "Spooktacular" three times without thinking. The on-air light flickers, the tape on the mic peels off by itself and the ad finishes in a voice that is not yours. Sal loves it. You don't sleep well.
failure.art: A strip of tape peeling off a microphone by itself in a dim radio booth, an on-air light flickering red

choices.label: Rewrite it fast into something less cursed

success.text: You cut every Spooktacular and write a jingle on the spot. Sal's sales double. The station manager pins your copy on the wall and asks if you want a job writing ads. The tape on the mic is quietly replaced with fresh tape.
success.art: A teenager scribbling furiously on a page of ad copy in a radio booth, a station manager reading over their shoulder delighted

failure.text: You run out of time mid-rewrite and read half of each version. The ad makes no sense, Sal threatens to sue and the manager pays you in mints. Somewhere in the transmitter, something laughs once.
failure.art: A station manager angrily on the phone in a radio office, a teenager slumped holding a crumpled page and a handful of mints

beats.title: Martians Over Glimmer Falls
beats.place: The production booth, KGLM 103.3, Halloween afternoon
beats.text: For Halloween, the station manager is re-staging the famous 1938 Martian-invasion radio play at six o'clock with local voices, and you've been cast as the reporter at the crash site. During the afternoon rehearsal, the old teletype in the corner starts chattering on its own. It's typing your lines a beat before you read them. Then it types one that isn't in the script: LIGHTS OVER CRYSTAL STREET. LOOK UP.
beats.art: A cramped radio production booth on Halloween afternoon, a teenager at a microphone holding a script and a pair of headphones, a vintage teletype machine in the corner chattering on its own and spitting a long curl of paper onto the floor, the station manager frozen with a sound-effects board, and through the window behind a hilltop water tower against an orange Halloween sky with three pale lights above the valley, wide shot

choices.label: Ham it up and finish the rehearsal on script

success.text: You give the crash-site reporter everything: the gasps, the crackle, the "Ladies and gentlemen, it's indescribable!" The teletype goes quiet to listen. When you finish, it types one word, APPLAUSE, then a perfectly normal weather report. The station manager says you're the best Martian victim KGLM has ever had.
success.art: A teenager dramatically clutching a radio microphone with wide eyes mid-scream, a station manager in shirtsleeves applauding, a teletype quietly printing behind them

failure.text: You flub the big line, and the teletype finishes it for you in capital letters, then keeps going: a second reporter, a second crash site, an address on Crystal Street. The station manager tears the paper off, laughing too loudly. "Kids," he says, and locks the roll in a drawer.
failure.art: A long curl of teletype paper spilling across a radio booth floor, a station manager laughing nervously as he tears it off, a teenager staring at the printed words

choices.label: Climb the water tower and look up

success.text: From the top of the tower the whole valley is gold and orange. Over Crystal Street, three pale lights hang in a perfect triangle, then drift apart and wink out one by one, as if they only wanted to be noticed. You climb down steady and tell Mix, who puts the sighting on air as a Halloween bonus. The phones light up with people who saw them too.
success.art: A teenager on the catwalk of a hilltop water tower at golden hour gazing at three pale lights in a triangle above a suburban cul-de-sac far below

failure.text: Halfway up the ladder, every radio in the station below blares the same Martian sound effect at once, and you freeze with both arms locked around a rung. By the time your hands work again, the sky is ordinary and empty. Mix helps you down and pretends he can't tell you're shaking.
failure.art: A teenager clinging tight to the rungs of a water tower ladder, a small cinderblock radio station below with its door flung open, an empty orange evening sky

choices.label: Unspool the teletype roll back to the start

success.text: You unroll the paper across the whole booth. Hidden in the gibberish, every thirteenth letter spells a sentence: WE ARE ONLY LISTENING. You show Mix, who decides he'll end tonight's broadcast by saying hello back. It feels like the most polite thing anyone has said to the sky all week.
success.art: A long strip of teletype paper unrolled across a radio station floor, a teenager on hands and knees circling letters with a red pencil, a young DJ with headphones leaning over to look
success.alone: You unroll the paper across the whole booth. Hidden in the gibberish, every thirteenth letter spells a sentence: WE ARE ONLY LISTENING. You leave a note for tonight's announcer: end the broadcast by saying hello back. It feels like the most polite thing anyone has said to the sky all week.

failure.text: The paper goes back much farther than today. At the very start of the roll, dated October 31, 1938, someone typed a single line: SEE YOU IN FORTY-EIGHT YEARS. You count it on your fingers twice. Then you roll the paper back up and decide you're bad at math.
failure.art: A teenager holding the yellowed start of a teletype roll under a desk lamp, an old radio station console glowing behind them

beats.title: Play It Backward
beats.place: The record library, KGLM 103.3
beats.text: A committee of Concerned Parents has marched up the KGLM hill with a petition and a cardboard box. In the box: every heavy metal album in the station library, plus Mix's whole Glitter Box disco set, which they call "a gateway." They insist the records hide satanic messages when played backward. The station manager is sweating. Mix is very, very calm, which is how you know he's furious.
beats.art: A wood-paneled radio station record library lined with album shelves, a group of stern parents in cardigans and windbreakers holding a clipboard and a cardboard box full of vinyl records, a 17-year-old Black DJ with headphones around his neck standing calmly with folded arms, a sweating station manager between them, a teenager at a turntable with one hand on the platter, warm overhead light, wide shot

choices.label: Play the "evidence" backward, live on air

success.text: You drop the needle, spin the platter backward by hand and lean into the mic. Out comes a slurry of garbled vowels that, if you squint, says "Pass the potato salad." The committee's leader turns pink. Half the parents start laughing, and one admits she owns that album. The box goes back on the shelf.
success.art: A teenager spinning a vinyl record backward by hand on a radio station turntable, red-faced parents in cardigans, one mother laughing behind her clipboard

failure.text: You spin it backward and, under the garble, a voice that isn't on the record says your name, slowly, twice. The committee gasps in triumph. The station manager pulls the plug and agrees to "review the library." Mix doesn't blame you, but the box spends the night in the manager's office.
failure.art: A record turntable in a radio station with its tonearm lifted, a teenager recoiling from the speaker, stern parents leaning forward with satisfied expressions

choices.label: Sit down with the parents and actually listen

success.text: You ask what they're afraid of, and it all spills out: kids who don't talk at dinner, a son who locks his door, the evening news. You tell them these records are how half the kids you know find each other. One dad goes quiet, then asks Mix the name of the dance song his daughter plays. The committee leaves with its petition unsigned.
success.art: A teenager on a stool talking earnestly with a small group of parents in a radio station library, one father listening thoughtfully, a young DJ writing down a song title for him

failure.text: You try, but the committee's leader talks over you, then over Mix, then over the station manager, until he signs a promise to "keep it wholesome" just to make it stop. The box goes into the back of a station wagon. Mix spends the afternoon taping a new show called Requests Nobody Can Ban.
failure.art: A cardboard box of vinyl records being loaded into the back of a wood-paneled station wagon, a young DJ watching from the radio station steps with his jaw set

choices.label: Smuggle the box out to the tower shed

success.text: While everyone argues about the devil, you walk the box out the back door, across the gravel and into the padlocked shed under the water tower. When the committee goes looking, the shelves have a suspiciously tidy gap. Mix slips you two quarters and a wink: "Lost in the archive. Tragic."
success.art: A teenager sneaking across a gravel lot carrying a heavy cardboard box of records toward a small shed beneath a towering water tank, a radio station back door ajar behind them

failure.text: The box bottom gives out halfway across the gravel, and forty albums fan out at the feet of the committee's leader. She picks up a disco record in a sequined sleeve and holds it up like evidence at a trial. The station manager makes you carry them all back in, one by one, while she watches.
failure.art: Dozens of vinyl albums scattered across a gravel lot, a stern woman with a clipboard holding up a glittering record sleeve, a teenager kneeling among the records

name: Rusty's Junkyard
blurb: Acres of rust behind a chain-link fence: a maze of stacked cars three high, a crusher that groans like a whale, Joey Benally's cinderblock garage, and a basset hound who howls before trouble arrives.
art: A sprawling junkyard of rusted 1950s and 1970s cars stacked in towering rows behind a chain-link fence, a hulking car crusher, a cinderblock garage with tools hanging outside, a basset hound napping by the gate in hazy afternoon sun

beats.title: The Car Maze
beats.place: The stacks, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Joey Benally needs a hubcap off a '57 Bel Royale somewhere in the car maze, and he'll pay three quarters for it. The stacks are three cars high, the paths fork every twenty feet, and the junkyard maps never agree. Barnaby the basset hound plants himself at the entrance and refuses to go one step farther.
beats.art: A towering maze of rusted 1950s and 1970s cars stacked three high in a junkyard, narrow dirt paths forking into shadow, chalk arrows on a fender at the first turn, a teenager standing at the entrance with a piece of chalk, a tricolor basset hound with long ears and a red bandana sitting stubbornly beside them, a lean Diné teenager in an orange work shirt pointing into the maze, hard afternoon sun and deep shadows, wide shot

choices.label: Go in with a plan and a chalk mark at every turn

success.text: Chalk arrow, chalk arrow, Bel Royale. You pop the hubcap, follow your arrows back out and hand it to Joey, who nods his highest compliment: "Not bad." Three quarters, and he lets you sit in the garage and drink his good soda.
success.art: A teenager holding up a gleaming chrome hubcap in a junkyard maze, chalk arrows marked on the rusted cars behind them

failure.text: Your chalk arrows are pointing the wrong way when you turn around. All of them. The path behind you is a wall of cars that wasn't there. You walk for an hour, and come out somewhere the maze shouldn't lead.
failure.art: A narrow junkyard path where every chalk arrow on the rusted cars points back the way a lost teenager came, a dead end of stacked cars ahead

choices.label: Coax Barnaby along and follow his nose

success.text: With half a hot dog and a lot of praise, Barnaby leads you on a crooked path that avoids every place he growls at. The Bel Royale is right where he finally sits down. Moral of the story: always trust the dog.
success.art: A basset hound leading a teenager through a junkyard car maze, nose to the ground, a classic chrome car at the end of the path

failure.text: Barnaby leads you in, then stops, howls and bolts. You're alone in the stacks, and somewhere ahead, a car door creaks open and slams. You leave without the hubcap and Joey says, "Yeah, the dog knows."
failure.art: A basset hound running away down a junkyard path with ears flying, a teenager alone between towering stacks of rusted cars

beats.title: Something in the Trunk
beats.place: The crusher, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Rusty is about to drop a 1959 Cadwell into the crusher, and from the trunk comes a knock. Three slow knocks. Rusty can't hear it over the engine and won't stop the job for "a teenager's imagination." The crusher plates are already grinding open like the jaws of something hungry.
beats.art: A hulking junkyard car crusher with its steel plates grinding open, a crane lowering a pink 1959 tail-finned sedan toward it, its trunk lid rattling, a gruff old man in a trucker cap in the operator's seat, a teenager waving both arms frantically at the edge of the pit, a lean teenager in an orange work shirt running toward the control panel, dust and diesel smoke, bright afternoon sun, wide shot

choices.label: Climb onto the Cadwell and pop the trunk

success.text: You leap onto the tailfin and yank the trunk open. A family of raccoons pours out, along with a dusty steel box: a 1959 time capsule from the Glimmer Falls Elementary class, never buried. Rusty stops the crane and turns very red. He pays you not to tell anyone.
success.art: A teenager clinging to the tailfin of a pink 1959 car dangling from a crane, the trunk open, raccoons tumbling out with a dusty metal box

failure.text: You slip off the bumper and hit the dirt hard. The Cadwell drops into the crusher. The knocking stops before the plates close. You'll never know. That's the worst part.
failure.art: A teenager lying in junkyard dirt looking up at a crushed pink car between steel plates, dust hanging in the air

choices.label: Get Joey to make Rusty shut it down

success.text: Joey walks up, turns the key in the crusher's panel himself and says "Hear that?" Rusty finally hears the knocking. Inside the trunk: an old radio still tuned to KGLM, playing a station ID from 1959. Rusty gives it to you, spooked.
success.alone: You walk up, turn the key in the crusher's panel yourself and say "Hear that?" Rusty finally hears the knocking. Inside the trunk: an old radio still tuned to KGLM, playing a station ID from 1959. Rusty gives it to you, spooked.
success.art: A young mechanic with a key in a crusher control panel, a gruff junkyard owner staring at an opened vintage car trunk revealing a glowing vintage radio

failure.text: Rusty brushes you both off and drops the Cadwell. As the plates close, every car radio in the junkyard switches on at once to the same song, and then off. Rusty shuts down for the day without a word.
failure.art: Dozens of junked car dashboards lighting up at once across a dusk junkyard, a crushed vintage car in the crusher

beats.title: Pay by the Pound
beats.place: The scrap scale, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Rusty pays by the pound for copper and aluminum, and the old station wagons at the back are full of it. You have a wagon, a pair of pliers and the whole afternoon. The trouble is the back of the lot, where the wagons are parked in a circle facing inward, like they're having a meeting.
beats.art: A teenager pulling a rusty little red wagon heaped with copper wire and crushed aluminum cans through a junkyard, passing a circle of old wood-paneled station wagons parked nose to nose facing inward, one with its dashboard radio glowing, a pair of pliers in the teen's back pocket, long late-afternoon shadows and golden light, wide shot

choices.label: Strip wire fast and haul it to the scale

success.text: Two full wagonloads. Rusty weighs it, grumbles and pays you four quarters. In the last wagon you find a pair of walkie-talkies still in the box. Nobody's going to miss them.
success.art: A grimy, grinning teenager beside a junkyard scale stacked with copper wire, holding up a boxed pair of walkie-talkies

failure.text: You cut the wrong wire in the third wagon and every horn in the circle honks at once. You drop everything and run. When you go back for your wagon, it's parked in the middle of the circle, with them.
failure.art: A little red wagon sitting in the middle of a circle of old station wagons facing inward, headlights on in daylight

choices.label: Find the working radio and hum along while you work

success.text: One of the wagons has a radio that still works. You hum along, the circle of cars seems to settle, and the job goes easy. The radio's dial is stuck on a station that doesn't exist, playing a weather report for October 31, 1986. You write it down.
success.art: A teenager humming while stripping wire in the open door of a wood-paneled station wagon, its dashboard radio glowing, other cars around it

failure.text: You hum, and the radio hums back, a half-beat behind, in your voice. You haul one load and leave the rest. Rusty pays you a quarter and asks why you look like you saw a ghost.
failure.art: A junkyard car radio glowing alone on a dashboard in an empty car, a teenager walking briskly away with a half-empty wagon

beats.title: Wade's Van Won't Start
beats.place: Joey's garage, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Wade Whitfield's van, a black panel van with a wizard airbrushed on the side, won't start, and tonight is open-mic night at the Glitter Box. He's never read a poem out loud before. He's been trying to back out for a week, and now the van is giving him the excuse. He doesn't look relieved.
beats.art: An 18-year-old with a long feathered dirty-blond mullet and a patched denim vest slumped against a black custom van with a wizard airbrushed on its side, the hood propped open, a crumpled spiral notebook in his hand, a teenager leaning into the engine with a wrench, a cinderblock garage behind them with tools hanging outside, dusk light, medium shot

choices.label: Get under the hood and fix it

success.text: It's the starter. You tap it with a wrench the way Joey taught you, and the van roars. Wade looks at the notebook, then at you. "Guess I gotta go now." He doesn't go up, not tonight, but he sits in the front row with the notebook on his knee and claps for every poet who does.
success.art: A teenager with a wrench under a van's hood as the engine roars to life, a metalhead in the driver's seat grinning nervously, a notebook on the dash

failure.text: You fix the starter and break the alternator. Joey sighs and promises to have it running by next week. Wade says "There's always next open mic," and you both know that's the excuse winning.
failure.alone: You fix the starter and break the alternator. You sigh and promise to have it running by next week. Wade says "There's always next open mic," and you both know that's the excuse winning.
failure.art: A young mechanic sighing at a smoking van engine, a metalhead and a teenager standing beside it in the evening light

choices.label: Give him a ride on your handlebars

success.text: Two miles on handlebars with a six-foot metalhead is not a ride, it's a sport. You make it to the Glitter Box with three minutes to spare. Wade doesn't go up, not tonight, but he mouths along with every poet who does, and when Glory squeezes his shoulder he almost cries.
success.art: A teenager pedaling a bicycle with a long-haired metalhead perched on the handlebars clutching a notebook, a sparkling theatre marquee ahead at dusk

failure.text: You hit a pothole on Elm and both go down. Wade's notebook goes into a storm drain. He sits on the curb a long time, then starts reciting the poem from memory to you, right there. It's good. He still doesn't go.
failure.art: A metalhead sitting on a curb beside a fallen bicycle reciting from memory to a teenager under a streetlight, a storm drain nearby

beats.title: Instant Pets, Some Assembly Required
beats.place: The Sunday swap meet in the front lot, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: On Sundays, Rusty opens the front lot to a swap meet: card tables of hubcaps, eight-tracks and lawn gnomes. One vendor found a crate of 1962 Brine Buddies, the mail-order instant sea pets, and dumped every packet into a kiddie pool to see what would happen. What happened is that they're now the size of hamsters, pink, cheerful and wearing tiny crowns, exactly like the ad promised. Barnaby is howling his head off.
beats.art: A sunny Sunday swap meet in a junkyard front lot, folding tables loaded with hubcaps, eight-track tapes and lawn gnomes, a plastic kiddie pool full of cheerful pink sea creatures the size of hamsters wearing tiny gold crowns, a vendor in a straw hat looking pleased with himself, a tricolor basset hound with a red bandana howling beside the pool, a teenager and a mustached veterinarian in a lab coat leaning over it, bright daylight, wide shot

choices.label: Buy the whole pool and set them free

success.text: You talk the vendor down from ten quarters to one and a pack of gum. Then you and Joey wheel the kiddie pool to the drainage creek behind the lot and tip it in. The Buddies wave tiny fins and paddle off in a line like a parade. Rusty says if they ever come back as big as dogs, that's on you.
success.art: A teenager and a teen mechanic tipping a kiddie pool into a reedy creek behind a junkyard, a line of small pink crowned sea creatures paddling away waving their fins

failure.text: You haggle so long that the vendor gets bored and sells the whole pool to a man who runs a bait shop. As his pickup pulls away, two hundred tiny crowned heads turn to look at you over the tailgate, betrayed. You'll see that look in your sleep.
failure.art: A rusty pickup truck driving away from a junkyard lot with a kiddie pool in its bed, rows of tiny pink crowned sea creatures peering sadly over the tailgate

choices.label: Fetch Dr. Haddad and his vet bag

success.text: Dr. Haddad takes one look, rolls up his sleeves and says, "Brine shrimp. Very ambitious brine shrimp." He tests the water, adds a box of salt from his car and prescribes shade. By noon the Buddies have shrunk back to fingernail size, and the vendor is selling them in jars with care instructions you lettered in marker. She pays you two quarters for the copywriting.
success.art: A veterinarian in rolled shirtsleeves kneeling by a kiddie pool of pink crowned sea creatures pouring in salt, a teenager lettering care instructions on cardboard under a beach umbrella
success.alone: You remember Dr. Haddad saying that anything living in water needs salt and shade. You pour in a box of rock salt from Rusty's shed and rig a beach umbrella. By noon the Buddies have shrunk back to fingernail size, and the vendor is selling them in jars with care instructions you lettered in marker. She pays you two quarters for the copywriting.

failure.text: Dr. Haddad says "more salt," you hear "more water" and blast the pool with Rusty's hose. The Buddies love it. They grow another inch, start chirping in harmony and spend the rest of the swap meet following you around the lot in a line. Barnaby will never forgive you.
failure.art: A teenager walking across a junkyard lot followed by a chirping line of plump pink sea creatures with tiny crowns, a basset hound glaring from under a card table
failure.alone: You half remember something about salt, decide it was "more water" and blast the pool with Rusty's hose. The Buddies love it. They grow another inch, start chirping in harmony and spend the rest of the swap meet following you around the lot in a line. Barnaby will never forgive you.

choices.label: Charge a nickel a look: SEE THE BRINE ROYALTY

success.text: You drape a bedsheet over two sawhorses, letter a cardboard sign and bark like a carnival pro: "Behold the crowned monarchs of the briny deep!" The line wraps around the hubcap table twice. You split a coffee can of nickels with the vendor, and the Buddies seem to enjoy the applause.
success.art: A teenager in a top hat barking at a line of kids outside a bedsheet tent on sawhorses, a hand-lettered cardboard sign, a kiddie pool of pink crowned sea creatures inside

failure.text: Your big unveiling is the exact moment the Buddies decide to molt. Two hundred tiny pink shells pop off at once with a sound like popcorn, and the front row gets a faceful of sea glitter. Parents want their nickels back. The vendor wants her cut of the nickels you no longer have.
failure.art: A crowd of startled kids sprinkled with sparkly pink flakes in front of a bedsheet tent, a kiddie pool erupting with tiny shells, a teenager in a top hat wincing

beats.title: Glory's Getaway Car
beats.place: Joey's garage, Rusty's Junkyard
beats.text: Glory Hallelujah is riding in Friday's Halloween parade as the Bride of Glimmerstein, and she wants to arrive in style: a 1961 Cadwell hearse Rusty dragged out of the back lot. Joey has the engine purring. The problem is the back door. It keeps unlatching by itself, and every time it swings open, the rolling casket tray glides out toward whoever is standing closest. Right now, that's you.
beats.art: A long black 1961 hearse parked outside a cinderblock junkyard garage, its rear door swinging open by itself and a chrome casket tray rolling out toward a startled teenager, a lean Diné teenager in an orange work shirt wiping his hands on a red rag at the engine, a pile of purple sequins and a pink feather boa on the workbench, late afternoon light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Rebuild the latch with Joey

success.text: You and Joey pull the latch apart on the workbench. Wedged in the spring is a folded parade ribbon from 1961: GRAND MARSHAL. The hearse was meant to lead a parade once and never made it. Joey rebuilds the latch, you tie the ribbon to the hood ornament, and the back door stays shut, like a car that's finally satisfied.
success.art: A teen mechanic and a teenager at a cluttered garage workbench examining a car door latch, a faded blue parade ribbon unfolded between them, a black hearse visible through the bus windows
success.alone: You pull the latch apart on Joey's workbench. Wedged in the spring is a folded parade ribbon from 1961: GRAND MARSHAL. The hearse was meant to lead a parade once and never made it. You rebuild the latch, tie the ribbon to the hood ornament, and the back door stays shut, like a car that's finally satisfied.

failure.text: The new latch holds for ten minutes. Then, with both of you bent over the engine, the back door creaks open and the casket tray rolls out and nudges you gently behind the knees. You sit down on it hard. Joey says, "It likes you," and doesn't sound like he's joking.
failure.art: A teenager sitting down hard on a chrome casket tray that has rolled out of the back of a black hearse, a teen mechanic leaning on the open hood looking amused
failure.alone: The new latch holds for ten minutes. Then, while you're bent over the engine, the back door creaks open and the casket tray rolls out and nudges you gently behind the knees. You sit down on it hard. Somewhere in the stacks, Barnaby howls once, like he told you so.

choices.label: Lie down in the back and see what it wants

success.text: You climb in, lie back on the tray and pull the door shut. It's dark and smells like carnations. After a long minute, the dome light flickers on by itself and the radio clicks over to a slow, dignified march. Then the door unlatches gently, like an invitation to step out. It never opens on its own again, and Glory insists you ride up front in the parade.
success.art: A teenager lying on their back on a casket tray inside a dim vintage hearse, the dome light glowing softly, carnation petals scattered on the carpet

failure.text: You lie down and pull the door shut, and the locks drop on every door at once. The engine turns over by itself. For one long minute the hearse idles, patient as a taxi waiting for an address, until Joey pops the lock with a coat hanger and hauls you out by the sneakers.
failure.art: A teen mechanic prying open the rear door of a black hearse with a bent coat hanger, a teenager's sneakers poking out, exhaust curling from the tailpipe

choices.label: Bedazzle it until it can't possibly be scary

success.text: Purple sequins on the fenders, a pink feather boa on the grille, glitter on every inch of chrome. The hearse seems stunned into good behavior. When Glory sweeps in to see it, she screams with joy, and the back door swings open slowly, like a gentleman holding it for a lady. She tips you two quarters and names you her costume department.
success.art: A black vintage hearse covered in purple sequins with a pink feather boa on its grille, a glamorous drag queen in a towering wig clapping with delight, glitter drifting in the junkyard sunlight

failure.text: The hearse does not want to be fabulous. Every sequin you glue on pops off within a minute, one by one, like it's spitting them out, and the boa ends up knotted around the antenna like a sulking flamingo. Joey sweeps up glitter for an hour and will be finding it in his toolbox for years.
failure.art: Sequins scattered across junkyard dirt around a stubbornly plain black hearse, a pink feather boa tangled on its antenna, a teen mechanic sweeping up glitter with a push broom

name: Oddment and Daughters
blurb: A traveling pawnshop that is never in the same lot twice: crammed shelves, a bell that rings before you touch the door, and Ms. Oddment behind the counter, who always has exactly what you need and always wants something odd in trade.
art: A narrow, crooked little shop wedged into an empty lot, its windows crammed with clocks, music boxes, dolls and brass curiosities, a hand-painted sign reading Oddment and Daughters, warm lamplight inside in broad daylight

beats.title: The Appraisal
beats.place: The counter, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: Ms. Oddment is a tall woman in a velvet waistcoat with a jeweler's loupe on a chain and eyes the color of tea. She looks you up and down as if you were an estate sale. "I don't buy things, dear. I buy afternoons. Memories. A little bit of the way you laugh." She taps a brass scale. "What will you sell me?"
beats.art: A tall slender woman in a dark velvet waistcoat with tea-colored eyes and a jeweler's loupe on a long chain leaning over a cluttered antique pawnshop counter toward a teenager, a brass balance scale with empty pans between them, a small glass jar with a curl of gray mist inside, shelves of clocks, music boxes and dolls glowing in warm lamplight, medium shot

choices.label: Sell her the memory of your worst birthday

success.text: She draws it out of you with a silver spoon, a little gray cloud, and drops it in a jar. You can't remember why you ever hated that cake. She pays you in quarters and throws in a deck of tarot cards. "They were already looking for you."
success.art: A tall woman lifting a small gray glowing cloud from a teenager's forehead with a silver spoon into a glass jar, a deck of tarot cards and coins on the counter

failure.text: She takes the wrong memory, the one of your best birthday. You can feel the gap where it was. She frowns, apologizes, and gives you three quarters you'd trade back in a heartbeat. "My hand slipped. It does, near Halloween."
failure.art: A glass jar on a pawnshop counter holding a warm golden glowing cloud, a woman looking apologetic, a teenager touching their temple

choices.label: Haggle her down to something harmless

success.text: You offer her your worst knock-knock joke. She laughs, a real laugh, and the lamps flare. "Done." She hands you a can of Aqua-Glow Max Hold. "Hairspray burns brighter than you'd think, and a bad joke is priceless."
success.art: A tall woman laughing behind a pawnshop counter, lamps flaring brightly, sliding a can of hairspray across to a grinning teenager

failure.text: Every offer you make, she counters with a stranger one: your shadow on Tuesdays, your middle name, the sound of your footsteps. You leave with nothing, and for an hour your footsteps make no sound at all.
failure.art: A teenager walking out of a crooked pawnshop onto a sunny sidewalk, oddly shadowless in the bright sun, a woman watching from the window

choices.label: Ask her what she does with it all

success.text: She looks at you a long moment. "Some things the world forgets, I keep. Some things the world should forget, I keep somewhere safer." She shows you a locked case at the back, very full and very quiet. "Everything cursed passes through a shop like mine eventually, dear. I only make sure it finds the right owner."
success.art: A tall woman holding a lamp beside a locked glass case at the back of a pawnshop, shadowy objects inside, a teenager peering in

failure.text: "Curiosity is a lovely currency," she says, and the brass scale tips as if you'd paid. You feel a little lighter and can't remember the name of your second-grade teacher. She smiles politely and rings up the sale.
failure.art: A brass pawnshop scale tipping under an invisible weight, a woman's long fingers ringing up a sale on an antique register

beats.title: All Sales Final
beats.place: The front door, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: A sweating man in a golf visor is trying to return a snow globe of Glimmer Falls. "It shows tomorrow's weather," he babbles, "and tomorrow's weather has my house on fire in it." Ms. Oddment points at a sign: ALL SALES FINAL. He turns to you, holding it out, shaking. Inside the globe, tiny flames flicker over a tiny roof.
beats.art: A cramped pawnshop at the front door, a frantic sweating man in a golf visor holding out a snow globe of a little town with tiny orange flames flickering over one roof inside the glass, a tall woman in a velvet waistcoat behind the counter pointing at a small framed placard, a teenager reaching for the snow globe, cluttered shelves of curios, warm lamplight, medium shot

choices.label: Take the globe off his hands for a quarter

success.text: The second it's yours, the flames inside go out and snow falls instead. The man nearly faints with relief. You set the globe on your windowsill. Every morning it shows the weather, honestly, and once, a warning you were glad to have.
success.art: A teenager holding a snow globe in which gentle snow falls over a tiny peaceful town, a relieved man in a golf visor sagging against a counter

failure.text: The moment you touch the glass, the tiny flames move from his roof to yours. Your roof. You put it down fast. Ms. Oddment takes it back for free with a sigh. "That's the trouble with gifts that see. They never lie, only change their minds."
failure.art: A snow globe on a pawnshop counter showing tiny flames over a different house, a teenager snatching their hand away

choices.label: Run to his house and check the wiring

success.text: His furnace has a cracked flue and a pile of dry newspapers stacked right against it. You move them, he calls a repairman and the flames in the globe shrink to a candle on a birthday cake. He tips you two quarters and a first-aid kit from his trunk.
success.art: A teenager pulling stacks of old newspapers away from a rusty basement furnace, a man in a golf visor on the phone, a snow globe on a shelf showing a small birthday candle

failure.text: You check everything and find nothing. That night, a fire truck rolls past your window with its siren off. In the morning, the man's house is fine, but his garage is a black square. The snow globe is back in Ms. Oddment's window.
failure.art: A suburban house with a burned-out garage beside it at dawn, a fire truck pulling away, smoke drifting

beats.title: One of the Daughters
beats.place: The back room, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: Behind the beaded curtain a girl about your age is restocking a shelf of glass eyes. She has Ms. Oddment's tea-colored eyes and a name tag that says WEDNESDAY. "There are seven of us. We're never allowed out of the shop." She lowers her voice. "I want to see the mall. Just once. Will you take me?"
beats.art: A dim pawnshop back room behind a beaded curtain, a teenage girl in an old-fashioned gray smock with tea-colored eyes restocking a shelf of glass eyes in little velvet trays, looking back over her shoulder, a teenager peeking through the beads, a single oil lamp and dust in the air, medium shot

choices.label: Sneak her out the back for an hour

success.text: You take Wednesday to Starlight Mall. She eats a pretzel, rides the escalator six times and laughs at the fountain. When you bring her back, Ms. Oddment is waiting, arms crossed, then sighs and gives you a box of glow-stick bracelets. "For keeping her safe. Don't do it again. Do it again."
success.art: A girl with tea-colored eyes laughing on a mall escalator with a pretzel, a teenager beside her, neon lights all around

failure.text: The back door opens onto a different street, then a different town, then a field you don't recognize. Wednesday drags you back inside before the door forgets where it is. "It does that," she says, disappointed. "Next time."
failure.art: A pawnshop back door opening onto an unfamiliar misty field at noon, a girl yanking a teenager back inside by the sleeve

choices.label: Ask Ms. Oddment to let her go

success.text: Ms. Oddment listens, very still. Then she takes off her loupe. "My mother never let me out either." She hands Wednesday a coat. They walk out together, mother and daughter, for the first time in a very long time. The shop smells like rain.
success.art: A tall shopkeeper helping a girl into a coat at the door of a crooked pawnshop, both stepping out into afternoon sunlight

failure.text: "The world is not kind to things like us, dear," Ms. Oddment says gently, and closes the curtain. Wednesday waves through the beads. You hear a lock click, and you feel you just made something worse.
failure.art: A beaded curtain swaying closed in a dim pawnshop, a girl's hand waving through the beads, a tall shadow behind her

beats.title: The Things on the Shelves
beats.place: The aisles, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: Ms. Oddment will pay a quarter a shelf to dust. "Don't touch anything that hums. Don't answer anything that asks you a question. And if the monkey with the cymbals starts clapping, leave the aisle at once." The first shelf has a music box, a baby shoe and a lighter engraved KEEP ME. The music box hums.
beats.art: A teenager with a feather duster in a narrow pawnshop aisle crammed with curios, a humming wooden music box with its lid half open, a single small baby shoe, an engraved silver lighter, and on a high shelf a wind-up cymbal monkey watching with its cymbals held apart, warm lamplight and deep shadows between the shelves, medium shot

choices.label: Dust every shelf slowly and follow the rules

success.text: Four shelves, no touching, no answering. The music box asks you its question three times and you never answer. At the end, Ms. Oddment counts out four quarters and nods. "Most people answer." You don't ask what happens to them.
success.art: A teenager carefully dusting a pawnshop shelf around curios with careful fingertips, a shopkeeper counting coins into their palm at the end of the aisle

failure.text: The music box asks, "Do you want to know how it ends?" and you say "What?" before you can stop yourself. The cymbal monkey starts clapping. You run. Ms. Oddment pays you anyway, minus one quarter "for the excitement."
failure.art: A wind-up monkey clashing its cymbals on a high pawnshop shelf, a teenager sprinting down the aisle dropping a feather duster

choices.label: Slip the KEEP ME lighter into your pocket

success.text: You pocket it. It's warm. At the door, Ms. Oddment says without looking up, "Keep the flashlight too, then. You'll want light more than fire." When you check your pocket, the lighter is gone, and a heavy six-cell flashlight is in its place.
success.art: A teenager at a pawnshop door pulling a heavy flashlight out of their jacket pocket in surprise, a shopkeeper absorbed in her ledger

failure.text: The lighter burns your fingers, and you drop it. When you pick it up, the engraving reads KEEP ME AWAY. Ms. Oddment is standing right behind you. "Thieves dust for free, dear." You finish the shelves unpaid.
failure.art: An engraved silver lighter lying on a pawnshop floor, a teenager blowing on burnt fingertips, a tall shopkeeper standing right behind them

beats.title: Redeemable Through Friday
beats.place: The counter, Oddment and Daughters
beats.text: A pawn ticket falls out of your jacket pocket as you walk in, and it's in your own handwriting. ITEM: one (1) courage, pawned for two quarters. DATED: Friday, October 31, 1986. Ms. Oddment sees it and raises one elegant eyebrow. "Ah. You haven't done that yet," she says. "But you will. Would you like it back early?"
beats.art: A cluttered pawnshop counter with a brass scale and a jeweler's loupe, a tall woman in a velvet waistcoat raising one eyebrow, a teenager holding up a small paper pawn ticket at arm's length with a stunned face, a small glass jar with a glowing speck of gold light on a high shelf behind her, warm lamplight, medium shot

choices.label: Pay the two quarters and redeem it now

success.text: You slide two quarters across the counter. Ms. Oddment fetches a small glass jar from a high shelf, and inside it a warm little light is pacing like a firefly. She uncorks it under your nose. You breathe in, and for the first time all week your shoulders come down from around your ears.
success.art: A tall shopkeeper in a velvet waistcoat uncorking a small glass jar holding a warm golden glow, a teenager leaning close to breathe it in, shelves of curios behind

failure.text: You pay. She uncorks the jar, and the little light zips straight past your nose and out through the mail slot into the street. "Oh dear. It isn't ready to come home yet," Ms. Oddment says, and refunds you one quarter for the trouble. You can feel it out there somewhere, waiting for Friday.
failure.art: A tiny golden light zipping out through the brass mail slot of a pawnshop door, a teenager lunging after it, a shopkeeper in velvet holding an empty uncorked jar

choices.label: Argue that a ticket from the future can't count

success.text: You cite the date, the missing witness signature and the ancient principle that you can't sell what you haven't done yet. Ms. Oddment listens with growing delight, then tears the ticket in half. "Void. Nobody has out-argued me since 1891." She gives you a lucky quarter for the performance. Whatever you meant to pawn on Friday, now you'll have to keep.
success.art: A teenager arguing passionately across a pawnshop counter, a delighted shopkeeper in a velvet waistcoat tearing a small paper ticket in half, a brass scale between them

failure.text: Ms. Oddment hears you out, then turns the ticket over. On the back, also in your handwriting, it says: I KNEW YOU'D TRY THAT. You have no comeback for yourself. She hands the ticket back with a sympathetic smile, and it sits in your pocket all day like a stone.
failure.art: A teenager staring at the back of a small paper pawn ticket covered in handwriting, a shopkeeper in velvet smiling sympathetically across a cluttered counter

choices.label: Get Wednesday to check the ledger in back

success.text: Wednesday flips the ledger open behind the beaded curtain while her mother is busy. "Friday, you trade your courage for a flashlight battery and a head start," she whispers. "You don't use the head start. You go back for somebody instead." She closes the book. "So you get it back anyway. That's what it says." The ticket in your hand goes warm.
success.art: A girl with tea-colored eyes and a name tag reading WEDNESDAY whispering to a teenager behind a beaded curtain, a thick leather ledger open on a shelf of glass eyes

failure.text: Wednesday opens the ledger, and Ms. Oddment's voice comes from directly behind you both: "Customers do not read the ledger, dear." Wednesday is sent to restock the glass eyes. You get a lecture on the ethics of futures trading that lasts until closing time.
failure.art: A tall shopkeeper in a velvet waistcoat looming at a beaded curtain, a teenager and a girl with a name tag caught over an open leather ledger

beats.title: Everything Must Fit
beats.place: The back lot, Oddment and Daughters, Halloween afternoon
beats.text: On Halloween afternoon, Oddment and Daughters is packing up. Every shelf is going into seven steamer trunks, one per daughter, because at midnight the shop moves on to whatever town needs it next. Ms. Oddment hires you to help. "Two rules," she says. "Wrap everything that ticks. And whatever you do, don't let the locked case see you leave."
beats.art: Seven open steamer trunks in a gravel lot behind a crooked little pawnshop on Halloween afternoon, clocks, music boxes and snow globes being packed in straw, a wind-up cymbal monkey lying face down in a trunk, a tall woman in a velvet waistcoat directing a teenager who carries a wrapped mantel clock, a locked glass curio case turned to face the wall, orange Halloween sky, wide shot

choices.label: Pack every trunk like a jigsaw puzzle

success.text: Clocks wrapped, music boxes muffled, the cymbal monkey packed face-down with its hands taped. Every trunk shuts with a satisfying click. Ms. Oddment inspects your work through her loupe, pays you two quarters and gives you a small, formal bow. "The next town will never know you helped," she says. "That's the highest compliment I have."
success.art: Neatly packed steamer trunks lined with straw holding wrapped clocks and music boxes, a cymbal monkey toy lying face-down, a shopkeeper inspecting through a jeweler's loupe

failure.text: One mantel clock goes into a trunk unwrapped, and it starts ticking backward. Everything in that trunk unpacks itself in reverse, item by item, back onto the shelves, while you watch. Ms. Oddment sighs, rolls up her velvet sleeves and helps you start over. You finish with blisters and straw in your hair.
failure.art: Curios floating up out of an open steamer trunk back onto pawnshop shelves, a teenager staring with an armful of straw, a ticking mantel clock sitting on top of the pile

choices.label: Ask what she'll leave behind for Glimmer Falls

success.text: Ms. Oddment pauses with a snow globe in each hand. "Nobody has ever asked me that." She digs through the last trunk and presses a heavy pouch into your hands: rock salt, coarse and gray. "Old-country recipe. Something tonight will need a line it can't cross." Then she does something you've never seen her do. She hugs you.
success.art: A tall shopkeeper in a velvet waistcoat pressing a heavy cloth pouch of coarse gray salt into a teenager's hands beside open steamer trunks, golden late-afternoon light

failure.text: "Leave behind?" Ms. Oddment looks honestly puzzled. "Dear, a shop like mine only ever takes things with it." Then she glances at the locked case, which has turned its glass front toward you. "Best you go home early," she says gently. "It's started looking at people."
failure.art: A tall glass-fronted locked display case in a half-empty pawnshop turned toward a teenager, a shopkeeper in velvet laying a hand on the teen's shoulder to steer them away

choices.label: Say goodbye to the daughters while the case faces the wall

success.text: You make your rounds while the case's glass is turned to the wall: a handshake from Monday, a fist bump from Thursday, a thank-you note folded into a pretzel from Wednesday. You slip out the back with your heart thudding, and the bell over the door stays perfectly still. Some goodbyes are better small.
success.art: A teenager tiptoeing between steamer trunks waving to a row of girls with tea-colored eyes, a tall locked glass case turned to face the wall in the background

failure.text: The bell rings on its own as you reach the door, and behind you the locked case turns, glass creaking. For a second your reflection in it is wearing a Halloween costume you don't own yet. Seven daughters say "Bye!" in perfect unison. You run all the way to the corner.
failure.art: A teenager's reflection in the glass of a tall locked display case, the reflection wearing an unfamiliar costume, seven girls waving in unison behind

name: Mercy Valley Clinic
blurb: A flat-roofed 1960s walk-in clinic with a lollipop jar on every counter, a waiting-room TV stuck on one channel, and Nurse Inez Duarte, who has patched up every kid on Crystal Street and believes every word they tell her about the monsters.
art: A low flat-roofed 1960s walk-in clinic of pale green brick with a red cross painted above wide glass doors, potted marigolds and a wooden bench out front, a parked bicycle, a warm waiting room of orange plastic chairs glowing through big windows in bright afternoon sun

beats.title: Wipeout on Larkspur Hill
beats.place: The front walk, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: A kid in a homemade daredevil cape comes off his BMX at the bottom of Larkspur Hill and skids right up to the clinic doors, howling. Nurse Inez is elbow-deep in a waiting room full of sniffles, so she points at you and then at the first-aid cart. "You. Wash your hands. Go." Behind the kid, his bike is still rolling. Uphill. Pedals turning all by themselves.
beats.art: A small boy in a homemade star-spangled cape sitting on the front walk of a pale green brick clinic with a scraped knee, a teenager kneeling beside him with a white first-aid kit and a bandage, a brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls and a teal cardigan waving through the glass doors, and behind them a riderless dirt bike rolling uphill with its pedals turning by themselves, sunny autumn afternoon, wide shot

choices.label: Clean the scrape and bandage it like a pro

success.text: You keep your voice low and calm, dab on the stinging stuff, count to three and fib that it's two. One butterfly bandage, one grape lollipop. Inez checks your work over the top of her glasses and nods. "Steady hands. Come back in a couple years and I'll put you on the schedule."
success.art: A teenager pressing a bandage onto a grinning boy's knee on a sunny clinic step, a brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls and a teal cardigan peering approvingly over her glasses, a purple lollipop clutched in the boy's fist, his cape spread on the concrete

failure.text: You get a good look at the scrape and your knees go to jelly. The kid ends up patting your back and telling you to breathe into a paper bag. Inez patches him up in forty seconds flat and hands the lollipop to you instead.
failure.art: A woozy teenager sitting on a clinic bench with their head between their knees breathing into a brown paper bag, a small caped boy patting their back, a nurse in a teal cardigan briskly bandaging the boy's knee in afternoon sun

choices.label: Distract him with a death-defying stunt special

success.text: You narrate his crash like a TV daredevil special: the jump, the wind, the cape, the crowd on its feet. By the slow-motion replay he's laughing too hard to notice the bandage going on. His mom tips you a quarter for the show, and he asks for your autograph on his knee.
success.art: A teenager gesturing like a TV announcer into a rolled-up magazine microphone, a caped boy laughing on a clinic step while a nurse in a teal cardigan wraps his knee, his mother in a windbreaker clapping, golden afternoon light

failure.text: Your dramatic reenactment ends with you tripping over the curb. Now there are two patients. Inez sighs the sigh of a woman who has seen this exact thing every Halloween since 1961 and hands you an ice pack shaped like a pumpkin.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled on a curb outside a green brick clinic holding a pumpkin-shaped ice pack to one elbow, a caped boy giggling on the step, a nurse with silver-streaked curls shaking her head with hands on her hips

choices.label: Chase the bike before it reaches the woods

success.text: You sprint up Larkspur Hill and grab the bike by the seat just as it noses into the pines. It shudders once, like a dog shaking off water, and goes still. There's a pinecone jammed in the spokes, and it's warm. You wheel it back down to a kid who now believes you can fly.
success.art: A teenager sprinting uphill and grabbing the seat of a riderless BMX bike at the edge of a pine forest, autumn leaves whirling around them, a small green brick clinic far below at the bottom of the hill, bright afternoon sky

failure.text: The bike beats you to the treeline and rolls into the shade under the pines. You stop at the edge, lungs burning. Somewhere in the dark between the trunks, something rings the bike bell twice, politely. The kid's mom says she'll just buy him a new one.
failure.art: A winded teenager bent over at the edge of a shadowy pine forest, a BMX bike vanishing between dark tree trunks, a chrome bike bell glinting deep in the gloom, late afternoon sun slanting across the hillside

beats.title: Candy Striper for a Day
beats.place: The short-stay ward, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: Inez's volunteer called in sick, so you get the red-and-white striped smock and the gelatin cart. The three-bed short-stay ward holds a snoring mailman, a girl recovering from her tonsils with a stack of comic books, and Mrs. Esperanza Ochoa, 88, who says her late husband Teo visits every day at four. The ward clock says 3:58.
beats.art: A teenager in a red-and-white striped volunteer smock pushing a cart of wobbling lime gelatin cups into a small sunny three-bed clinic ward, a mailman snoring in one bed, a girl with a stack of comic books in another, an 88-year-old woman in a crocheted shawl sitting up in the third bed watching the doorway with hope, a round wall clock nearly at four, warm afternoon light, wide shot

choices.label: Pull up a chair and ask Mrs. Ochoa about Teo

success.text: She tells you how Teo danced the mambo at the Grange Hall in 1949 and hummed while he fixed the sink. At four o'clock the curtain by her bed sways, and the room smells like aftershave and motor oil for exactly one minute. She squeezes your hand. "See? He likes you."
success.art: A teenager in a striped smock holding hands with a smiling elderly woman in a clinic bed, the curtain beside the bed swaying gently in golden afternoon light, a vase of carnations on the windowsill

failure.text: She tells you about Teo until four o'clock comes and goes with nothing at all. Her face falls. "He's never late." You stay with her until the dinner trays come, and you can't stop glancing at the empty chair by the window.
failure.art: An elderly woman in a clinic bed gazing at a vacant vinyl chair beside a sunny window, a teenager in a striped smock sitting quietly at her bedside, a dinner tray with a covered plate cooling on the side table

choices.label: Check the front desk's visitor sheets

success.text: Every day since September, at 4:00 on the dot, in shaky old-fashioned cursive: T. Ochoa, in and out. Inez reads it over your shoulder and doesn't blink. "He signs in, he signs out, he wipes his feet. Best-behaved visitor I've got." She pours you a cup of coffee like you're staff.
success.art: A teenager in a striped smock and a brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls leaning together over a clipboard at a clinic front desk, a long column of identical looping ink cursive, a mug of coffee steaming beside it

failure.text: You flip through the visitor sheets: T. Ochoa, every day at four, in the same shaky hand. Then you turn the last page and find tomorrow's date, already signed. The paper is cold as a freezer door. You put the clipboard down very carefully.
failure.art: A teenager in a striped smock holding a yellowed clipboard at arm's length over a clinic front desk, old visitor sheets fanned out across the counter, chilly blue light falling through the window blinds

choices.label: Wait in the hallway at four and see who comes

success.text: At four on the dot the hall lights hum and dim. Unhurried footsteps you can't see pass you, pause, and something pats your shoulder the way an old man thanks a kid who held the door. From the ward comes Mrs. Ochoa's laugh, bright as a girl's at a dance.
success.art: A teenager in a striped smock standing tall in a dim clinic hallway, overhead lights glowing low and amber, a trail of faint shining footprints on the polished linoleum leading toward a sunlit ward doorway

failure.text: The hall lights dim and you lose your nerve, ducking into the supply closet with the mops. Slow footsteps pass, and somebody hums a mambo. When you come out, there's a fresh red carnation on the gelatin cart, and you're pretty sure it's for you.
failure.art: A teenager in a striped smock peeking out of a cramped clinic supply closet full of mops into a dim amber hallway, a single red carnation resting on a cart of lime gelatin cups

beats.title: The Nose Jar
beats.place: The exam room cabinet, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: Mercy Valley turns twenty-five this week, and Inez wants a lobby display of the Nose Jar: every object she has pulled out of a Glimmer Falls kid's nose, ear or sneaker since 1961. Marbles. A tiny silver board-game top hat. Forty-one popcorn kernels. Each has a paper tag in Inez's tidy hand. One small purple pebble has a tag with your name on it, dated November 1, 1986.
beats.art: A big glass apothecary jar tipped open on a clinic exam table, colorful marbles, a tiny silver top hat token, popcorn kernels and a small glowing purple pebble spilling out, each tied to a little paper tag on a string, a teenager leaning in close under a hanging exam lamp, a nurse with silver-streaked curls watching from the doorway, close medium shot

choices.label: Show Inez the tag and ask what it means

success.text: Inez turns the tag over and over. "That's my handwriting. I didn't write it." Then she does the most comforting thing any adult has done all week: she believes you completely, writes her home phone number on your hand, and says, "Whatever's coming, you come here first."
success.art: A brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls and a teal cardigan holding a small paper tag up to the window light, her other hand pressing a ballpoint pen to a teenager's open palm, a glass jar of marbles on the exam table

failure.text: Inez reads the tag, goes pale and tears it in half. "Somebody's idea of a joke." She says it too fast. For the rest of the afternoon she keeps finding reasons to walk past the exam room, checking that you're still there.
failure.art: A pale nurse in a teal cardigan tearing a small paper tag in half beside a glass jar of marbles, a worried teenager sitting on a crinkly exam table, afternoon sun striping through window blinds

choices.label: Catalog the whole jar for the anniversary display

success.text: You sort twenty-five years of nose treasures into a display a museum would envy, with a chart of the top objects by decade: marbles own the sixties, crayons the seventies. Inez is so delighted she hands you a tin of bandages and antiseptic spray "for the week you're about to have."
success.art: A teenager arranging marbles, crayons, buttons and tiny toys in neat rows on a felt-lined tray at a clinic counter, a smiling nurse with silver-streaked curls holding out a white tin first-aid kit

failure.text: You sort for an hour. Every time you look away, the purple pebble is back on top of the pile, no matter where you put it. Inez finds you staring at it, and without a word she locks the whole jar in the cabinet.
failure.art: A small purple pebble perched on top of a heap of marbles and buttons on a clinic counter, a teenager staring at it with narrowed eyes, a nurse in a teal cardigan reaching for a ring of cabinet keys

choices.label: Slip the humming pebble into your pocket

success.text: It hums against your leg all afternoon like a purring cat. It goes quiet by the lollipop jar and buzzes by any window that faces Crystal Street. Somebody filed this pebble under your name, and you intend to find out why. Until then, it's a pretty good weirdness detector.
success.art: A teenager walking down a clinic hallway with a faint violet glow shining through their jeans pocket, a glass lollipop jar on the counter beside them, a sunny window looking out on a suburban cul-de-sac

failure.text: Inez clocks it the second the pebble leaves the jar. "Pocket," she says, palm out, the way she's said it to every Crystal Street kid since Kennedy. You hand it over. It's warm, and her eyebrows climb all the way up.
failure.art: A brisk nurse with silver-streaked curls holding out an open palm toward a sheepish teenager, a small glowing purple pebble resting in the teenager's hand between them, a glass jar of marbles on the exam table

beats.title: The Halloween Binder
beats.place: The night desk, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: Inez's night desk hides a fat orange binder marked HALLOWEEN WEEK, one page per kid, every year since 1961. Glitter burns that won't wash off. A lunchbox chewed by something with far too many tiny teeth. A boy who walked in with his shadow on backwards. She catches you looking. "Nobody else believes them," she says. "So I write it all down."
beats.art: A fat orange three-ring binder lying open on a cluttered clinic night desk under a gooseneck lamp, instant photos of grinning kids with bandaged elbows taped to its pages, a mug of coffee beside it, a nurse in her sixties with silver-streaked curls, cat-eye glasses and a teal cardigan leaning on the counter beside a curious teenager, dark windows behind, warm lamp light, medium shot

choices.label: Tell her what you've seen this week

success.text: You tell her everything, even the parts that sound ridiculous out loud. Inez doesn't laugh once. She takes a fresh page, writes your name across the top and underlines it twice. "Now it's on the record," she says. "And now somebody's watching your back."
success.art: A teenager talking earnestly across a clinic night desk, a nurse with silver-streaked curls listening intently with a pen poised over an open orange binder, warm gooseneck lamplight pooling between them

failure.text: You start to tell her, and the words jam up somewhere behind your teeth. Inez waits, then slides a cherry lollipop across the desk. "When you're ready. I'm here till midnight and back at seven." You leave with the lollipop and the story still stuck.
failure.art: A teenager slumped at a clinic night desk turning a red lollipop in their fingers, a patient nurse in a teal cardigan waiting with folded hands under a gooseneck lamp, an orange binder closed between them

choices.label: Read the binder cover to cover

success.text: Twenty-five Halloweens of patterns. The worst nights cluster on the same few streets, and the kids who came in together always healed faster than the ones who came in alone. You copy the useful parts into your notebook. Inez's binder is the best monster manual in California.
success.art: A teenager curled in an orange plastic waiting-room chair poring over a fat orange binder, a spiral notebook balanced on one knee, taped instant photos of smiling bandaged kids on the open pages, afternoon light through the windows

failure.text: Somewhere around 1979 the pages start describing kids you know, with dates that haven't happened yet. You shut the binder fast. Inez takes it back and doesn't ask what you saw, which is somehow worse.
failure.art: A wide-eyed teenager snapping a fat orange binder shut at a clinic night desk, a nurse with silver-streaked curls reaching to take it back, the gooseneck lamp flickering over a cold cup of coffee

beats.title: Captain Cosmo Wants a Volunteer
beats.place: The waiting room, Mercy Valley Clinic
beats.text: The waiting-room TV has been stuck on Channel 11 since 1974, and Channel 11 went off the air in 1975. Today it's showing Captain Cosmo's Rocket Club, the after-school kids' show from 1963, in fuzzy black and white. Captain Cosmo leans into the camera, looks straight at you over the heads of the coughing patients and says, "You there. Yes, you. Come on up, space cadet."
beats.art: A small 1960s clinic waiting room with orange plastic chairs and coughing patients, a wall-mounted wooden television showing a smiling black-and-white kids' show host in a fishbowl space helmet leaning out of the fuzzy screen and pointing at one teenager, the teen half standing from a chair, a nurse with silver-streaked curls at the reception window, fluorescent light, wide shot

choices.label: Salute and play along like a real space cadet

success.text: You stand, salute and recite the Rocket Club pledge as he feeds it to you line by line: brush your teeth, mind your mother, never fly alone. The whole waiting room joins in. A boy with an ear infection stops crying. Captain Cosmo beams, says "Club dismissed!" and the set switches to a soap opera for the first time in twelve years.
success.art: A teenager standing in a clinic waiting room saluting a black-and-white television, patients of all ages saluting along, a small boy with a bandaged ear grinning

failure.text: You salute, the picture zooms in, and suddenly you're on the screen too, fuzzy and black and white in a cardboard space helmet, standing next to the Captain. The real you blinks. The TV you doesn't. Nurse Inez turns the set to face the wall, firmly, and doesn't say a word.
failure.art: A wall-mounted clinic television showing a black-and-white teenager in a cardboard space helmet beside a smiling host, the real teenager staring up at it, a nurse reaching for the set

choices.label: Climb up and unstick the channel knob

success.text: You stand on a chair, pry the back off the cabinet and find the knob gummed up with twenty years of lollipop residue. Scratched into the dial underneath: FOR GRANDPA WALT, WHO WATCHED WITH ME HERE. You free the knob, but you leave it on 11. Inez slips you a quarter and two lollipops. "Good call," she says.
success.art: A teenager standing on an orange plastic chair peering into the open back of a wall-mounted television, a nurse with reading glasses holding out lollipops below

failure.text: The knob turns freely now, and every channel is Channel 11. The news, the game show, the cartoons: Captain Cosmo hosts all of them, and he looks a little hurt that you tried. Inez pockets the knob and says she'll call the repairman, the one who doesn't ask questions.
failure.art: A wall television in a clinic waiting room showing a black-and-white space-helmeted host as a teenager twists the dial, a nurse pocketing the knob

choices.label: Ask Nurse Inez who Captain Cosmo was

success.text: Inez smiles, a little sad. "Cosmo was Harold Pike from the pharmacy counter. He brought his Rocket Club here every Halloween to visit the kids stuck in bed." She points to a faded photo by the door: a man in a cardboard helmet surrounded by kids in casts. "He hasn't missed a Halloween since. I just leave the set on."
success.art: A nurse with reading glasses pointing to a faded photo by a clinic door of a smiling man in a cardboard space helmet surrounded by children in casts

failure.text: Inez opens her mouth to answer, and the TV cranks its own volume to full: "NO SPOILERS, NURSE!" Every patient jumps. Inez sets her jaw, says "Later," and goes back to her clipboard, but she keeps glaring at the set like it owes her money.
failure.art: A wall television blaring with a black-and-white host in a space helmet wagging his finger, startled patients jumping in their chairs, a nurse frowning over her clipboard

beats.title: Free Candy X-Rays Tonight
beats.place: The X-ray room, Mercy Valley Clinic, Halloween afternoon
beats.text: Ever since the 1982 scare stories, Mercy Valley has offered free X-rays of trick-or-treat candy on Halloween night, and tonight the line will wrap around the block. This afternoon Nurse Inez needs a test run, so she slides a sample bag of fun-size bars under the machine. The film comes back clean: no pins, no razor blades. Except one Choco-Lotta bar has a tiny skeleton inside it, and the tiny skeleton is waving.
beats.art: A 1960s clinic X-ray room, a wall lightbox glowing white behind an X-ray film of fun-size candy bars, one bar on the film holding a tiny skeleton that is waving, a nurse with silver-streaked curls and cat-eye glasses and a teenager leaning in close to the lightbox, the big X-ray machine arm overhead, cool white light, medium shot

choices.label: Unwrap the bar and meet whoever's in there

success.text: You peel back the wrapper. Inside is an ordinary chocolate bar, and stuck to its bottom, a tiny glow-in-the-dark plastic skeleton from a cereal-box prize. Inez laughs so hard she has to sit down. You keep the skeleton for luck, and that night it waves at you from your bedpost, very slightly.
success.art: A teenager holding up a tiny glow-in-the-dark plastic skeleton peeled from a chocolate bar, a nurse in cat-eye glasses laughing in her chair, an X-ray lightbox glowing behind

failure.text: You unwrap the bar and it's hollow: a skeleton-shaped space in the chocolate and a trail of tiny chocolate footprints across the counter, leading to the heating vent. Inez stares at the vent a long time, then tapes a fresh candy bar beside it. "Tribute," she says.
failure.art: Tiny chocolate footprints trailing across a clinic counter to a metal heating vent, an empty candy wrapper, a nurse taping a fresh chocolate bar beside the vent

choices.label: Help Inez set up the line before the crowd comes

success.text: You tape arrows on the floor, set out a table of free apple slices, letter a sign that says CANDY GOES IN, FUN COMES OUT and practice your everything's-fine smile. When the doors open at six, the line moves like a dream. Inez slips you two quarters and the title Head of Halloween Operations.
success.art: A teenager taping orange arrows on a clinic floor beside a folding table of apple slices and a hand-lettered sign, a nurse setting up a lightbox in the background

failure.text: You get the line set up, but the practice bag you run comes back with every single candy holding a tiny waving skeleton. You hide the film. Inez finds it. "We tell no one," she says, and you both smile far too brightly at the first parents through the door.
failure.art: An X-ray film on a clinic lightbox showing a pile of candy bars each holding a tiny waving skeleton, a nurse and a teenager standing in front of it with stiff smiles

choices.label: Talk down the parents who think every bag is poisoned

success.text: An early dad is already shouting about razor blades in apples. You tell him what Inez told you: in twenty-five years she's never found one, but she's patched up plenty of kids who tripped over their own capes. Reflective tape, walk in groups, check the bag, then let them eat it. He actually writes it down.
success.art: A teenager calmly talking to a worried father in a clinic lobby, the father writing in a small notebook, a bowl of candy and a roll of reflective tape on the counter

failure.text: The dad won't hear it, and his panic spreads down the early line like a cold. Within ten minutes six parents have sworn off Halloween forever and one wants Inez to X-ray their kid's costume. Inez does it, sighing. The costume, a cardboard robot, has a tiny skeleton waving inside it too.
failure.art: A line of anxious parents with candy bags in a clinic lobby, a nurse aiming an X-ray machine at a child's cardboard robot costume, a teenager wincing at the counter

name: Thriftee-Mart
blurb: The biggest supermarket in Glimmer Falls: buzzing fluorescent aisles, a Halloween candy aisle stacked to the ceiling, a manager who flinches at every price, and a bag boy who hears every rumor in town before it happens.
art: A sprawling 1980s supermarket storefront with wide plate-glass windows, a pyramid of orange pumpkins and a row of shopping carts out front, bright fluorescent aisles glowing inside, a bag boy in a red apron pushing a long train of carts across a sunny parking lot

beats.title: Sticker Shock
beats.place: Aisle 2, canned goods, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: Mr. Pettibone, the manager, is sweating through his short-sleeved dress shirt. His pricing gun has gone haywire: every sticker it spits out says 13 cents, the price of a can of ham at the 1959 grand opening, and half the aisle is already tagged. Shoppers are filling carts like it's the end of the world. "It's possessed," he whispers. "Or it's under warranty."
beats.art: A canned-goods aisle in a 1980s supermarket, a sweating balding manager in a short-sleeved dress shirt and clip-on tie clutching a hand-held pricing gun that spits a long curling ribbon of orange stickers, cheerful shoppers piling canned hams into carts, a teenager peeling stickers off cans with a fresh roll, buzzing fluorescent lights, wide shot

choices.label: Grab a sticker roll and re-price the aisle by hand

success.text: You go shelf by shelf at a speed that makes the stock boys whistle, peeling off 13-cent stickers and slapping on real ones. By noon the aisle is sane again. Mr. Pettibone presses two quarters into your hand like he's donating a kidney.
success.art: A teenager racing along a supermarket shelf of canned goods peeling off orange price stickers, a manager in a clip-on tie watching in grateful awe, two stock boys whistling from a rolling ladder under fluorescent light

failure.text: You re-price the entire aisle. When you step back to admire it, every new sticker has quietly changed to 13 cents too. Mr. Pettibone has to sit down on a case of creamed corn and breathe into his tie.
failure.art: A supermarket manager slumped on a cardboard case of creamed corn holding his clip-on tie to his face, a teenager staring at a long shelf of cans dotted with identical orange stickers

choices.label: Talk Mr. Pettibone down off the ledge

success.text: You walk him to the break room, get him a paper cup of water, and point out that a town that buys cheap ham today will buy full-price mustard all week. He laughs for the first time since 1983 and makes you an honorary assistant manager, plastic name tag and all.
success.art: A teenager handing a paper cup of water to a frazzled supermarket manager in a tiny break room with a dented coffee maker and a cluttered corkboard, the manager smiling weakly, a plastic name tag in his other hand

failure.text: Halfway through your pep talk, the pricing gun fires on its own and tags the intercom, which squeals like a stuck pig. Mr. Pettibone locks himself in the walk-in freezer to "think," and you get stuck covering the courtesy desk, getting yelled at about coupons.
failure.art: A teenager stuck behind a supermarket courtesy desk facing a line of annoyed shoppers waving clipped coupons, a heavy walk-in freezer door shut tight in the background, frost curling from its seams

choices.label: Pull the trigger yourself and see what it wants

success.text: You squeeze the trigger and the gun prints one sticker that says THANK YOU in a curly old store font, then a normal price, then another. Folded tight behind the roll you find a yellowed 1959 grand-opening coupon. Old store, old ghosts, small favors. The gun behaves after that.
success.art: A teenager holding a hand-held pricing gun up to the fluorescent light, a tiny yellowed coupon unfolding from inside its roll, a curl of orange stickers drifting down around them like confetti

failure.text: The gun bucks in your hand and fires a sticker square onto your forehead: 13 cents. It will not come off. Kids in the parking lot point and laugh, and for the rest of the day every stray cat in Glimmer Falls follows you at a respectful distance.
failure.art: A teenager with a bright orange price sticker stuck to the middle of their forehead walking across a sunny supermarket parking lot, a parade of curious stray cats trailing behind them, kids pointing from a station wagon

beats.title: Paper, Plastic or Rumor
beats.place: Checkout lane 4, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: Dez Farrow has bagged groceries for half of Glimmer Falls, and he hears everything: who's getting divorced, who bought forty cans of hairspray, who keeps buying cat food with no cat. He trades rumors for favors, never money. Today he leans over the bagging counter and whispers that one shopping cart in the lot rolls off toward the old quarry end every night, by itself.
beats.art: A lanky teen bag boy in a red apron and paper hat leaning over checkout lane four toward a listening teenager, brown paper grocery bags and a conveyor belt of cereal boxes between them, and through the big front window a single shopping cart drifting by itself across the parking lot toward the far end, late afternoon light and fluorescent glow, medium shot

choices.label: Help him round up the carts in the lot

success.text: You and Dez snake a train of thirty carts across the blacktop and slam it home. He pays up with a whole afternoon of gossip, including which houses on Crystal Street keep their porch lights on all night, and why. Hold a rumor right and it's a map.
success.art: A teenager and a bag boy in a red apron pushing a long snaking train of shopping carts across a sunny supermarket parking lot, autumn leaves skittering under the wheels, the store windows glowing behind them

failure.text: The cart train jackknifes and rolls into the side of Mr. Pettibone's station wagon. Dez winces. "Rumors are on hold until I'm not fired." One cart breaks loose and rolls away toward the quarry end of the lot, in no hurry at all.
failure.art: A tangle of shopping carts crashed against the side of a wood-paneled station wagon, a bag boy in a red apron covering his face with both hands, a single cart rolling away across the far end of the parking lot

choices.label: Trade him a juicy rumor of your own

success.text: You tell him the one about the vice principal and the karaoke contest, with voices and a dance break. Dez is so delighted he pays you back three rumors and a free Bolt Cola from the checkout cooler. "You," he says, "are wasted on honesty."
success.art: A teenager acting out a dramatic story with jazz hands at a supermarket checkout lane, a bag boy in a paper hat doubled over laughing and holding out a cold bottle of cola from a glowing cooler

failure.text: Your rumor bombs. Worse, Dez already heard it, and a better version. By closing time there's a brand-new rumor going around the Thriftee-Mart about you, and somehow it involves a llama.
failure.art: A deflated teenager at a checkout lane while a bag boy in a paper hat whispers behind his hand to a giggling cashier with a teased perm, paper grocery bags stacked high between them

choices.label: Watch the wandering cart at closing time

success.text: At closing, the cart rolls out of its corral and heads for the quarry end of the lot, and you walk right beside it. It stops at a storm drain, wheels pointed down, waiting. You wheel it back and tie it to the corral with your shoelace. In the morning it's still there, and Dez looks at you like you hung the moon.
success.art: A teenager walking calmly beside a lone shopping cart rolling across a dusky supermarket parking lot toward a storm drain, long shadows stretching under tall sodium lights, a violet sunset over the foothills

failure.text: The cart turns to face you. That's all it does. It just faces you, for a long time, one wheel squeaking softly, while the parking-lot lights buzz on one by one. You walk home the long way, and you don't look back until your own porch.
