failure.art: A shopping cart sitting alone in a vast dusky parking lot turned toward a frozen teenager, a row of tall parking lot lights flickering on one after another into the distance

beats.title: The Last Bag of Full-Size Bars
beats.place: Aisle 7, Halloween candy, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: The candy aisle is a fortress of orange and black: Three Muskrateers, Reesey's Pieces, Kit-Kaboom and, at the very end, one last bag of full-size Choco-Lotta bars. Two Crystal Street moms have their hands on it and neither one is letting go. Meanwhile, from somewhere deep inside the giant candy-corn pyramid, comes a steady, happy crunching.
beats.art: A supermarket Halloween candy aisle with orange and black bags stacked to the ceiling beside a giant pyramid of candy corn, two determined moms in pastel sweatsuits tugging one bag of full-size chocolate bars between them, a few candy corns tumbling from a hole in the pyramid, a teenager stepping in with both hands raised, fluorescent light, wide shot

choices.label: Broker a peace treaty between the moms

success.text: You propose joint custody: they split the bag and team up on one haunted garage for both houses, double the scares. They shake on it like heads of state. Each one slips you a quarter, and one of them asks if you're available to babysit.
success.art: A teenager holding up a bag of chocolate bars between two moms in pastel sweatsuits shaking hands in an orange and black candy aisle, each mom pressing a coin into the teenager's free palm

failure.text: Both moms turn on you at once. They storm off in opposite directions, and you're left holding the bag, which Mr. Pettibone makes you pay for because "it's been squeezed."
failure.art: A teenager left holding a crumpled bag of chocolate bars in an orange and black candy aisle, two moms storming away in opposite directions, a manager in a clip-on tie approaching with his hand out

choices.label: Dig into the candy-corn pyramid to find the cruncher

success.text: You plunge both arms into the pyramid and haul out a raccoon in a tiny striped sweater, fat as a pillow and deeply unbothered. The whole aisle laughs. The sweater is stitched BANDIT. You carry him out to the parking lot, where a very relieved old man has been calling his name for an hour.
success.art: A teenager hauling a plump raccoon in a little striped sweater out of a collapsing pyramid of candy corn, kernels cascading everywhere, laughing shoppers crowding the bright supermarket aisle

failure.text: The pyramid collapses on you in an avalanche of candy corn. When you dig yourself out, the crunching has stopped, and every kernel within a yard of you has one neat little bite taken out of it. Whatever it was, it has very small teeth, and it got away.
failure.art: A teenager buried to the shoulders in a heap of spilled candy corn in a supermarket aisle, nibbled kernels scattered all around, a small furry striped tail disappearing under the bottom shelf

choices.label: Build a display so spectacular nobody wants to fight

success.text: You build a candy castle with turrets of Kit-Kaboom, a drawbridge of Choco-Lotta bars and a moat of Bolt Cola cans. Shoppers stop to take pictures. Mr. Pettibone doesn't know what to do with his face, so he hands you a six-cell flashlight off the endcap. "For the week," he mutters.
success.art: A teenager placing the final candy bar on a towering castle built of Halloween candy bags with a moat of soda cans, a supermarket manager staring open-mouthed, shoppers snapping instant photos in bright fluorescent light

failure.text: Your castle looks magnificent for nine whole seconds. Then a toddler pulls one bar out of the bottom row. They hear the collapse in the parking lot. Mr. Pettibone just points at the mop.
failure.art: A collapsed heap of Halloween candy bags and rolling soda cans spread across a supermarket floor, a triumphant toddler holding up a single candy bar, a teenager gripping a mop and bucket

beats.title: Price Check, Aisle Zero
beats.place: The courtesy desk, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: Thriftee-Mart has twelve aisles. The intercom keeps calling for a price check on aisle zero. It's Mr. Pettibone's voice, and Mr. Pettibone is standing right next to you holding a cantaloupe, looking ill. "I haven't touched that microphone," he says. "I'm a produce man." At the back of the store, past frozen foods, a pair of swinging doors you've never noticed is gently swaying.
beats.art: A pale supermarket manager in a clip-on tie holding a cantaloupe and staring up at a ceiling speaker at the courtesy desk, a teenager beside him, and at the far end of a long fluorescent frozen-food aisle a pair of dented swinging stockroom doors gently swaying, cold freezer light, long wide shot

choices.label: Push through the swinging doors and find aisle zero

success.text: Behind the doors is a 1959 grocery aisle, perfectly stocked and mint: tins of things they don't make anymore, a crank cash register, glass bottles of soda with the old formula. A radio plays a doo-wop song you almost know. You tip your head to the aisle like a guest, back out, and the doors settle shut, calm and satisfied.
success.art: A teenager with a flashlight standing in a perfectly stocked 1959 grocery aisle of tin cans and glass soda bottles, a brass crank cash register and a wooden tabletop radio, dust glittering in a single warm beam of light

failure.text: Behind the doors is a stockroom that goes back much farther than the building does. The fluorescent tubes buzz on ahead of you one at a time, inviting. You back out and let the doors swing shut. The intercom says, very softly, "Price check cancelled."
failure.art: A teenager backing out through swinging doors from an impossibly long stockroom of stacked cardboard boxes, fluorescent tubes flickering on one by one into the far distance

choices.label: Grab the courtesy-desk microphone and answer it

success.text: "Attention, Thriftee-Mart shoppers," you purr in your best late-night DJ voice, "aisle zero is closed for the season. Please enjoy ten percent off courage." The whole store applauds. The intercom crackles once, like a laugh, and goes back to soft-rock elevator music.
success.art: A teenager leaning into a gooseneck microphone at a supermarket courtesy desk with a sultry late-night DJ grin, shoppers in the aisles turning to applaud, a manager hiding a laugh behind a cantaloupe

failure.text: You key the mic, and your own voice comes out of the ceiling speakers a full second before you speak, saying something slightly different. The whole store hears it. Mr. Pettibone gently takes the microphone and puts it in a drawer.
failure.art: A startled teenager pulling back from a gooseneck microphone at a supermarket courtesy desk, a manager reaching to take it, shoppers frozen mid-aisle staring up at the ceiling speakers

choices.label: Dig the store blueprints out of the manager's office

success.text: The 1959 plans show thirteen aisles. Aisle zero was walled off after the grand opening because "customers reported feeling watched by the canned peaches." You and Mr. Pettibone agree to leave it be and stack pumpkins in front of the wall. He's so relieved he tips you two quarters.
success.art: A teenager and a supermarket manager unrolling yellowed architectural blueprints across a cluttered office desk, a coffee mug pinning one corner and a cantaloupe holding down another, a desk lamp glowing

failure.text: You find the blueprints, but someone has been at them first: aisle zero is circled over and over in red grease pencil. Mr. Pettibone swears he's never seen those circles. You both agree, out loud, to stop looking at blueprints for the day.
failure.art: Yellowed store blueprints spread across a desk with one narrow aisle circled again and again in red grease pencil, a teenager and a supermarket manager staring down at it under a buzzing desk lamp

beats.title: Free Samples, Aisle 5
beats.place: The demo table, aisle 5, Thriftee-Mart
beats.text: Doreen Mulcahy, in a paper hat and apron, is handing out free samples of Sunny Acres Fluff-Whip, "the dessert topping of tomorrow," on little crackers. Every shopper who tries one walks off humming the same jingle with the same calm, glassy little smile. Doreen's own smile hasn't moved in an hour. She holds out a cracker. "Free," she says. "Everybody's doing it."
beats.art: A supermarket aisle demo table, a woman in a paper hat and apron with a fixed smile holding out a tiny cracker topped with fluffy white whipped spread, tubs of topping stacked on the table, shoppers strolling away with identical calm glassy smiles, a teenager eyeing the cracker, buzzing fluorescent lights overhead, medium shot

choices.label: Eat the cracker and find out what's so great

success.text: It tastes like marshmallow, vanilla and, faintly, a sunny afternoon you've never actually had. The jingle starts up in your head, and you hum one bar before you shake it off like water from your ears. Now you know what it feels like from the inside, which means you'll know it when you hear it again.
success.art: A teenager biting a small cracker heaped with white whipped spread, eyes squeezed shut and shaking their head, a smiling woman in a paper hat at the demo table

failure.text: It's delicious. You hum the jingle all the way to the dairy case before you notice you're smiling like Doreen and can't stop. Your cheeks ache. It wears off around dinner, but for the rest of the day every grown-up who smiles at you looks like they know a secret you almost joined.
failure.art: A teenager standing in a supermarket dairy aisle with a fixed wide smile and glazed eyes, rows of milk cartons, a half-eaten cracker in hand

choices.label: Read the fine print on the tub

success.text: Ingredients: sugar, corn syrup, whipped vegetable oil and, in tiny type at the very bottom, "a proprietary sense of belonging." You show Mr. Pettibone, who reads it twice, goes pale and pulls the whole display. Doreen blinks, rubs her cheeks and asks why her face is so tired. Mr. Pettibone gives you two quarters out of pure relief.
success.art: A teenager squinting at the tiny print on a plastic dessert tub, a sweaty supermarket manager in a short-sleeved dress shirt reading over their shoulder in alarm

failure.text: The ingredients list goes on and on, wrapping around the tub and onto a second tub, and somewhere in the middle it starts listing the names of people who live on Crystal Street. You put the tub down. Doreen picks it up and sets it back exactly in its place, smiling, smiling.
failure.art: A plastic dessert tub covered in a spiraling list of tiny printed words, a teenager setting it down nervously, a smiling woman in a paper hat reaching to straighten it

choices.label: Make Doreen laugh, a real laugh

success.text: You do the worst Mr. Pettibone impression ever attempted: the sweating, the tie, "It's under warranty!" Doreen's frozen smile cracks into a real, snorting laugh, and the jingle in the aisle cuts off like a needle lifted from a record. She takes off the paper hat. "Three jobs," she says. "I just wanted one easy shift." She gives you the whole box of crackers.
success.art: A teenager doing a goofy impression with a loosened tie at a supermarket demo table, a woman in an apron doubled over laughing with her paper hat in her hand

failure.text: You do your best bit. Doreen watches politely with her perfect smile. Then every shopper in the aisle laughs at exactly the same moment, for exactly the same length, and stops. Doreen offers you the cracker again. You buy a candy bar instead and leave by the far door.
failure.art: A row of supermarket shoppers laughing in eerie unison beside a demo table, a teenager mid-joke frozen in confusion, a woman in a paper hat holding out a cracker

beats.title: The Great Pumpkin Weigh-In
beats.place: The parking lot, Thriftee-Mart, Saturday morning
beats.text: Saturday morning is Thriftee-Mart's Great Pumpkin Weigh-In, and the favorite is Mr. Albert Voss's backyard giant: a lumpy orange monster on a flatbed trailer, wider than a compact car. Every few minutes it thumps from somewhere deep inside, like something knocking to come out. Mr. Voss says it's settling. At the end of the line, a seven-year-old named Rosie Delgado holds her entry, the size of a softball, in both hands.
beats.art: A supermarket parking lot on a Saturday morning with hay bales and a big platform scale, a giant lumpy orange pumpkin wider than a compact car on a flatbed trailer with a torn green vine stub, a proud old man in suspenders beside it, a teen bag boy in a red apron and a teenager at the ramp, and at the end of the line a seven-year-old girl holding a softball-sized pumpkin in both hands, crisp autumn sun, wide shot

choices.label: Help heave the giant onto the scale

success.text: You, Dez and three stock boys roll it up the plywood ramp on the count of three. The scale reads 666 pounds, which makes the crowd gasp and then crack up. The thumping stops the moment it's weighed, like it only wanted to know. Mr. Voss pumps your hand and pays you two quarters from his overalls.
success.art: A teenager and a group of stock boys straining to roll a giant orange pumpkin up a plywood ramp onto a big platform scale, a cheering crowd in a supermarket parking lot

failure.text: Halfway up the ramp, the giant thumps hard enough to shove all five of you backward into the hay bales. It rolls back down onto the trailer and settles with a satisfied thud. Mr. Voss says it doesn't like being rushed. Your back disagrees with everyone.
failure.art: A teenager and stock boys tumbling backward into hay bales as a giant pumpkin rolls down a plywood ramp, an old man in suspenders wincing

choices.label: Look at where the vine was cut

success.text: The stem isn't cut. It's torn, and the vine stub is still green and reaching, wet with sap. Mr. Voss admits the vine crawled across his whole yard from the direction of the Heartstone roundabout in six weeks, and he had to saw it loose. You talk him into burning the vine and keeping the seeds in a jar, far from any soil. He looks relieved someone finally asked.
success.art: A teenager crouching to inspect a thick torn green vine curling from the stem of a giant pumpkin, beads of sap on the end, an old man in suspenders looking guilty

failure.text: You lean close to the stem, and the vine stub twitches and curls gently around your wrist, warm as a hand. You jerk free. The crowd is busy cheering at the scale, but by the time you're back in line there's a thin green ring on your skin that takes all weekend to fade.
failure.art: A green pumpkin tendril curling gently around a teenager's wrist beside a giant pumpkin, the teen pulling back in alarm, a parking-lot crowd cheering at a scale in the distance

choices.label: Talk up Rosie's tiny pumpkin to the judges

success.text: You get the judges to invent a brand-new category on the spot: Most Loved Pumpkin. Rosie explains that she grew hers in a coffee can and sang to it every night. She wins a ribbon and a free cupcake, and as she walks past the giant on the trailer, it stops thumping, as if it's listening to her too.
success.art: A beaming little girl holding a softball-sized pumpkin and a blue ribbon in a supermarket parking lot, a teenager and smiling judges clapping, a giant pumpkin on a trailer behind them

failure.text: The judges smile politely and move on. Rosie's lip trembles. You sit with her on a hay bale and help her name the pumpkin, which she decides is Lord Pumpkington. It isn't a ribbon. She still holds your hand until her mom comes back from the checkout.
failure.art: A small girl sitting on a hay bale in a supermarket parking lot holding a tiny pumpkin, a teenager sitting beside her, her small hand in theirs
